Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Abstract > Background
The comparative efficacy of different types of electric toothbrushes relative to each other and to manual toothbrushes remains a subject of clinical investigation. This network meta-analysis (NMA) aims to rank the efficacy of various electric toothbrush technologies for plaque and gingivitis reduction.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Abstract > Methods
A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Web of Science was conducted from inception to June 2025. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing electric (oscillating-rotating, sonic, ultrasonic, other) and manual toothbrushes were included. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment. A frequentist NMA was performed, and treatments were ranked using Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking (SUCRA) values. Consistency between direct and indirect evidence was evaluated.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Abstract > Results
Nineteen RCTs were included. In terms of plaque reduction, oscillating-rotating brushes were ranked first (SUCRA = 89.2%), followed by sonic (SUCRA = 72.4%), ultrasonic (SUCRA = 54.1%), other electric (SUCRA = 45.3%), and manual toothbrushes (SUCRA = 18.3%). A similar ranking was observed for gingivitis reduction. Subgroup analyses indicated superior benefits for orthodontic patients and children. The overall risk of bias was low, and no significant inconsistency was detected.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Abstract > Conclusion
Oscillating-rotating electric toothbrushes demonstrated the highest probability of being among the most effective interventions for reducing plaque and gingivitis among the compared technologies. This evidence suggests that they may be considered a preferred choice for improved oral hygiene in clinical practice, particularly in high-risk groups such as orthodontic patients and children.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Introduction
Dental plaque is the primary etiological factor for prevalent oral diseases such as gingivitis and caries [1–3]. Its mechanical removal through toothbrushing constitutes the cornerstone of daily oral care. Although the manual toothbrush is the most widely used tool, its efficacy is highly dependent on user technique and compliance [4–6].

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Introduction
Electric toothbrushes were developed to offer a standardized brushing action, thereby addressing the limitations associated with manual brushing techniques. Systematic reviews and pairwise meta-analyses have consistently concluded that electric toothbrushes are more effective than manual ones in terms of plaque removal (Yaacob et al., 2014; Elkerbout et al., 2020; de Jager et al., 2017) [7–9]. However, these previous analyses were limited to pairwise comparisons (e.g., electric vs. manual) and did not provide a direct, quantitative ranking among different electric technologies such as oscillating-rotating, sonic, and ultrasonic brushes. Consequently, a significant gap persists in the direct comparison and ranking of various electric toothbrush technologies. For clinicians and patients to make informed decisions, it is essential to establish a hierarchical ranking of these interventions.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Introduction
Network meta-analysis (NMA) is a robust statistical technique that facilitates the simultaneous comparison of multiple interventions by integrating both direct and indirect evidence [10]. Unlike traditional pairwise meta-analyses, NMA allows for the ranking of multiple treatment modalities within a unified framework, thereby directly addressing the aforementioned evidence gap [11]. Consequently, this systematic review and NMA aims to evaluate and rank the efficacy of various types of electric toothbrushes compared to manual toothbrushes in reducing plaque and gingivitis, thereby offering evidence-based guidance for clinical practice.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Search strategy and selection criteria
This systematic review was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251273484). A comprehensive literature search was conducted across several electronic databases, including PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov, to identify relevant studies published from the inception of these databases until June 2025. The search strategy employed a combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and free-text keywords pertaining to “electric toothbrush,” “manual toothbrush,” “plaque,” “gingivitis,” and “randomized controlled trial,” and was limited to publications in the English language. The complete search strategy, including the exact MeSH term combinations for each database, is provided in Supplementary Table S1.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Search strategy and selection criteria
Studies were included if they met the following PICOS criteria: (1) Population: Children or adults with permanent or mixed dentition. (2) Intervention: The use of an electric toothbrush, which may include oscillating-rotating, sonic, ultrasonic, or other specified types. Other electric toothbrushes refer to powered brushes that do not conform to the definitions of oscillating-rotating, sonic, or ultrasonic technologies, such as basic side-to-side motion brushes. (3) Comparator: The use of a manual toothbrush. (4) Outcomes: Changes in a validated plaque index (PI) and/or gingivitis index (GI). (5) Study Design: Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs), which encompass both parallel-group and crossover designs. The exclusion criteria for this study encompassed non-randomized studies and those lacking sufficient data for comprehensive analysis. Studies that compared various types of electric toothbrushes without a corresponding manual toothbrush control group were not automatically excluded; instead, they were included if they reported at least one outcome of interest (plaque or gingivitis index) and facilitated direct head-to-head comparisons between electric technologies (e.g., oscillating-rotating vs. sonic). This methodology enabled the network to be connected via a common comparator (manual brushing), while also integrating direct electric versus electric evidence, which is crucial for ranking interventions within the framework of network

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Data extraction and quality assessment
Two independent reviewers screened the titles, abstracts, and full texts according to pre-defined criteria. Data were extracted using a standardized form, which captured the following information: first author, publication year, country, study design, sample size, participant characteristics, intervention and control details, follow-up duration, and outcome data, including baseline and follow-up means and standard deviations for both PI and GI. In studies reporting multiple plaque or gingival indices, a single primary index was prioritized according to the following hierarchy: (1) the index designated as primary by the study authors; (2) the most frequently reported index in the field—specifically, the Rustogi Modified Navy Plaque Index (RMNPI) for plaque and the Modified Gingival Index (MGI) for gingivitis; and (3) whole-mouth scores over site-specific scores.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Data extraction and quality assessment
The risk of bias for each included study was independently assessed by two reviewers using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool 2.0 (RoB 2.0). This tool evaluates five domains: the randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported results.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Data synthesis and statistical analysis
For studies that reported multiple follow-ups, the longest follow-up period within each study was selected for analysis. Standardized Mean Differences (SMDs) with 95% Confidence Intervals (CIs) were calculated as the effect measure for continuous outcomes, specifically Plaque Index (PI) and Gingival Index (GI), due to the varying indices utilized across the studies.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Data synthesis and statistical analysis
For crossover and split-mouth trials, we extracted paired data whenever available. In instances where paired data were not reported, we approximated the standard deviation of the change using the method recommended by the Cochrane Handbook, assuming a correlation coefficient of 0.5 between period measurements. We assessed period effects and found them to be non-significant in all included crossover trials. Additionally, no carryover effects were reported by the original study authors.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Data synthesis and statistical analysis
A frequentist network meta-analysis was conducted using a random-effects model. The network geometry was visually represented, with nodes indicating interventions and edges representing direct comparisons; the thickness of the edges was scaled according to the number of studies for each comparison [12, 13]. The primary aim was to construct a connected evidence network to compare the efficacy of manual, oscillating-rotating, sonic, ultrasonic, and other electric toothbrushes in reducing plaque and gingivitis.In addition to direct comparisons against the manual toothbrush, the model quantified effects between electric technologies without direct trial evidence (e.g., sonic vs. ultrasonic) through indirect comparisons. Direct evidence between oscillating-rotating and sonic brushes was included to evaluate consistency. Both global and local inconsistency were assessed using node-splitting methods. The analysis yielded effect estimates for all pairwise comparisons and cumulative ranking probabilities, thereby addressing questions regarding the optimal technology and the differences among technologies within a unified framework.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Data synthesis and statistical analysis
The relative ranking of interventions for each outcome was estimated using the Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking (SUCRA) values, where a higher SUCRA percentage (ranging from 0% to 100%) indicates a greater likelihood of being the optimal treatment. Subgroup analyses were pre-specified and conducted based on population age (children, adults, elderly), specific conditions (orthodontic patients), and follow-up duration.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Data synthesis and statistical analysis
To address potential violations of the transitivity assumption arising from the inclusion of both short-term single-use and long-term home-use trials, we conducted a prespecified stratified NMA. Studies were categorized into two strata based on follow-up duration and study setting: (1) short-term single-use studies, involving a single brushing episode with outcomes assessed immediately post-brushing ; and (2) longer-term home-use studies, characterized by an intervention period of at least one week, reflecting habitual use and the accumulation of plaque and gingivitis over time. A separate frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis was performed for each stratum, adhering to the same analytical framework as the primary analysis. The relative rankings of interventions within each stratum were estimated using SUCRA values. To satisfy the transitivity assumption underlying valid indirect comparisons, we compared the distribution of key effect modifiers across different types of direct comparisons (manual vs. electric, and electric vs. electric). The potential modifiers examined included baseline plaque severity (mean plaque index), brushing supervision (supervised vs. unsupervised), and follow-up duration (single-use vs. ≥1 week). No substantial imbalances were observed across the comparison types, which supports the plausibility of the transitivity assumption. Detailed comparisons are reported in the "Results" section. All statistical analyses were executed using R

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Assessment of reporting biases
Publication bias was assessed using a combination of methods suitable for a network of this size. First, comparison-adjusted funnel plots were visually inspected to identify small-study effects. Second, Egger’s regression test was conducted for the most common comparison (oscillating-rotating vs. manual toothbrush). Third, sensitivity analyses were performed by excluding smaller studies (sample size < 50) to evaluate the robustness of the rankings. The assessment of publication bias adheres to the recommendations set forth by the PRISMA-NMA guidelines [Hutton et al., 2015] and the Cochrane Handbook [Sterne et al., 2011]. We acknowledge that the statistical power to detect asymmetry is diminished when the number of studies per comparison is small (k < 10), and that the possibility of unpublished null findings cannot be entirely discounted.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Assessment of reporting biases
We planned to assess publication bias through visual inspection of funnel plots and Egger’s regression test for the primary comparison between electric and manual toothbrushes. However, due to the limited number of studies available for each specific comparison in the network (k < 10), the statistical power to detect asymmetry was low. Therefore, the results of these analyses should be interpreted with caution.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Assessment of reporting biases
Due to the unavailability of study-specific variance estimates across all comparisons, conventional funnel plot analysis was not feasible. Therefore, we implemented a comprehensive multi-method assessment framework that included: (1) precision-weighted regression using sample size as a proxy for study precision [14]; (2) p-curve analysis to detect selective reporting of significant results [15]; (3) comparison of prospectively registered versus published outcomes [16]; (4) network asymmetry tests [17]; and (5) sensitivity analyses that excluded small studies and incorporated data from unpublished trials [18]. This systematic review and network meta-analysis is reported following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses for Network Meta-Analyses (PRISMA-NMA) guidelines, and the completed checklist is provided as Supplementary File Table S5.

Body > Results > Network geometry
The evidence network for comparing interventions is illustrated in Fig. 3. This network comprises five nodes: Manual, Oscillating-Rotating (O-R), Sonic (S), Ultrasonic (U), and Other Electric (OE). The manual toothbrush serves as the common comparator that links all types of electric toothbrushes. Notably, direct comparisons between oscillating-rotating and sonic brushes were available from two included trials (Van der Weijden et al., 1996; Erbe et al., 2019), which contributed directly to the network and the estimation of relative effects between these two electric technologies. These direct comparisons, along with indirect evidence from the manual node, enabled the establishment of a fully connected network. Additionally, a new supplementary figure (Figure S1) illustrates the same network geometry with node sizes scaled proportionally to the number of studies per intervention, thereby providing a clearer visualization of the evidence base. The network is well-connected, which facilitates a robust NMA. To support the transitivity assumption, we compared key effect modifiers across different comparison types. The mean baseline plaque index ranged from 0.62 to 0.65 in studies comparing oscillating-rotating to manual brushing, and from 0.60 to 0.63 in studies comparing oscillating-rotating to sonic brushing. Body > Results > Results of the network meta-analysis
The league table for plaque reduction is presented in Table 2. The network meta-analysis demonstrated that all types of electric toothbrushes significantly outperformed manual toothbrushes in reducing plaque, with Standardized Mean Differences (SMDs) ranging from moderate to large effect sizes. Among these, oscillating-rotating brushes exhibited the largest effect size in comparison to manual brushing (SMD [95% CI]: -1.24 [-1.56, -0.92]), followed by sonic brushes (SMD: -0.87 [-1.15, -0.59]).The relative ranking of interventions based on SUCRA values is illustrated in Fig. 4. For plaque reduction, the order of efficacy is as follows: Oscillating-Rotating (SUCRA = 89.2%) > Sonic (72.4%) > Ultrasonic (54.1%) > Other Electric (45.3%) > Manual (18.3%). A similar hierarchy was observed for gingivitis reduction, with oscillating-rotating brushes again ranking highest (SUCRA = 86.5%), followed by sonic (70.1%), ultrasonic (52.8%), other electric (43.9%), and manual (16.7%).

Body > Results > Results of the network meta-analysis
To facilitate clinical interpretation, we translated the standardized mean differences (SMDs) into absolute effect sizes using the most commonly reported in dices. For plaque reduction, measured by the Rustogi Modified Navy Plaque Index (RMNPI) on a scale of 0 to 1, the estimated mean difference between oscillating-rotating and manual toothbrushes was − 0.18 (95% CI: -0.24 to -0.12), indicating an approximate 18% greater reduction in plaque score. In terms of gingivitis reduction, assessed using the Modified Gingival Index (MGI) on a scale of 0 to 4, the mean difference was − 0.32 (95% CI: -0.45 to -0.19), which represents a clinically significant reduction in inflammation.Interpretive caution is warranted for the ‘other electric’ category (SUCRA = 45.3%), which was represented by only two studies (k = 2) with small sample sizes. Consequently, the SUCRA ranking for this intervention is derived from very limited evidence and should be interpreted with extreme caution. As indicated by the confidence intervals crossing zero in the longer-term stratified analysis (Supplementary Tables S3 and S4), the observed difference between ‘other electric’ and manual toothbrushes was not statistically significant. The imprecision surrounding its effect estimate is substantial.

Body > Results > Stratified analysis by study duration
To assess the robustness of the primary findings and address potential violations of the transitivity assumption, we conducted a stratified NMA that separated short - term single - use trials (n = 7) from longer - term home - use trials (n = 12). The results are summarized in Supplementary Tables S3 and S4. In the short-term single-use stratum, oscillating-rotating brushes emerged as the top-ranked intervention for plaque reduction (SUCRA = 91.5%), followed by sonic (SUCRA = 74.2%), ultrasonic (SUCRA = 52.3%), other electric (SUCRA = 44.1%), and manual brushes (SUCRA = 16.8%). The effect sizes compared to manual brushing were larger in this stratum (oscillating-rotating: SMD = -1.52, 95% CI: -1.98 to -1.06) than in the primary analysis, indicating an immediate mechanical cleaning advantage.In the longer-term home-use stratum, the ranking was similar, but the differences between technologies were narrower. Oscillating-rotating brushes retained the top position (SUCRA = 86.7%), followed by sonic (SUCRA = 70.8%), ultrasonic (SUCRA = 55.2%), other electric (SUCRA = 46.1%), and manual (SUCRA = 19.5%). The effect size compared to manual brushing was more modest in this stratum (oscillating-rotating: SMD = -0.96, 95%

size compared to manual brushing was more modest in this stratum (oscillating-rotating: SMD = -0.96, 95% CI: -1.35 to -0.57), reflecting behavioral and compliance factors over extended use. Importantly, the relative ranking of electric technologies remained consistent across both strata, thereby supporting the robustness of the primary analysis.

Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore heterogeneity (Fig. 5). The superiority of electric toothbrushes was consistent across most subgroups. Notably, the largest effect sizes were observed in orthodontic patients and children, while the effect was non-significant in the elderly subgroup. Furthermore, the results remained robust in sensitivity analyses that excluded studies with a high risk of bias.

Body > Results > Age-specific subgroup analysis for gingivitis reduction
Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore heterogeneity across different age groups, illustrated in the forest plot (Fig. 6). To further elucidate the differential effects of electric versus manual toothbrushes across the lifespan, we conducted a focused subgroup analysis stratified by age categories. This analysis specifically evaluated gingivitis reduction efficacy in distinct age groups, providing insights for age-tailored clinical recommendations.The forest plot presents the results of a subgroup analysis comparing the efficacy of electric versus manual toothbrushes in reducing gingivitis across different age groups. Overall analysis indicates that electric toothbrushes are significantly superior to manual toothbrushes in reducing gingivitis (SMD = 0.82, 95% CI [0.65, 0.98], P < 0.001), suggesting a moderate beneficial effect of electric toothbrushes.

Our comprehensive assessment did not reveal significant evidence of publication bias or small-study effects. The distribution of p-values was right-skewed (χ² = 43.0, p = 0.03), suggesting that the body of evidence possesses evidential value beyond the selectively reported significant findings. Precision-weighted regression indicated no significant association between effect size and study precision (β = 0.15, 95% CI: −0.23 to 0.53, p = 0.42). Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Main findings and interpretation
This network meta-analysis of 19 RCTs synthesizes the current best evidence to provide a direct comparative ranking of major electric toothbrush technologies. The principal finding is unequivocal: all electric toothbrushes demonstrate statistically significant superiority over manual toothbrushes in reducing both dental plaque and gingivitis, with oscillating-rotating technology consistently ranking as the most efficacious option. This hierarchy is robust, as evidenced by high SUCRA values for plaque (89.2%) and a similar order for gingivitis outcomes.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Main findings and interpretation
The biological plausibility of this ranking further strengthens our conclusions. The superior performance of oscillating-rotating brushes is mechanistically supported by their unique three-dimensional cleaning action, which involves simultaneous oscillation and rotation. This action generates high-frequency, focused shear forces that effectively disrupt and detach the supragingival biofilm matrix, particularly from concave surfaces, fissures, and the critical gingival margin area [38, 39]. In contrast, the primarily lateral, sweeping motion of sonic brushes and the microstreaming activity of ultrasonic brushes, while effective, may be less efficient at mechanically dislodging firmly adherent plaque in these challenging anatomical sites [40]. This interpretation is corroborated by several included trials that specifically noted the superior cleaning efficacy of oscillating-rotating brushes on approximating surfaces compared to other modalities [41, 42].

content:
Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Comparison with previous research and innovation
Our findings consolidate and significantly advance the existing evidence base. Previous high-quality systematic reviews and pairwise meta-analyses have definitively established that electric toothbrushes are more effective for plaque removal than manual brushes [7–9]. This study not only confirms that conclusion but also provides a crucial, novel extension: a direct, quantitative ranking among the electric subtypes themselves.This represents a substantial step forward. Prior evidence could guide clinicians in recommending “an electric toothbrush,” but it could not inform the choice between, for example, a sonic and an oscillating-rotating model when both options are available. By employing a frequentist network meta-analysis, we have integrated both direct head-to-head comparisons (e.g., oscillating-rotating vs. sonic) and indirect evidence via a common comparator (manual brushing) to generate a unified hierarchy. This methodological approach directly addresses a persistent and clinically relevant evidence gap, transforming the clinical question from “whether to use an electric brush” to “which electric brush technology to select for optimal results.”

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Clinical implications and subgroup insights
The stratified results of this analysis provide nuanced and actionable guidance for personalized preventive oral care, moving beyond a one-size-fits-all recommendation.Our findings for orthodontic patients are particularly compelling, as this subgroup demonstrated the most pronounced benefits from using oscillating-rotating electric toothbrushes. Fixed appliances significantly hinder plaque control, thus elevating the risk of gingivitis, enamel demineralization, and white spot lesions [43]. The mechanized, three-dimensional action of oscillating-rotating brushes appears uniquely effective at navigating the complex topography around brackets and archwires, disrupting plaque biofilms in areas that are exceptionally challenging to clean manually. Therefore, these devices should be strongly advocated as a cornerstone of home-care regimens for individuals undergoing fixed orthodontic therapy.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Clinical implications and subgroup insights
Transitioning to pediatric populations, the significant treatment effect underscores the role of electric toothbrushes as potential enablers. Children often lack the manual dexterity and sustained motivation required for consistently effective brushing. An oscillating-rotating electric toothbrush can serve as a ‘skill-equalizer,’ delivering a standardized cleaning action that compensates for variable technique. This may not only enhance immediate plaque control but also help instill positive long-term oral hygiene habits by making the process more efficient and potentially more engaging. Although the literature does not uniformly define established minimal clinically important differences (MCID) for these indices, the absolute differences presented (e.g., 18% greater plaque reduction) serve as clinically interpretable benchmarks that can inform practice and facilitate shared decision-making. Given the limited number of studies within each subgroup (e.g., only three trials involving orthodontic patients), the findings from these subgroups should be interpreted as generating hypotheses rather than providing definitive evidence. The effect of gingivitis reduction in adults was not statistically significant, as indicated by the confidence interval crossing the null (Fig. 6). Due to the limited sample sizes in the subgroups, formal interaction tests were not conducted; thus, the observed difference between subgroups (e.g., orthodontic patients vs. adults) are exploratory and should not be interpreted as statistically significant

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Clinical implications and subgroup insights
subgroups (e.g., orthodontic patients vs. adults) are exploratory and should not be interpreted as statistically significant without confirmatory studies. However, the attenuated effect observed in the elderly subgroup introduces a critical note of caution. This finding highlights that technological superiority does not automatically translate into effectiveness for all users. In older adults, factors such as impaired grip strength, arthritic limitations, cognitive decline, or visual deficits can compromise the ability to use any toothbrush properly. Consequently, recommending an advanced electric toothbrush must be part of a broader, individualized assessment. Success may depend on combining the tool with tailored instruction, caregiver assistance, or adaptive aids to handle the device, emphasizing that the prescription of technology must align with the user’s capacity and support system.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Strengths and limitations
The credibility of our findings is enhanced by several methodological strengths: adherence to PRISMA-NMA reporting guidelines, a comprehensive search without language restrictions, dual independent reviews at all stages, utilization of the updated Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool, and rigorous statistical methodologies, including consistency checks and sensitivity analyses.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Strengths and limitations
Several limitations warrant consideration. First, clinical heterogeneity arises from significant variations in population characteristics, which may limit the generalizability of our findings. Additionally, the use of various plaque and gingival indices across studies may have introduced further heterogeneity. Although we employed a prioritization hierarchy and calculated standardized mean differences (SMDs) to mitigate this issue, the absolute effect sizes derived from the most commonly utilized indices (RMNPI and MGI) should be regarded as approximate. Future studies should adopt a standardized core outcome set to enhance comparability.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Strengths and limitations
Second, the relative rankings of interventions are determined by Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking (SUCRA) values. It is important to understand that SUCRA values reflect the probability of a particular intervention achieving the highest rank among those being compared. However, they do not provide a direct assessment of clinical effectiveness or the absolute magnitude of benefit. Readers should interpret the ranking hierarchy within this probabilistic context.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Strengths and limitations
Third, despite employing a multi-faceted approach to assess reporting biases, we cannot entirely exclude the possibility that unpublished null findings may influence the network. We acknowledge the limited statistical power of publication bias tests within a network of this size, with k being less than 10 for most comparisons. The non-significant results of Egger’s test, along with the observed symmetry in funnel plots, should be interpreted with caution, as small-study effects may still be present but undetectable. Future updates of this network meta-analysis, supported by a larger evidence base, may enable more robust assessments of publication bias.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Strengths and limitations
Fourth, our decision to extract the longest follow-up from each study for the primary analysis, while clinically relevant for assessing sustained efficacy, may have introduced bias by homogenizing different time points across studies. This could potentially overlook significant temporal variations in treatment outcomes, such as initial learning effects or waning efficacy over time.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Strengths and limitations
As with all Network Meta-Analyses (NMAs), the validity of indirect comparisons relies heavily on the assumption of transitivity, which posits that studies comparing different interventions share sufficient similarities in their study designs and patient characteristics. We endeavored to uphold this assumption by implementing strict and uniform inclusion criteria. To address concerns regarding transitivity, we conducted a stratified analysis that distinguished between short-term single-use trials and longer-term home-use studies. However, clinical heterogeneity within each stratum, such as variations in brushing durations and levels of supervision, may still exist. Nevertheless, the consistent ranking observed across strata reinforces the robustness of our primary conclusions. Even within the longer-term stratum, follow-up durations varied from 4 weeks to 12 months, potentially introducing residual heterogeneity. The lack of a temporal trend analysis, such as meta-regression on follow-up length, represents a limitation of the current study. Future research should investigate whether treatment effects diminish or accumulate over time by employing more granular temporal models. The limited number of direct head-to-head trials comparing electric technologies, specifically oscillating-rotating versus sonic toothbrushes, constrains the precision of the estimated differences between these technologies. Only two head-to-head randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have directly compared oscillating-rotating and sonic

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Strengths and limitations
between these technologies. Only two head-to-head randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have directly compared oscillating-rotating and sonic toothbrushes. This limited direct evidence introduces uncertainty regarding the estimated differences between these two technologies, highlighting the need for future large-scale direct comparisons. To validate the observed hierarchy and assess patient-centered outcomes, including compliance and adverse events, future large-scale, long-term randomized trials that directly compare oscillating-rotating, sonic, and ultrasonic brushes are essential. Another limitation is the potential influence of industry sponsorship, as the majority of the included trials received funding from manufacturers of electric toothbrushes. Although the RoB 2.0 assessment prioritized methodological quality over funding sources, we acknowledge that sponsorship may introduce bias favoring the sponsor’s product.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Future research directions
To build upon this work, future research should: (1) Standardize outcome reporting by utilizing a core set of validated indices to enhance the clarity of meta-analyses; (2) Conduct longitudinal, real-world studies that evaluate not only efficacy but also long-term adherence, durability, and cost-effectiveness of these technologies; (3) Investigate emerging innovations, such as brushes with integrated artificial intelligence that provide feedback on brushing quality and coverage; and (4) Develop and test targeted interventions for special needs populations, including the elderly and individuals with disabilities, for whom current designs may be inadequate. Such research will be essential for evolving precise, patient-centered clinical guidelines and informing healthcare policy.

Comparative efficacy of electric toothbrush technologies in plaque and gingivitis reduction: a network meta-analysis
Body > Conclusion
This network meta-analysis synthesizes both direct and indirect comparative evidence to establish a potential efficacy hierarchy among major toothbrush technologies. The findings suggest that oscillating-rotating electric toothbrushes may represent among the most effective interventions for reducing dental plaque and gingivitis, followed by sonic, ultrasonic, other electric technologies, and, lastly, manual toothbrushes. However, direct head-to-head comparisons between electric technologies are limited, with only two trials comparing oscillating-rotating technologies to sonic technologies. Furthermore, the evidence supporting the ‘other electric’ category is particularly sparse. Consequently, this ranking should be interpreted as provisional. This study provides a comprehensive ranking of these modalities, contributing to evidence-based guidance for clinical practice and consumer choice. The pronounced benefits observed in high-risk populations, particularly orthodontic patients and children, highlight the potential value of this hierarchy. For these groups, where conventional brushing poses distinct challenges, the adoption of an oscillating-rotating electric toothbrush could be considered a useful strategy for enhancing preventive care and mitigating oral health risks. Therefore, based on the current evidence, oscillating-rotating electric toothbrushes may be preferred for optimal mechanical plaque control in daily oral hygiene, particularly in populations where manual brushing is challenging. This recommendation offers a reasonable evidence-based rationale to guide clinical decision-making and public health advice.

Abstract > Aim
To synthesize evidence on gingival diseases and conditions in children and adolescents (< 18 years) without known systemic disorder involvement, focusing on their distribution, aetiology, diagnosis, management and oral health–related quality of life (OHRQoL).

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Abstract > Materials and Methods
A systematic review was carried out following PRISMA guidelines, including PubMed Central, Scopus, EMBASE and LILACS, up to January 2025. Clinical trials and observational studies addressing gingival diseases or conditions in healthy individuals under 18 years were included.

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Abstract > Results
The search identified 33,180 studies. Title and abstract screening narrowed these to 2264, of which 433 were full‐text‐reviewed. Ultimately, 269 studies, all restricted to biofilm‐induced gingivitis, were included. Considerable heterogeneity was observed in diagnostic criteria and study quality. Dental biofilm–induced gingivitis was common (52%) and associated with poorer OHRQoL. Key determinants for gingival inflammation included socioeconomic status, oral hygiene behaviours, pubertal changes and malocclusion. Based on current evidence, effective management of gingivitis in children should combine supervised toothbrushing with a fluoridated toothpaste and school‐ or caregiver‐based oral health education. Adjunctive use of chlorhexidine may provide additional benefit in certain clinical situations.

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Abstract > Conclusion
Dental biofilm–induced gingivitis is frequent among children and adolescents and influenced by numerous determinants. Prevention and treatment should emphasise accessible, behaviour‐focused and education‐based strategies for biofilm control.

Body > Introduction
Periodontal tissues in children and adolescents exhibit anatomical and developmental features that differ markedly from those of adults. These features influence the clinical appearance of gingival inflammation and may modify disease expression during growth and tooth eruption (Bimstein and Matsson 1999).

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Introduction
Gingivitis is a reversible inflammatory reaction of gingival tissues, occurring without periodontal attachment loss, often arising from dental biofilm accumulation on the tooth surface. It results from interactions between the dental biofilm and the host immune–inflammatory reaction (Murakami et al. 2018), as well as local and systemic modifying factors and behavioural influences such as oral hygiene practices (Chapple et al. 2018). It is estimated that everybody experiences gingivitis during their lifetime (Trombelli 2025). In addition to dental biofilm–induced gingivitis, gingival diseases encompass a broad group of conditions with diverse aetiologies, including immune‐mediated, hypersensitivity, infectious, traumatic and neoplastic disorders. These conditions may be localised or may signify underlying systemic involvement, bearing in mind that the absence of evidence of underlying systemic diseases is not proof of its absence (Bell 1897). Although not caused by dental biofilm, their severity may be exacerbated by biofilm‐related inflammation (Chapple et al. 2018). Distinguishing these lesions from dental biofilm–induced gingivitis is critical for accurate diagnosis, appropriate management and timely referral when necessary.

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Determinants > Socioeconomic Variables
One cohort study found that adolescents from lower socioeconomic backgrounds had more gingival bleeding at a 2‐year follow‐up (Sfreddo et al. 2019).

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Determinants > Socioeconomic Variables
Lower education in adolescents (Knack et al. 2019), lower parental education (Amarasena and Ekanayake 2010; Koga et al. 2020; Medina‐Vega et al. 2024; Nicolau et al. 2003; Olczak‐Kowalczyk et al. 2024; Ravera et al. 2012; Simangwa et al. 2018; Tomazoni et al. 2017; Wang et al. 2024) and attending public schools (Elias‐Boneta et al. 2018; Nagarajappa et al. 2012) were positively associated with gingivitis.

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Determinants > Socioeconomic Variables
Several studies found lower bleeding scores among children of professionals (white‐collar workers) (e.g., physicians, lawyers, academics), compared to those of skilled, partly skilled and unskilled workers (blue‐collar workers) (Anagnou‐Vareltzides et al. 1983; Dummer et al. 1987; Lawal and Dosumu 2021). However, some studies found no association (Amarasena and Ekanayake 2010; Bashirian et al. 2018; Kyaw Myint et al. 2020). Low family income was positively associated with gingivitis in some studies (Cortellazzi et al. 2008; Knack et al. 2019; Koga et al. 2020), while in others it was not (Medina‐Vega et al. 2024; Nicolau et al. 2003; Tomazoni et al. 2017).

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Determinants > Age
Increasing occurrence of gingivitis is associated with increasing age (Agbaje et al. 2016; Bashirian et al. 2018; Fan et al. 2021; Jessri et al. 2013; Knack et al. 2019; Lawal and Dosumu 2021; Liu, Xu, et al. 2022; Pathivada et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2024).

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Determinants > Gender
In most studies, boys presented more frequently with gingivitis than girls (Agbaje et al. 2016; Antunes et al. 2008; Bashirian et al. 2018; Cortellazzi et al. 2008; Dummer et al. 1987; Jurgensen and Petersen 2009; Lawal and Dosumu 2021; Simangwa et al. 2018; Thwin et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2024). Three studies found no gender differences (Fan et al. 2021; Liu, Xu, et al. 2022; Wolf et al. 1996), whereas one found higher occurrence among girls (Jessri et al. 2013).

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Determinants > Immigrant Status and Ethnicity
Immigrant children and children from non‐White or minority groups had significantly more gingival inflammation, independently of other determinants (Antunes et al. 2008; Jurgensen and Petersen 2009; Knack et al. 2019; Simangwa et al. 2018; Sivakumar et al. 2016; Wang et al. 2024). In one study, the association with ethnicity was not significant (Tomazoni et al. 2017). One study found ‘lighter black‐skinned’ children presented less gingivitis than ‘White’ children (Chiapinotto et al. 2013).

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Determinants > Oral Health Behaviour
Brushing teeth at least twice daily and supervised toothbrushing were significantly associated with improved gingival health (Amarasena and Ekanayake 2010; Berenie et al. 1973; Bjarnason et al. 1997; Gao et al. 2014; Jessri et al. 2011; Kumari et al. 2021; Kyaw Myint et al. 2020; Liu, Xu, et al. 2022; Nagarajappa et al. 2012; Olczak‐Kowalczyk et al. 2024; Pourhashem et al. 2007; Sharva et al. 2014; Smadi 2017; Vadiakas et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2024; Weissenbach et al. 1995).

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Determinants > Oral Health Behaviour
A cross‐sectional study compared the modified Bass technique with vertical, roll, horizontal and mixed brushing and found that, while higher brushing frequency predicted less plaque, the modified Bass technique was associated with slightly more gingival inflammation despite similar plaque levels, possibly due to a traumatic effect of bristle activity in the gingival sulcus (Lavstedt et al. 1982). Children who seldom or never used fluoride toothpaste had significantly higher odds for developing moderate to severe gingivitis (Folayan et al. 2022). Children who reported infrequent flossing suffered from gingivitis more frequently than children who reported frequent flossing (Jessri et al. 2013; Liu, Xu, et al. 2022).

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Determinants > Oral Health Behaviour
Lack of regular annual dental check‐ups (once per year) (Fan et al. 2021; Liu, Xu, et al. 2022; Olczak‐Kowalczyk et al. 2024) or never visiting the dentist (Jessri et al. 2011; Liu, Xu, et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2024) was significantly associated with a higher occurrence of gingivitis.

content:
Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Determinants > Oral Health Knowledge and Perception of Oral Health
Lower awareness and oral health knowledge among parents and children were associated with poorer gingival health (Fan et al. 2021; Gao et al. 2014; Koga et al. 2020; Liu, Xu, et al. 2022; Ravera et al. 2012; Tomazoni et al. 2017).

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Determinants > Oral Microbiota
Changes in the composition of the sulcular microbiota related to pubertal maturation (Gusberti et al. 1990) and selected microbial profiles, that is, the relative abundance of some bacterial species (Ashley et al. 1988; Kyaw Myint et al. 2020; Mitova et al. 2019; Morinushi et al. 2000; Nadkarni et al. 2015; Pomes et al. 2000; Tankova et al. 2024; Vega‐Chin et al. 2022; Weissenbach et al. 1995), were significantly associated with gingival inflammation.

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Other Determinants
Living conditions (Liu, Xu, et al. 2022; Bashirian et al. 2018; Frencken et al. 1986; Giacaman et al. 2018; Jurgensen and Petersen 2009; Kaur et al. 2014; Narang et al. 2016; Ravera et al. 2012; Thwin et al. 2024; Tomazoni et al. 2017; Vadiakas et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2024; Koga et al. 2020; Simangwa et al. 2018; Antunes et al. 2008; Knack et al. 2019; Tomazoni et al. 2017; Nicolau et al. 2003), diet (El Tantawi et al. 2021; Folayan et al. 2021; Kyaw Myint et al. 2020; Liu, Xu, et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2024) and malocclusions (Antunes et al. 2008; Buckley 1981; Cortellazzi et al. 2008; Feldens et al. 2006; Kolawole and Folayan 2019; Kukletova et al. 2012; Liu, Xu, et al. 2022; Medina‐Vega et al. 2024; Tomazoni et al. 2017) were positively associated with gingivitis. Detailed results can be found in Appendix 3.

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Management
Eighty‐nine studies reported information on the management of gingivitis (Tables 2 and 3). Forty‐one articles were excluded because of high risk of bias.

heading_path: Oral Health Education and Supervised Toothbrushing
content:
Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Management > Oral Health Education and Supervised Toothbrushing
School‐ and home‐based oral health education primarily reduced gingival inflammation among children who already presented gingivitis, as shown by decreases in gingival bleeding or index scores (Bhardwaj et al. 2013; D'Cruz and Aradhya 2013; Leghrouz et al. 2024; Subedi et al. 2021; van Palenstein Helderman et al. 1997). Supervised brushing, real‐time coaching and instruction by trained personnel were effective therapeutic strategies (Englander 1979; Saied‐Moallemi et al. 2009; Telford and Murray 1974). Digital tools and parent‐focused programmes (Alves et al. 2018; Arafa et al. 2025; Ozoemena et al. 2022; Sarayuthpitak et al. 2022; Shirmohammadi et al. 2022) led to improvements in gingival health, while game‐based or puzzle‐based interventions showed mixed or non‐significant effects on gingival bleeding (Santhosh et al. 2024; Shirahmadi et al. 2024).

heading_path: Oral Health Education and Supervised Toothbrushing
content:
Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Management > Oral Health Education and Supervised Toothbrushing
In a study, three brushing strategies were compared: (i) habitual brushing without instruction, (ii) brushing with instruction and demonstration and (iii) differential learning in which children brushed with guided variations and challenges (Pabel et al. 2018). All groups brushed under supervision during school hours. The differential learning group showed a significantly greater reduction in papillary bleeding index (PBI) scores.

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Management > Electric Versus Manual Toothbrush
Concerning the superiority of electric versus manual toothbrushes on the reduction of gingivitis scores, the results were split, with two earlier studies finding no clinically relevant differences between the two (Owen 1972; Silverman et al. 2004) whereas two recent studies reporting that electric toothbrushes led to significant reductions in mean gingival index (GI, MGI) scores compared to manual toothbrushes (Anamika and Kumar 2024; Davidovich et al. 2024). Only one study reported using rotating‐oscillating toothbrushes, while the others did not report which technology was used, only mentioning electric toothbrushes.

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Management > Mouthwashes
Four studies reported a significant decrease in GI scores after 0.1%–0.2% chlorhexidine (CHX) use, as well as after the use of herbal mouthwashes (Bajaj and Tandon 2011; Bhattacharjee et al. 2015; Bhor et al. 2021; Fahim and Zarnigar 2024). A herbal formulation with Achyranthes aspera and Trachyspermum ammi was compared with 0.2% CHX, which showed non‐inferiority in gingival improvement (Kumar et al. 2024). Neem and mango extract mouthwashes compared to 0.2% CHX all led to significant reductions in gingival scores after 2 months, but only CHX after 3 months (Sharma et al. 2014).

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Management > Mouthwashes
Honey‐based mouthwashes and 0.2% CHX were assessed, showing significant reduction in gingival scores, although CHX outperformed honey‐based mouthwashes (Singhal et al. 2018). When 0.2% CHX mouthwash was compared with aloe vera, the former was seen to significantly reduce gingival scores (Alnouri et al. 2020) or both aloe vera and CHX showed significant reductions in gingival scores (Kamath et al. 2020). A stevioside mouthwash was compared was 0.2% CHX, sodium fluoride and a placebo. GI scores declined slightly less than CHX and sodium fluoride (Vandana et al. 2017).

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Management > Mouthwashes
CHX‐fluoride with or without strontium showed no significant differences between the groups (Spets‐Happonen et al. 1985). Magnetised water was studied for its effectiveness in reducing GI score in comparison with 0.2% CHX, with one study finding CHX more effective (Nagpal et al. 2020) and another one finding no significant difference between the two (Nezam et al. 2022).

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Management > Dental Flossing
In a 4‐week school‐based RCT, adding supervised flossing to daily toothbrushing did not improve gingivitis or plaque outcomes compared with brushing alone (Rich et al. 1989).

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Results > Management > Professional Tooth Cleaning
Professional tooth cleaning every 2 weeks for a year showed significant reductions in gingival scores in the intervention group compared to controls (Poulsen et al. 1976). Dental biofilm–induced gingivitis is very common among individuals under 18. However, owing to considerable heterogeneity in the methods used, comparisons of different occurrence estimates across study groups are not possible.

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Discussion > Occurrence and Determinants
This review highlights that gingivitis in children is influenced by sociodemographic, behavioural and biological determinants. Socioeconomic disadvantage—reflected by lower income, lower parental education, parental occupation, school type, ethnicity and immigration status—was positively associated with gingival inflammation (Antunes et al. 2008; Cortellazzi et al. 2008; Koga et al. 2020; Lawal and Dosumu 2021; Liu, Xu, et al. 2022; Medina‐Vega et al. 2024; Simangwa et al. 2018; Sivakumar et al. 2016; Tomazoni et al. 2017). Behavioural factors, such as toothbrushing with a fluoride‐containing paste twice daily, supervised brushing and regular dental visits, were positively associated with better gingival health (Gao et al. 2014; Jessri et al. 2013; Olczak‐Kowalczyk et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2024). In contrast, low oral health knowledge, poor hygiene routines and inadequate dental care access mediated the effects of low socioeconomic status (Koga et al. 2020). These findings emphasise the need for preventive strategies that target both individual behaviours and caregiver involvement through education and support. Health beliefs and self‐efficacy seem to play a role, often shaped by socioeconomic and cultural backgrounds. This interplay of direct and indirect effects highlights the complexity behind sociodemographic

socioeconomic and cultural backgrounds. This interplay of direct and indirect effects highlights the complexity behind sociodemographic determinants: exerting influence through multiple mechanisms such as hygiene practices, healthcare utilisation and psychosocial environment.

Studies in this review suggest that the occurrence of gingivitis increases with age during childhood and early adolescence (Agbaje et al. 2016; Bashirian et al. 2018; Fan et al. 2021; Jessri et al. 2013; Knack et al. 2019; Lawal and Dosumu 2021; Liu, Wong, et al. 2022; Pathivada et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2024). One reason for this could be changes in the oral microflora related to puberty (Gusberti et al. 1990) and to hormonal changes during puberty, particularly elevated levels of sex steroid hormones, which modulate the host immune–inflammatory response and result in an exaggerated gingival reaction to dental plaque (Murakami et al. 2018). Another explanation can be behavioural changes related to adolescence. Boys experience gingivitis more frequently than girls, maybe due to differences in oral health behaviours (Furuta et al. 2011).

Numerous studies have found that school‐ and caregiver‐based oral health education can reduce gingival inflammation and improve oral hygiene behaviours. School‐based programmes, particularly those incorporating interactive elements like real‐time plaque disclosure (Telford and Murray 1974) or supervised brushing (Englander 1979; Pabel et al. 2018), can improve gingival health. This is consistent with Kim and Kim's meta‐analysis, which found that educational interventions yielded substantial improvement of plaque and gingival indices (Kim and Kim 2024). Several studies highlight that the effectiveness of health education is influenced not only by its content but also by its delivery and surrounding social context (D'Cruz and Aradhya 2013; Saied‐Moallemi et al. 2009). Furthermore, maternal education programmes, continuing from birth through early childhood, have shown significant improvements in children's gingival health, underscoring the benefits of engaging caregivers over time (Alves et al. 2018).

Studies reporting an association between self‐reported dental flossing and lower gingivitis frequency relied on questionnaire data, with the consequent risk of reporting bias (Jessri et al. 2013; Liu, Xu, et al. 2022). Flossing may function as a proxy indicator for overall oral health awareness or higher socioeconomic status, and children who report flossing are also likely to brush more effectively or more frequently. Rich et al. (1989) evaluated flossing under controlled conditions, concluding that toothbrushing alone achieved clinical results comparable to combined toothbrushing and flossing. Evidence suggests that flossing does not significantly reduce gingivitis in children, whereas supervised toothbrushing and regular use of fluoridated toothpaste improve gingival health. Despite professional tooth cleaning every second week or once a month resulted in some improvement of gingival health in children, these interventions were unrealistic and not commensurate with the occurrence of gingivitis (Poulsen et al. 1976; Zickert et al. 1982).

Although honey‐based mouthwashes showed gingival health benefits, their sugar content raises concerns about caries risk (Singhal et al. 2018).

When different components of OHRQoL were considered, significant associations with impacts on relaxing, smiling and social contact were reported (Krisdapong, Prasertsom, Rattanarangsima, and Sheiham 2012). These associations can be attributed to both the subjective nature of the concept and the effect of patient‐related confounding factors. However, it should be noted that they were only evident in younger children, which might indicate that as children get older, they tend to focus on things related to their appearance rather than their oral health. Previous studies have also reported an impact on an eating component (Berhan Nordin et al. 2019; Zahra et al. 2024), related to dental pain caused by bleeding gingiva.

Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis in Children and Adolescents Without Known Systemic Involvement: A Systematic Review
Body > Conclusions
From this review, we found that gingivitis among children and adolescents without known systemic disorder involvement was common and influenced by a complex interplay of biological, behavioural and sociodemographic determinants. Socioeconomic disadvantage, inadequate oral hygiene practices, limited oral health knowledge, pubertal changes and malocclusions contribute to gingival inflammation. Effective prevention and management strategies should be based on interventions early in life, focusing on education and behavioural changes, particularly those delivered through schools and caregivers. Supervised toothbrushing remains the cornerstone of gingivitis control, with selective adjunctive use of antimicrobial mouth washes showing additional benefit.

A structured literature search was conducted for randomised or non‐randomised controlled trials (RCTs and CTs) assessing gingival inflammation at patient level within 2–6 weeks after treatment in adults with gingivitis.

Clinical Efficacy of Interventions Based on Professional Mechanical Plaque Removal in the Treatment of Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
Abstract > Results
Heterogeneous evidence shows with low certainty that PMPR has no efficacy in patients continuing with ineffective self‐performed oral hygiene regimens but enhances OHI outcomes (FQ1; three RCTs, one CT). Split‐mouth RCTs consistently indicated with very low certainty that ultrasonic scaling (US) plus air polishing is as effective but less time consuming than US plus polishing with rubber cup and prophylaxis paste. Furthermore, diode laser shows no adjunctive benefit (FQ2; five RCTs). Although some professionally administered local adjuncts have shown positive outcomes in patients receiving PMPR, their broader clinical application is limited due to unresolved clinical issues and uncertain cost effectiveness (FQ3; two RCTs).

Clinical Efficacy of Interventions Based on Professional Mechanical Plaque Removal in the Treatment of Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
Abstract > Conclusions
OHI should be the first‐line treatment for dental biofilm–induced gingivitis. Combination of PMPR and OHI provides an adjunctive benefit over OHI alone. Air polishing may be combined with US to reduce the time for PMPR administration.

Clinical Efficacy of Interventions Based on Professional Mechanical Plaque Removal in the Treatment of Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
Body > Introduction
Dental biofilm–induced gingivitis is acknowledged by the Classification of Periodontal Diseases and Conditions (Caton et al. 2018; Trombelli 2025) as a patient‐related disease entity characterised by an extent of gingival inflammation beyond a specific threshold (i.e., 10% bleeding on probing [BOP]) occurring on an intact or reduced periodontium in the absence of a history of periodontitis (Trombelli et al. 2018; Chapple et al. 2018). Reversion to a periodontally healthy condition (full‐mouth BOP score < 10%) currently represents the main treatment endpoint of gingivitis (Trombelli et al. 2018, Chapple et al. 2018). The rationale for gingivitis treatment comes from the impact that gingivitis has on patient perceptions of bleeding gums and from the oral health–related quality of life, especially when the disease is present in a generalised form (Krisdapong et al. 2012; Tomazoni et al. 2014; Kaewkamnerdpong et al. 2023; Al‐Bitar et al. 2024; Dikilitaş et al. 2024; Pupovac et al. 2024; Ripardo et al. 2025). However, and more importantly, gingivitis treatment is considered as the main strategy for the primary prevention of periodontitis (Chapple et al. 2015), gingivitis being regarded as the necessary precursor

Clinical Efficacy of Interventions Based on Professional Mechanical Plaque Removal in the Treatment of Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
Body > Introduction
the primary prevention of periodontitis (Chapple et al. 2015), gingivitis being regarded as the necessary precursor of periodontitis (Kinane and Attström 2005).

Clinical Efficacy of Interventions Based on Professional Mechanical Plaque Removal in the Treatment of Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
Body > Introduction
Along with the control of patient and local factors modulating the severity of the gingival inflammatory response to the dental plaque biofilm (Tatakis and Trombelli 2004; Trombelli et al. 2004, 2005, 2006; Trombelli and Farina 2013), mechanical plaque biofilm disruption and removal is the primary, essential component of gingivitis treatment, self‐administered by the patient and/or performed by an oral health professional (referred to as professional mechanical plaque removal [PMPR]). For the former, clear recommendations for oral hygiene instructions (OHIs) are currently available, consisting of behaviours including toothbrushing twice per day for at least 2 min with a fluoride toothpaste, interdental cleaning (mainly flossing in most gingivitis cases, due to the integrity of the interdental tissues, but otherwise interdental brushes, should space permit) once daily and, in some cases, implementing oral hygiene with agents for chemical plaque control (Needleman et al. 2015; Chapple et al. 2015). In this respect, two systematic reviews have recently shown that self‐performed mechanical oral hygiene, eventually implemented with chemical agents, may be effective in controlling gingivitis (Suvan et al. 2025; Figuero et al. 2025). Although it has been shown that OHI may be effective in controlling gingivitis irrespective of the additional use of PMPR (Hugoson et al. 2007),

Clinical Efficacy of Interventions Based on Professional Mechanical Plaque Removal in the Treatment of Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
Body > Introduction
be effective in controlling gingivitis irrespective of the additional use of PMPR (Hugoson et al. 2007), it can be speculated that in specific conditions OHI alone may be insufficient to restore gingival health, thus supporting the administration of PMPR in addition to OHI. In this respect, a single session of PMPR following OHI may successfully restore gingival health and improve self‐efficacy scores (Ying et al. 2025).

Clinical Efficacy of Interventions Based on Professional Mechanical Plaque Removal in the Treatment of Dental Biofilm–Induced Gingivitis: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
Body > Introduction
To date, there is a lack of clarity on when and how to administer PMPR to optimise the outcomes of gingivitis treatment. This consideration comes from the observation that a fraction of patients may not shift to a gingivally/periodontally healthy condition, with treatment success rates being partly associated with the baseline extent of gingivitis (Ying et al. 2025). Also, the scientific evidence on PMPR modalities in the treatment of gingivitis has never been comprehensively reviewed with a systematic approach to evaluate whether some PMPR interventions (when administered once) are superior to others in restoring periodontal health while potentially reducing the time required to undertake the procedure. Therefore, the present systematic review was performed to evaluate the efficacy of protocols based on PMPR for the treatment of naturally occurring dental biofilm–induced gingivitis, with emphasis on their rationale, modality (i.e., technique and/or technology) and implementation with the professional administration of adjuncts.

Intervention (for FQ1 and FQ2): Clinical procedures incorporating PMPR, where PMPR is defined as the professional, non‐surgical removal of dental plaque and calcified deposits, as performed using technologies with a prevalently mechanical, disrupting effect on the dental biofilm (e.g., sonic/ultrasonic/manual instrumentation; air‐abrasive devices) in single (full‐mouth) or multiple (partial‐mouth) sessions. The intervention may also incorporate risk‐factor control, either performed (e.g., elimination of plaque‐retentive local factors) or suggested (e.g., behavioural change) by the oral health professional; any measure to improve self‐performed plaque control (e.g., OHI, provision of devices) either prior to PMPR or within the same appointment; (for FQ3): Clinical procedures incorporating PMPR and adjunctive therapies administered

PMPR or within the same appointment; (for FQ3): Clinical procedures incorporating PMPR and adjunctive therapies administered locally by an oral health professional in the attempt to enhance PMPR effects through debris removal (e.g., water irrigation), an alteration of biofilm structure (e.g., desiccants) or an antimicrobial effect (e.g., chlorhexidine, photodynamic therapy).
Comparison (for FQ1): No treatment, that is, continuation of routine oral hygiene procedures (if PMPR was administered without OHI in the Intervention) or OHI alone (if PMPR was administered with OHI in the Intervention); (for FQ2): Any of the aforementioned Interventions; (for FQ3): Same as intervention, but without professional administration of adjunct/s.
Outcome measures: Although primary interest was given to the proportion of patients reverting from gingivitis (as defined by Chapple et al. 2018; Trombelli et al. 2018) to periodontal health (Chapple et al. 2018, Trombelli et al. 2018), any clinical measure of gingival inflammation expressed at the patient level (e.g., BOP score, gingival index) as either a post‐treatment change or a value at the follow‐up visit was considered among the primary

Body > Materials and Methods > Study Selection Criteria
either a post‐treatment change or a value at the follow‐up visit was considered among the primary outcomes. For studies reporting data on at least one primary outcome measure, supragingival plaque scores and treatment invasiveness were also considered as secondary outcome measures. For the latter, a broad definition was used, including intra‐ and post‐operative morbidity, complications, incidence of adverse events/harms either local or systemic (in case of adjuncts), chair time for treatment administration, costs related to the procedure and patient‐reported outcomes (Farina et al. 2023). Studies that assessed outcomes only after repeated administrations of the intervention at regular intervals were included but used only for data following the first administration; if this was not possible, they were excluded.
Timing: Studies including the assessment of a primary outcome between 2 and 6 weeks following the completion of the administration of the Intervention.
Study design: Prospective randomised controlled trials (RCTs) or controlled trials (CTs) with a split‐mouth or parallel‐arm design. Only studies with a per protocol population of at least five subjects per investigated treatment were considered.

Body > Materials and Methods > Literature Search > Electronic and Hand Searches
According to the strategy reported in Appendix S1, Medline, Elsevier Scopus and Embase databases were searched for relevant literature from inception up until 2 May 2025. A separate search of the Cochrane Oral Health Group Specialty Trials' Register was conducted, and the reference lists of relevant systematic reviews were screened for the presence of eligible studies. Grey literature was retrieved through the Proquest database. The Journal of Clinical Periodontology, the Journal of Periodontology, the Journal of Periodontal Research and the Journal of Dental Research—Clinical and Translational Research were hand‐searched. The reference lists of the selected publications were screened for the presence of eligible studies. No language restrictions were applied. Titles and abstracts from the electronic searches were managed using Zotero (v7.0.7; Corporation for Digital Scholarships).

The same reviewers selected full manuscripts for studies meeting the inclusion criteria. After identifying the studies to be included, the authors resolved disagreements by discussion. If consensus was not reached, disagreements were resolved by discussion with a third author (P.M.P.).

Body > Materials and Methods > Literature Search > Assessment of Reporting Quality and Risk of Bias in Individual Studies
For the included RCTs, a methodological quality assessment was performed according to the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (ROB 2.0) for randomised trials (Sterne et al. 2019). Five main domains for risk of bias were assessed: randomisation process, deviations from the intended interventions, missing outcomes data, measurement of the outcomes and selection of the reported results. A risk of bias judgement (among ‘low risk of bias’, ‘some concerns’, or ‘high risk of bias’) was assigned to each domain (depending on the descriptions given for each field) or to the entire study.

For the included CTs, a methodological quality assessment was performed according to the Cochrane risk of bias tool (ROBINS‐I) in non‐randomised studies of intervention (Sterne et al. 2016). The risk of bias was assessed for seven main domains: bias due to confounding, selection bias, classification of interventions, deviations from the intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of outcomes and selection of reported results. A risk of bias judgement (among ‘low’, ‘moderate’ or ‘serious’ risk of bias) was assigned for each domain and for the overall risk of bias of each included CT.

Body > Materials and Methods > Literature Search > Assessment of Reporting Quality and Risk of Bias in Individual Studies > Certainty Assessments
The quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations were evaluated by using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) (Guyatt et al. 2013; Meader et al. 2014). For each meta‐analysis, the certainty of the evidence was evaluated based on the inconsistency of results, indirectness of the evidence, imprecision and other considerations, which include publication bias, the effect size (ES), plausible confounding factors and the presence of dose–response effects. Inconsistency refers to unexplained heterogeneity in the results, potentially due to the differences in population, interventions, controls and outcomes among the contributing studies. The indirectness of evidence refers to the differences in population, intervention, comparison and outcomes of the contributing studies, compared to the review question. Imprecision refers to reduced certainty about the effect estimates due to wide confidence intervals or small sample sizes.
