The field of oral health treatment is witnessing the emergence of next-generation polyherbal and multi component nutraceutical combinations as a promising new therapeutic option. Unlike their conventional counterparts, next-generation probiotics/herbal formulations are designed to deliver targeted therapeutic benefits through microbiome modification, performing better than conventional probiotics and providing new treatment options. These advanced formulations differ from traditional probiotics by utilizing more refined biological mechanisms and being specifically created to manage particular health conditions through precise intervention at critical microbial pathways (Jan et al., 2024). Scientists Varoni and Iriti (2016) have proposed the term ‘odontonutraceuticals’ to describe plant chemicals that can help prevent and treat oral diseases. When herbal products are combined in formulations together, they show powerful antimicrobial effects that kill harmful bacteria, reduce inflammation in gum tissues and provide antioxidant protection to prevent tissue damage. These beneficial effects come from a complex mixture of plant compounds, including flavonoids, terpenoids, alkaloids, and phenolic substances that work together (Anwar et al., 2025)

Body > Conclusion
Gingivitis is one of the most widespread and common oral diseases worldwide. The modulation of the oral microflora and the development of antimicrobial resistance due to the chemicals and antibiotics used for the management of gingivitis have demonstrated that herbal and traditional medicine are a safer and effective approach for treating gingivitis. Phytochemicals from medicinal plants such as green tea, pomegranate, neem, aloe vera, and sage exhibit strong antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activities, and are comparable to conventional agents like chlorhexidine with fewer adverse effects. But the clinical translation of these traditional medicines faces several challenges. Some of the major challenges are lack of formulation standardization, inconsistent dosing strategies, variability in bioactive compound concentrations, and significant inter-individual differences in oral microbiome composition. In conclusion, the advancement of science and solving the current lacunae and drawbacks in the future can lead to odontonutraceuticals and advanced polyherbal formulations for the treatment and management of gingivitis.

Noninvasive Imaging Techniques as Modern Diagnostic Tools in Desquamative Gingivitis: Focus on RCM, OCT, and LC‐OCT
Abstract > Background
Desquamative gingivitis is a clinical condition characterized by erythema, blisters, and erosions within the gingiva. It may be a manifestation of oral lichen planus or autoimmune bullous diseases, such as pemphigus vulgaris and mucous membrane pemphigoid. The identification of the cause of desquamative gingivitis typically involves the analysis of clinical manifestations, histopathology, and immunopathology evaluation. This article reviews available data on the application of noninvasive imaging techniques (reflectance confocal microscopy, optical coherence tomography, and line‐field confocal optical coherence tomography) in identifying the cause of desquamative gingivitis.

Abstract > Materials and Methods
The review of the literature for desquamative gingivitis was performed by searching the PubMed, Scopus, and Wiley databases up to January 2025.

Abstract > Results
This study aimed to evaluate the applicability of noninvasive imaging techniques, including RCM, OCT, and LC‐OCT, in the differential diagnosis of desquamative gingivitis. Findings suggest these modalities offer characteristic diagnostic patterns across underlying diseases.

Abstract > Results
In oral lichen planus, RCM typically shows disrupted connective tissue papillae, obscured basement membranes, and inflammatory cell infiltrates. In pemphigus vulgaris, the key findings are acantholytic keratinocytes and intraepithelial clefts, while mucous membrane pemphigoid displays subepithelial clefts and signs of hemorrhage.

Noninvasive Imaging Techniques as Modern Diagnostic Tools in Desquamative Gingivitis: Focus on RCM, OCT, and LC‐OCT
Abstract > Results
OCT findings in desquamative gingivitis associated with oral lichen planus include maintained epithelial thickness in the erosive forms and multilocular blisters in the bullous variants of the disease. In pemphigus vulgaris, OCT reveals intraepithelial clefts and thinning of the epithelium, while mucous membrane pemphigoid is marked by subepithelial blister formation and fluid accumulation.

Abstract > Conclusion
New noninvasive imaging techniques, such as reflectance confocal microscopy and optical coherence tomography, may support clinical decision‐making, improve biopsy targeting, and enhance long‐term monitoring of desquamative gingivitis.

Body > Introduction
Desquamative gingivitis is a clinical symptom characterized by erythema, desquamation, erosions, and blistering of the gingival epithelium [1]. Several diseases may present with desquamative gingivitis. The clinical criteria for diagnosing desquamative gingivitis were first established by Nisengard in 1995. These criteria included the presence of erythema not associated with plaque and desquamation of the gingiva, along with additional oral or extraoral lesions and sensations of a sore mouth, primarily triggered by spicy foods [2].

Body > Introduction
The most common causes include oral lichen planus (75%), mucous membrane pemphigoid (9%), and pemphigus vulgaris (4%) [3]. Other causes include other autoimmune blistering diseases (paraneoplastic pemphigus, epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, linear IgA bullous disease, bullous pemphigoid, dermatitis herpetiformis), connective tissue disorders (systemic lupus erythematosus, dermatomyositis, polymyositis, mixed connective tissue disease), erythema multiforme, and toxic epidermal necrolysis. Conditions similar to desquamative gingivitis that can also exacerbate and overlap with other causes of the gingival condition include infections (chronic candidiasis, histoplasmosis, SARS‐CoV‐2) and allergic contact dermatitis [4, 5, 6]. The most common contact allergens are sodium lauryl sulfate and cinnamaldehyde, which are found in toothpastes and mouthwashes. [4, 7, 8]. Plaque accumulation also leads to an exacerbation of desquamative gingivitis [9].

Noninvasive Imaging Techniques as Modern Diagnostic Tools in Desquamative Gingivitis: Focus on RCM, OCT, and LC‐OCT
Body > Introduction
Recent studies have emphasized the complex interplay between local periodontal inflammation and systemic health, providing a broader context for understanding desquamative gingivitis, particularly in patients with coexisting periodontitis or peri‐implant diseases. Bibliometric analyses have highlighted a growing body of evidence linking periodontitis with systemic conditions such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and autoimmune disorders, all of which may modulate gingival immune responses and exacerbate local tissue damage [10]. Moreover, successful periodontal treatment—particularly when accompanied by effective biofilm control—has been shown not only to reduce local inflammation but also to positively influence systemic inflammatory markers. In peri‐implant mucositis, for instance, nonsurgical mechanical debridement augmented with chlorhexidine protocols significantly reduced bleeding on probing and bacterial loads of key pathogens such as Porphyromonas gingivalis and Tannerella forsythia [11]. These findings are clinically relevant to desquamative gingivitis, where plaque‐induced inflammation may overlap with or mimic mucocutaneous autoimmune processes.

Noninvasive Imaging Techniques as Modern Diagnostic Tools in Desquamative Gingivitis: Focus on RCM, OCT, and LC‐OCT
Body > Introduction
The diagnostic approach for desquamative gingivitis involves a combination of clinical presentation, extraoral involvement, immunopathological tests, and histopathological examinations [9, 12]. Performing biopsies on gingival tissue affected by desquamative gingivitis is particularly challenging due to the fragility and thinness of the tissues [12]. In this aspect, a real‐time, in vivo assessment of the gingiva could offer significant advantages. It would enhance the diagnostic accuracy by identifying the optimal biopsy site and enabling long‐term, noninvasive monitoring of patients with confirmed desquamative gingivitis [13]. Emerging optical imaging technologies, such as reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM) and optical coherence tomography (OCT), provide cross‐sectional images of tissue in a noninvasive way, providing high‐resolution microscopic images of biological tissues [14, 15]

Noninvasive Imaging Techniques as Modern Diagnostic Tools in Desquamative Gingivitis: Focus on RCM, OCT, and LC‐OCT
Body > Introduction
RCM offers detailed horizontal plane visualization of tissues at cellular‐level resolution, specifically 0.5–1.0 µm horizontally and 4–5 µm axially. The system utilizes a diode laser as a source of monochromatic and coherent light, which penetrates the tissue to illuminate a small internal point. The image contrast in RCM is based on variations in the tissue's reflectivity, which depends on its chemical and molecular composition. These differences in the refractive index result in only a portion of the light being reflected, with structures possessing a higher refractive index appearing brighter in the RCM images [14].

Noninvasive Imaging Techniques as Modern Diagnostic Tools in Desquamative Gingivitis: Focus on RCM, OCT, and LC‐OCT
Body > Introduction
OCT is a technique that produces optical cross‐sectional images by utilizing low‐coherence interferometry to measure both the echo time delay and the intensity of light backscattered from the surface under examination. When a light beam is directed at the surface, different structural elements reflect the light in distinct ways, generating interference patterns that are subsequently captured by a sensor. The penetration depth reaches up to 2 mm, enabling the visualization of the epidermis, dermis, skin appendages, and blood vessels. The OCT has a horizontal resolution of 7.5 µm and an axial resolution of 5 µm, with the scan covering a field of view of 6 × 6 mm. [15, 16].

Body > Introduction
Line‐field confocal optical coherence tomography (LC‐OCT) has been designed to merge the high horizontal resolution of RCM (1 µm) with the deep penetration of OCT (500 µm) [17].

This literature review examines the underlying causes of desquamative gingivitis, including oral lichen planus, mucous membrane pemphigoid, and pemphigus vulgaris. The distribution of mucosal involvement is explored, along with emerging diagnostic techniques, such as RCM and OCT, applied to the oral cavity in relation to these conditions. Emerging diagnostic tools may hold dual value—not only for differentiating diagnoses but also for tracking therapeutic outcomes in patients at the interface of oral and systemic pathology.

A review of the literature for desquamative gingivitis was performed by searching the PubMed, Scopus and Wiley databases up to January 2025 The following search terms were used: (“oral lichen planus,” “autoimmune bullous diseases,” “autoimmune blistering diseases,” “pemphigus vulgaris,” “mucous membrane pemphigoid,”) in combination with(“desquamative gingivitis,” “mucosal involvement,” “gingiva,” “reflectance confocal microscopy,” “optical coherence tomography,” “line‐field confocal optical coherence tomography,” “review”). The reference lists of the resulting contributions were also searched for additional relevant publications. The inclusion criteria were (1) studies addressing noninvasive imaging techniques (RCM, OCT, or LC‐OCT) in the diagnosis of desquamative gingivitis; (2) studies focusing on oral lichen planus, mucous membrane pemphigoid, or pemphigus vulgaris; and (3) English‐language publications. The exclusion criteria were (1) studies focusing exclusively on therapeutic interventions; (2) animal studies; and (3) opinion articles, editorials, conference abstracts, and commentaries.

Body > Introduction
Therefore, this review aims to synthesize current evidence on the diagnostic role of RCM, OCT, and LC‐OCT in distinguishing the underlying causes of desquamative gingivitis, particularly focusing on their applicability in differentiating oral lichen planus, mucous membrane pemphigoid, and pemphigus vulgaris.

Body > Discussion
Our literature review identified consistent, disease‐specific imaging patterns across the three major etiologies of desquamative gingivitis—oral lichen planus, mucous membrane pemphigoid, and pemphigus vulgaris—supporting the clinical utility of RCM, OCT, and LC‐OCT in differential diagnosis. The following sections summarize the findings for each condition individually.

Emerging evidence highlights the significant role of oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of periodontitis, suggesting that elevated levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) contribute to both local tissue breakdown and systemic inflammatory burden [10, 11]. In patients with desquamative gingivitis coexisting with periodontitis, oxidative stress may act as a common pathogenic mechanism, amplifying epithelial damage and modulating immune responses. Antioxidant imbalance may also influence the severity of gingival lesions, particularly in autoimmune‐related presentations [10, 11]. Future studies should explore whether targeted antioxidant therapy could serve as an adjunct in managing desquamative manifestations associated with periodontal inflammation.

Body > Oral Lichen Planus
Lichen planus is a chronic T cell‐mediated inflammatory disease of unknown etiology that causes tissue destruction through apoptosis of basal keratinocytes by Fas expression [18]. There are various clinical classifications of oral lichen planus. The first is based on six clinical types: reticular, erosive, atrophic, plaque, papular, and bullous. This classification was introduced by López‐Jornet and Bermejo‐Fenoll in 2005, categorizing oral lichen planus into these distinct forms, which may appear individually or in combination [19]. The second classification is a simplified approach, grouping oral lichen planus into three main categories: hyperkeratotic/reticular, erythematous/erosive/atrophic, and ulcerative. This version, highlighted by Hampel and Reichart, is easier to distinguish in clinical practice [20].

Body > Oral Lichen Planus
Patients with reticular lesions are often asymptomatic, but atrophic (erythematous) or erosive (ulcerative) oral lichen planus is associated with pain and burning sensation [21]. Oral lichen planus is typically localized on the buccal mucosa, gingiva, and tongue in a symmetric and bilateral distribution [22]. Gingival involvement is common and, in about 10% of cases, desquamative gingivitis is the only manifestation of oral lichen planus. The occurrence of desquamative gingivitis among patients with oral lichen planus varies between 10% and 25%, depending on the study [3, 22, 23, 24].

Body > Oral Lichen Planus
The typical clinical picture is chronic gingivitis surrounded at the periphery by Wickham's striae [20] (Figure 1). The risk of malignant transformation in oral lichen planus varies widely, with reported rates ranging from 0.3% to 14.3%, often averaging around 1% over follow‐up periods of 5–10 years. Erosive and atrophic forms are particularly at risk, as noted by Agha‐Hosseini et al., while Gandolfo et al. reported transformation rates between 0.5% and 2%, emphasizing these subtypes [25, 26]. Lodi et al. confirmed these findings, highlighting the importance of monitoring high‐risk subtypes [27].

Body > Oral Lichen Planus
Oral lichen planus has characteristic changes on histology, including hyperparakeratosis, hyperorthokeratosis, or a mix of both, with cytoid (Civatte) bodies, basal cell hydropic degeneration, and a predominantly lymphocytic band‐like infiltrate in the lamina propria [28]. This inflammatory pattern, known as interface mucositis, is also observed in oral lesions of lupus erythematosus and other oral lichenoid conditions [29]. Other notable features include saw‐tooth rete ridges, atrophy, acanthosis, eosinophilic deposits at the epithelium‐connective tissue junction, and ulceration. In contrast to skin lesions, oral lesions show less frequent saw‐tooth rete ridges and more frequent atrophy [30]. Regular follow‐up for oral lichen planus patients includes biopsies if progressive development with suspicious features is observed. If the lesions change their clinical appearance, a biopsy should be immediately considered [25].

RCM and OCT may represent promising noninvasive diagnostic tools and support tissue biopsy with increased accuracy in mucous membrane disorders. Alessi et al. compare findings in RCM in cases of desquamative gingivitis with histopathology to establish diagnostic criteria for this noninvasive technique. The authors use the term dermis for lamina propria. In our article, we will substitute dermis and dermal–epidermal junction for lamina propria in the quoted excerpts [1].

Body > Oral Lichen Planus
RCM has proven valuable in diagnosing and monitoring oral lichen planus. Alessi et al. [1] identified abnormal cornified and granular layers in desquamative gingivitis associated with oral lichen planus, appearing as intensely bright regions in the superficial epithelium. The spinous layer exhibited moderately bright spaces between keratinocytes, linked to inflammatory cell infiltration and a honeycomb‐like arrangement. Necrotic keratinocytes, lacking visible nuclei, appeared as isolated bright, polygonal structures, typically larger than surrounding cells. The lamina propria was challenging to discern; basal keratinocytes formed blurred, ring‐like structures without distinct edges. Sheets of bright, small inflammatory cells and melanophages—bright, reflective, plump, oval to star‐shaped cells—were present within the inflammatory infiltrate. Horizontally oriented, dilated blood vessels were also observed in the lamina propria. Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, irregular acanthosis, spongiosis, extensive erosive areas, apoptotic keratinocytes, and an inflammatory infiltrate with melanophages in the lamina propria.

Body > Oral Lichen Planus
Contaldo et al. further emphasized the significance of RCM in evaluating oral lichen planus, especially in the gingiva, where they observed a pronounced honeycomb pattern. Significant spongiosis and epithelial inflammatory cell infiltrates surrounded the connective tissue papillae, with horizontally oriented, dilated blood vessels identifiable within the connective tissue papillae. The reticular‐plaque pattern of oral lichen planus involving mucous membranes displayed all classical signs. RCM revealed ortho‐ and/or parakeratosis, with hypergranulosis characterized by large, polygonal keratinocytes and granules forming a crown‐like arrangement around the nuclear dark halo. Acanthosis and spongiosis in the spinous layers appeared as crowded, large keratinocytes and thickened intercellular spaces. Necrotic keratinocytes were seen as cloudy polygonal cells in the lower spinous layer. Junctional areas showed disrupted connective tissue papillae, likely due to exudate from inflammation and basal keratinocyte necrosis. In erosive‐atrophic lesions, inflammation and obscured connective tissue papillae were predominant, with hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, and acanthosis absent, and cells smaller than normal, revealing visible blood vessels below a few

Ardigò et al. highlighted the utility of RCM in diagnosing inflammatory oral mucosal diseases, including oral lichen planus, emphasizing its real‐time, noninvasive imaging capabilities, which facilitate differentiation of oral lichen planus from other mucosal conditions [32]. Additional studies, such as Contaldo et al. and Rajadhyaksha et al., further explored the application of RCM in identifying characteristic morphological features of oral lichen planus and its clinical relevance. Collectively, these studies underscore the importance of RCM as a noninvasive diagnostic tool, providing detailed visualization of epithelial and subepithelial changes characteristic of oral lichen planus [33, 34].

Body > Oral Lichen Planus
A systematic review of the literature explored the feasibility of using OCT for the initial assessment of desquamative gingivitis. OCT features of erosive oral lichen planus have been described as a normal stratified epithelial layer and epithelial thickness, an intact basal membrane and lamina propria, and the presence of intense inflammatory infiltrate. In cases of bullous oral lichen planus, OCT revealed multilocular subepithelial blisters, along with a normal stratified epithelial layer, normal epithelial thickness, an intact basal membrane, and lamina propria, as well as intense inflammatory infiltrate [35] (Figure 2).

Body > Oral Lichen Planus
Gambino et al. evaluated OCT as a diagnostic tool for atrophic‐erosive oral lichen planus by comparing OCT scans of healthy buccal mucosa with those of buccal mucosa affected by atrophic‐erosive oral lichen planus, using histopathology as the gold standard. En face scans, displayed in grayscale, revealed that the epithelium appeared narrower and more hyperreflective, indicating hyperorthokeratosis or hyperparakeratosis. The lamina propria exhibited an almost complete lack of distinct hyperreflectivity and an unclear transition between the epithelium and the lamina propria. Dynamic scans visualized vascularization, showing scattered red dots throughout the gray, nonhomogeneous, hyperreflective stratified squamous epithelium, which was likely due to intra‐ and inter‐cellular edema, a hallmark of acanthosis and spongiosis. Additionally, the lamina propria showed a loss of structural integrity and a denser vascular pattern, indicative of increased blood flow in chronically inflamed mucosa [36].

Panzarella et al. evaluated the diagnostic concordance between specific OCT patterns of desquamative gingivitis associated with oral lichen planus, mucous membrane pemphigoid, and pemphigus vulgaris. Among 43 gingival lesions examined, 33 (77%) were identified as oral lichen planus by both OCT and histopathological examination. Notably, OCT identified 11 cases (33%) of bullous oral lichen planus, whereas biopsy detected only one such case [37].

Comparing OCT features of the mucous membrane across different forms of oral lichen planus (reticular, reticular‐atrophic, atrophic, atrophic‐erosive, plaque‐like) and contrasting them with leukoplakia and oral squamous cell carcinoma in a cohort of 15 patients revealed significant diagnostic patterns. Reticular oral lichen planus exhibited increased epithelial surface reflectivity, reduced lamina propria reflectivity, limited basement membrane visibility, and an inconspicuous vascular network. Atrophic oral lichen planus demonstrated a hyporeflective epithelium, absent basement membrane visibility, lack of layer differentiation, and an enhanced vascular network. Reticular‐atrophic and atrophic‐erosive oral lichen planus showed epithelial surface hyperreflectivity, reduced epithelial thickness, decreased lamina propria reflectivity, vague basement membrane visibility, reduced layer differentiation, and fewer large vessels. Additionally, reticular‐atrophic oral lichen planus displayed visibly reduced lamina propria reflectivity. Plaque‐like oral lichen planus presented a hyperreflective epithelial layer but lacked basement membrane visibility, layer differentiation, and vascular network identification. In contrast, leukoplakia exhibited a hyporeflective surface, distinct

In contrast, leukoplakia exhibited a hyporeflective surface, distinct shadowing, absent basement membrane visibility, no layer differentiation, and no identifiable vascular network. Oral squamous cell carcinoma demonstrated a hyperreflective epithelial surface, significantly reduced imaging depth, a cloud‐like layered structure, distinct shadowing, an absent basement membrane and layers, and no vascular network. Diagnostic differentiation focused on epithelium integrity, epithelial thickness, the identifiability of the basement membrane and vascular network within the connective tissue, as well as the reflectivity and differentiation of the epithelium and lamina propria [38].

Body > Mucous Membrane Pemphigoid
Mucous membrane pemphigoid is a group of subepidermal bullous disorders mediated by autoantibodies against various antigens (180 kD, 230 kD, laminin 332, type VII collagen, α6 and β4 integrin subunits) and characterized by a chronic course with a predominant involvement of mucosal membranes. The severity of the disease can vary, from mild or moderate forms with slight gingival inflammation to severe cases affecting multiple mucosal areas [40].

Body > Mucous Membrane Pemphigoid
The most commonly involved sites in mucous membrane pemphigoid are the oral mucosa (80%–85% cases), followed by conjunctiva (64%), nasal mucosa, genital mucosa, gastroesophageal mucosa, and the skin [40]. Skin involvement is observed in only 25%–30% of patients [40]. According to Sultan et al., the majority of oral mucous membrane pemphigoid cases (84%) had gingival involvement, while non‐gingival sites were less common (16%). Gingival lesions were more prevalent in mucous membrane pemphigoid patients (64%) compared to pemphigus vulgaris patients (33%). Tongue involvement was rare in mucous membrane pemphigoid patients, with only 15% showing such involvement. In mucous membrane pemphigoid, the intraoral sites most commonly involved are: the gingiva (80%), buccal mucosa (58%), palate (26%), alveolar ridge (16%), tongue (15%), and lower lip (7%) [41].

Body > Mucous Membrane Pemphigoid
According to Bagan et al., the majority of oral mucous membrane pemphigoid lesions occurred on the gingiva (95%), followed by the palate and buccal mucosa (21% each). The lesions also affected the lips (5%), while tongue and floor of the mouth involvement were less common (3% each). Gingival mucous membrane pemphigoid typically manifests as desquamative gingivitis, with bullae present in the majority of cases, accompanied by erythematous‐erosive areas. Most cases (67%) presented with a single affected location, while a smaller proportion (15%) had three or more simultaneously affected sites [42].

Body > Mucous Membrane Pemphigoid
As reported by Parlatescu et al., desquamative gingivitis was found in 47.72% of patients diagnosed with autoimmune blistering diseases, with 79.41% from the subepithelial group and 27.77% from the intraepithelial group. It was the only oral manifestation in 5.55% of intraepithelial disease patients and 26.47% of subepithelial disease patients. In subepithelial diseases, the buccal mucosa was the second most affected site (41.17%), followed by the soft palate (32.35%) and hard palate (17.65%). All patients with subepithelial diseases had unilateral buccal mucosa involvement. In intraepithelial diseases, the buccal mucosa was most frequently affected (83.33%), followed by the soft palate (46.29%) and tonsillar pillar (27.77%). Oral lesions were limited to a single region in 12.96% of intraepithelial patients and 32.35% of subepithelial patients [43].

During the healing phase, fibrosis may occur on extra‐gingival lesions, leading to the appearance of reticulated white striations that resemble lichen planus [45, 46].

This dark area corresponds not only to the histopathological features of mucous membrane pemphigoid but also to the clinical aspect of hemorrhagic bullae observed in some patients. The reported OCT features for mucous membrane pemphigoid of the gingiva were the presence of multilocular subepithelial blister, a normal stratified epithelial layer and epithelial thickness, an altered/indistinguishable basal membrane and lamina propria, and the presence of inflammatory infiltrate [37]. In a documented case of desquamative gingivitis associated with mucous membrane pemphigoid, the OCT images revealed a dark region between the mucosa and submucosa. The fluid‐filled blisters appeared dark with a notable grayish hue, likely corresponding to blister fluid containing eosinophils [47, 48]. Neutrophil and eosinophil infiltration was also described as the alternation of black and gray areas [49]. The epithelial layer, measuring 300 µm and depicted as the initial horizontal band, exhibited low contrast with the underlying connective tissue and appeared to be well‐preserved [49] (Figure 5).

Body > Pemphigus vulgaris
Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune bullous disorder characterized by the production of autoantibodies against desmosomal proteins, desmogleins 1 (DSG1) and 3 (DSG3), leading to acantholysis, blister formation, and subsequent erosions [50, 51]. Diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris is based on a combination of clinical presentation, histopathology, direct immunofluorescence (DIF), and serological tests for anti‐Dsg1 and anti‐Dsg3 autoantibodies. A definitive diagnosis requires a clinical picture, histopathological evidence of suprabasal acantholysis, and positive DIF showing IgG and/or C3 deposits at the surface of epidermal keratinocytes. Additionally, serological tests, such as indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) or enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), are used to detect anti‐Dsg1 and/or anti‐Dsg3 autoantibodies, which are present in more than 95% of cases and correlate with disease activity [52].

Body > Pemphigus vulgaris
Oral lesions may appear before skin lesions or may be the sole manifestation of the disease [50]. Scully et al., discovered that only 28% of patients with pemphigus vulgaris exhibited desquamative gingivitis, while the majority, 72%, had involvement of non‐gingival sites. In a group of 55 pemphigus vulgaris patients with oral manifestations, desquamative gingivitis was present in 24% of cases and was the primary symptom in 9% of cases [53]. The pharynx was identified as the most common site of extra‐oral involvement, accounting for 38% of cases. Sultan et al., supported these findings, showing desquamative gingivitis in 28% of pemphigus vulgaris cases, with it being the sole manifestation in 6% of cases. Additionally, the pharynx was the most frequently affected extra‐oral site, observed in 55% of cases [41]. Mignogna et al., noted gingival involvement in 44% of oral pemphigus vulgaris cases, with desquamative gingivitis being the sole oral manifestation in 11% of the 18 cases studied [54]. Pemphigus vulgaris can affect any area of the oral mucosa, with a preference for the gingival papillary tips. This differs from mucous membrane pemphigoid, where there is more widespread gingival involvement [55]. Pemphigus vulgaris is characterized by extensive non‐gingival oral lesions

Pemphigus vulgaris is characterized by extensive non‐gingival oral lesions involving most frequently on the buccal mucosa (90%) and the retromolar trigone (72.5%), and also in a high number of cases on the soft palate (60%) and the gingiva (42.5%) [56]. In these cases, the oral mucosa is frequently eroded, leading to rapid rupture of superficial blisters, making intact blisters rare. Healing typically occurs without scarring. Other mucous membranes that may be involved include the less common pharyngeal and nasal mucosa, genital, ocular, laryngeal, and esophageal mucosa [56] (Figure 6).

Body > Pemphigus vulgaris
The identification of acantholytic keratinocytes is essential for pemphigus vulgaris diagnosis using RCM. This is especially crucial as the gingival presentation of pemphigus vulgaris often involves extensive erosions. Acantholytic keratinocytes are readily detectable with RCM and can be observed not only within pemphigus blisters but also at the transition between eroded and apparently unaffected gingival mucosa. Additionally, RCM is beneficial for selecting biopsy sites, as specimens are often taken from areas that do not yield sufficient diagnostic material. It also aids in patient follow‐up, as some persistent lesions, especially in the gingiva, may endure despite immunosuppressive treatment and can be mistaken for periodontal disease [1].

Body > Pemphigus vulgaris
In RCM of desquamative gingivitis in pemphigus vulgaris, an intraepithelial cleft containing rounded detached cells, which correspond with acantholytic keratinocytes, was observed, along with prominent, round or linear dark canalicular structures oriented horizontally in the lamina propria, reflecting dilated vessels. The lamina propria also showed inflammatory cells as round‐to‐polygonal, slightly refractive cells, which were smaller in size compared to melanophages and keratinocytes [1]. In the described case, a woman with pemphigus vulgaris presented with multiple erosions on the mucosa of her right cheek and the left lateral side of her tongue. RCM was used to examine the erosion on the cheek mucosa, revealing the presence of acantholytic keratinocytes and an intraepithelial cleft [32].

The OCT image of the gingiva in pemphigus vulgaris revealed dark superficial clefts within the stratified squamous epithelium. In this instance, an intraepithelial split could be clearly identified. These intraepithelial acantholytic blisters were likely fluid‐filled. The roof of these blisters appeared significantly thinner than the well‐defined epithelial layer [49]. The reported OCT features for pemphigus vulgaris involving the gingiva are: presence of unilocular intraepithelial blister, reduced stratified epithelial layer and epithelial thickness, normal basal membrane and lamina propria, and the presence of acantholytic cells in the blister [37] (Figure 7).

Body > Conclusions
Desquamative gingivitis is a clinical manifestation of a wide range of systemic and mucocutaneous diseases, including oral lichen planus, mucous membrane pemphigoid, and pemphigus vulgaris. An accurate diagnosis involves a combination of clinical assessment, immunopathological and histopathological examinations, and the emerging use of noninvasive imaging techniques. Noninvasive imaging techniques, particularly RCM, OCT, and LC‐OCT, have the potential to revolutionize the diagnostic approach to desquamative gingivitis by improving differential diagnosis, reducing the need for invasive biopsy, and enabling longitudinal monitoring of treatment response. Their integration into clinical practice could enhance early detection of underlying autoimmune and inflammatory conditions, contributing to improved patient outcomes.

For pemphigus vulgaris, acantholytic keratinocytes and intraepithelial clefts are the characteristic findings, while in mucous membrane pemphigoid, subepithelial clefts and hemorrhagic features can be visualized (Table 1).

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Abstract
Desquamative gingivitis (DG) is a clinical sign characterized by gingival erythema, epithelial desquamation, and erosion rather than a discrete diagnosis. It most commonly reflects underlying oral lichen planus, mucous membrane pemphigoid, or pemphigus vulgaris. As affected patients typically present to general dental practitioners, timely recognition and structured triage are essential for effective management. However, diagnostic delays remain common and can extend the management period by several months. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence on the clinical presentation, epidemiology, etiology, differential diagnosis, diagnostic workup, and management pathways relevant to general dentistry for this condition. Key findings indicate that a staged clinical history and examination can substantially narrow the differential diagnosis prior to biopsy, that histopathology combined with direct immunofluorescence offers superior diagnostic yield compared with histopathology alone, and that biopsy technique and site selection, favoring perilesional or uninvolved tissue and atraumatic sampling methods, meaningfully affect the diagnostic accuracy. Chronic ulcerative stomatitis and lichen planus pemphigoides are important but frequently overlooked mimics of more common causes. While disease-specific pharmacotherapy generally requires specialist oversight, professional oral hygiene reinforcement and gentle periodontal care delivered by general dental practitioners produce consistent, evidence-supported improvements in pain and

A structured, practical approach to recognition, biopsy planning, and prompt referral can shorten the diagnostic pathway and improve long-term outcomes in patients with this challenging clinical condition.

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Body > Introduction and background
Desquamative gingivitis (DG) was first proposed in 1932 to describe a clinical triad of erythema, epithelial desquamation, and erosion or blistering of the marginal and attached gingiva. It remains a frequently encountered but under-recognized presentation in general dental practice [1,2]. Rather than constituting a diagnosis in itself, DG is a shared clinical phenotype produced by a range of underlying mucocutaneous and systemic diseases, most commonly oral lichen planus, mucous membrane pemphigoid, and pemphigus vulgaris, which together account for the substantial majority of reported cases [1,3]. Because patients with DG typically present first to a general dental practitioner (GDP) rather than a dermatologist or oral medicine specialist, the GDP occupies a critical, often first-contact position in a diagnostic pathway that has historically been prolonged and inefficient, with studies documenting professional diagnostic delays averaging over seven months and involving consultations with multiple clinicians before a definitive cause is identified [4,5].

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Body > Introduction and background
The clinical significance of accurate and timely recognition extends beyond oral discomfort. Several conditions underlying DG pose a significant systemic risk. Mucous membrane pemphigoid can produce scarring at ocular and other extraoral mucosal sites with a risk of blindness, while pemphigus vulgaris can behave as a severe systemic mucocutaneous disease requiring urgent systemic immunosuppression [6,7]. Moreover, the chronic pain characteristic of DG frequently discourages effective oral hygiene, creating a secondary risk pathway for periodontal breakdown and tooth loss, which compounds the primary disease [8]. Despite this clinical importance, a persistent knowledge gap among GDPs regarding the differentiation, appropriate biopsy technique, and referral thresholds for DG remains, prompting calls for clearer diagnostic algorithms and structured clinical guides specifically tailored to non-specialist practice [1,3]. This narrative review aims to synthesize the current evidence on the clinical features, epidemiology, etiology, differential diagnosis, diagnostic workup, management, and referral pathway for DG, with a practical focus on equipping GDPs to recognize this presentation efficiently and initiate an appropriate diagnostic and therapeutic course.

Clinical features and epidemiology

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Body > Review
DG is a clinical descriptor, not a diagnosis, applied to gingiva showing erythema, epithelial desquamation, erosion, and occasional vesiculobullous changes affecting the marginal and attached tissues [1,5]. The condition typically spares nothing consistently; lesions may be localized to a few papillae or extend across the full width of the attached gingiva, most classically on the labial aspect of the anterior maxillary and mandibular teeth [3,5]. Gentle lateral pressure on apparently normal gingiva can separate the epithelium from the connective tissue, producing a positive Nikolsky sign that supports a vesiculobullous process, although its absence does not exclude it [3]. Symptoms range from mild discomfort to severe burning pain, which is exacerbated by acidic, spicy, or abrasive foods and tooth brushing. This discomfort frequently discourages effective plaque control, compounding erythema through superimposed plaque-induced inflammation [5,9]. Importantly, DG itself does not cause attachment loss or alveolar bone destruction; therefore, periodontal breakdown seen in affected patients usually reflects secondary plaque accumulation rather than the underlying mucocutaneous disease [1,5].

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Body > Review
Epidemiologically, DG shows a strong predilection for women, typically presenting in the fifth and sixth decades of life, coinciding with perimenopausal hormonal changes, although pediatric and adolescent cases have also been reported [1,2]. Across large retrospective series, mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP), oral lichen planus (OLP), and pemphigus vulgaris (PV) account for the substantial majority of DG presentations, with published estimates attributing approximately 80% of cases to these three entities [1,3]. In a case series, MMP has been reported as the underlying diagnosis in 35-60% of DG presentations, OLP in 24-45%, and PV in 3-15%, although these proportions vary with referral patterns and the diagnostic era [1,3]. A comparative retrospective analysis spanning 55 years of biopsy records found that immunologically mediated oral diseases accounted for only 1.18% of all specimens, with lichen planus being far more common than PV or MMP; however, DG was documented across all three diagnoses and was most frequent in MMP [9]. Consistent with this, a two-center cohort comparing oral MMP with PV found DG in 84% of MMP cases versus only 28% of PV cases, while non-gingival oral lesions were far more common in PV (55%) than in MMP (6%) [7]. A separate series of 100 low-risk oral MMP cases similarly found DG as the presenting

[7]. A separate series of 100 low-risk oral MMP cases similarly found DG as the presenting feature in 97% of patients, most often confined to a single oral site [10]. Collectively, these figures indicate that when DG is confined to the gingiva without other mucosal or cutaneous involvement, MMP should be ranked high on the differential diagnosis list, whereas widespread non-gingival oral disease should raise suspicion of PV.

The diagnostic course of DG is often prolonged. A cohort study of 41 patients presenting primarily with DG found an average patient delay of 10.8 months before the first professional consultation, followed by a further professional delay averaging 7.3 months, involving consultation with more than four healthcare providers before a definitive diagnosis was reached [4]. Less severe disease and female sex were both associated with longer patient-side delays, while professional delay was correlated with the number of clinicians consulted and the absence of extragingival lesions that might otherwise prompt an earlier suspicion of a systemic mucocutaneous disorder [4]. This prolonged diagnostic odyssey underscores the pivotal position of the general dental practitioner (GDP), who is frequently the first clinician to examine these lesions and, therefore, bears substantial responsibility for initiating a timely and structured diagnostic pathway [4,5].

Etiology and pathogenesis

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Body > Review
The etiological spectrum underlying DG is broad, spanning autoimmune dermatoses, lichenoid disease, endocrine disturbance, hypersensitivity reactions, and chronic infection; however, the overwhelming majority of cases converge on three immune-mediated conditions: OLP, MMP, and PV [1,11]. OLP is a T-cell-mediated mucocutaneous disease in which cytotoxic lymphocytes target the basal keratinocytes. When confined to the gingiva, it typically presents as an erosive or atrophic variant rather than the more familiar reticular and asymptomatic form observed in the buccal mucosa [11,12]. Lichenoid reactions clinically indistinguishable from OLP can also be triggered by dental restorative materials, particularly amalgam, or by systemic medications; therefore, a history of recent drug changes or contact with suspected materials should be obtained [3].

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Body > Review
MMP and PV are characterized by autoantibody-mediated subepithelial and intraepithelial blistering. In MMP, autoantibodies target basement membrane zone antigens including BP180, BP230, and laminin-332, producing subepithelial separation, while in PV, autoantibodies against desmogleins disrupt keratinocyte cell-to-cell adhesion, producing intraepithelial acantholysis [3,6]. This mechanistic distinction has direct clinical relevance because MMP carries a risk of scarring at extraoral mucosal sites, particularly conjunctival scarring that can progress to blindness, whereas PV, although potentially more acutely severe and mortality-associated when systemic, does not typically scar [3,6]. Beyond these three dominant entities, a minority of DG cases are related to plasma cell gingivitis, CUS, lupus erythematosus, erythema multiforme, linear IgA disease, epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, graft-versus-host disease, and drug- or contact-induced lichenoid lesions, several of which lack precise prevalence data owing to their rarity [1,3].

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Body > Review
Emerging evidence also implicates the oral microbiome as a modulating, rather than purely secondary, factor in DG-associated disease. Dysbiosis, characterized by reduced microbial diversity and an increase in proinflammatory bacterial genera, has been consistently observed in OLP. This dysbiosis is correlated with epithelial barrier disruption and increased cytokine production. Proposed mechanisms include Toll-like receptor activation and skewing of T-cell responses, which may sustain mucosal inflammation [12]. Evidence in MMP and PV remains preliminary, but a shared theme across these conditions is that local microbial ecology and immune dysregulation may interact bidirectionally, indicating that plaque control is unlikely to be a purely cosmetic adjunct and may influence disease activity [12,13]. For GDP, recognizing this dual burden, an immune-mediated disease process compounded by a plaque-driven inflammatory overlay, reframes oral hygiene reinforcement as a therapeutic rather than an incidental intervention.

Differential diagnosis

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Body > Review
Because the clinical appearance of DG is shared across multiple diseases, several less common but clinically important mimics merit specific consideration, including OLP, MMP, and PV. Chronic ulcerative stomatitis (CUS) is a rare immune-mediated disorder that closely resembles erosive OLP, both clinically and histologically. It most often affects middle-aged and older women, with cutaneous involvement in approximately one-fifth of the cases [14,15]. The key distinguishing features are serological and immunopathological, rather than clinical. CUS is characterized by stratified epithelium-specific antinuclear antibodies directed against the ΔNp63α isoform of p63, which are detectable on direct immunofluorescence (DIF), and by a comparatively poor response to conventional corticosteroids, with better outcomes reported for hydroxychloroquine [14,15]. This distinction is important because a patient labeled as having corticosteroid-refractory erosive OLP may have unrecognized CUS, requiring a different systemic agent [15].

Body > Review
Lichen planus pemphigoides (LPPs) represent a further diagnostic pitfall, combining the features of lichen planus with a subepithelial autoimmune blistering process. Oral involvement alone is rare, and diagnosis requires correlating clinical findings with histopathology showing features of both lichen planus and pemphigoid, supported by DIF, which demonstrates linear IgG and C3 deposition in the basement membrane zone [16]. A case series of four patients with oral LPP found that three had exclusive oral involvement, reinforcing that a gingival lesion resembling lichen planus should not automatically be assumed to be uncomplicated OLP if the biopsy features are atypical [16]. Beyond these entities, the dermatologic oral examination literature emphasizes that site-based pattern recognition, correlating the anatomical distribution of oral lesions with a structured differential, meaningfully narrows the diagnostic possibilities before biopsy is even undertaken, since certain conditions have characteristic zones of predilection within the oral cavity [13].

Table 1 summarizes the epidemiological, clinical, and histopathological features that help distinguish the principal diseases underlying DG. Given this overlap, the GDP's task is not to render a definitive histologic diagnosis but to recognize the DG pattern, exclude simple plaque-induced gingivitis, and initiate a structured referral for tissue-based confirmation.

Diagnostic workup for the general dental practitioner

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Body > Review
For GDP, the diagnostic workup of suspected DG begins with a structured clinical assessment before any invasive steps are considered. A validated approach involves three sequential stages: intraoral examination of lesion morphology, location, and Nikolsky sign; a detailed history covering onset, systemic health, current infections, topical product exposure, and medication changes; and assessment of extraoral involvement of the skin, eyes, nose, or genital mucosa [1]. This staged history-taking framework was shown in a pilot study of dental undergraduates to meaningfully improve diagnostic accuracy compared with unstructured routine assessment, supporting its transferability to general practice [1].

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Body > Review
When the clinical picture indicates an immune-mediated process, a biopsy is the pivotal next step. However, histopathology alone is frequently insufficient, and the diagnostic yield is substantially improved when paired with DIF, particularly for erosive, ulcerated, or diffusely erythematous presentations [17]. The French national guidelines for OLP explicitly recommend histological biopsy in the absence of reticular lesions and DIF biopsy for ulcerated, erosive, bullous, or diffuse erythematous gingival presentations [17]. A systematic review evaluating immunofluorescence performance found that DIF substantially outperformed indirect immunofluorescence, with sensitivity and specificity of 87.8% and 100% for PV, 92% and 98% for MMP, and 81% and 98.9% for DG-associated oral ulceration overlapping with OLP, while DIF sensitivity for OLP itself was more moderate at 64.3% with 88% specificity [19].

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Body > Review
The biopsy site and technique significantly affected the diagnostic yield. A large meta-analysis of gingival biopsies for MMP and PV with gingival expression found DIF positivity rates of 100% for PV and 90.2% for MMP when biopsies were taken from the gingiva. The authors concluded that the biopsied site should be selected primarily for tissue quality and lesion proximity rather than a fixed anatomical rule, favoring healthy tissue adjacent to active lesions [20]. Complementing this, a retrospective comparison of biopsy techniques found that a normal buccal punch biopsy from uninvolved mucosa was statistically equivalent in sensitivity to a perilesional biopsy for both PV and multisite MMP and was more sensitive than histology or indirect immunofluorescence serology alone, offering GDPs and specialists a technically simpler alternative to perilesional sampling [18]. Because the gingival epithelium is particularly fragile and prone to shearing during conventional punch or scalpel biopsy, a dedicated stab-and-roll technique was developed specifically to preserve epithelial integrity. In a retrospective review of 27 DG cases, this method maintained intact epithelium in 51 of 52 biopsy specimens (98.1%), enabling a definitive diagnosis of MMP, PV, or OLP in most cases [21]. Collectively, this evidence supports the referral of suspected DG for biopsy incorporating both routine histopathology and

Collectively, this evidence supports the referral of suspected DG for biopsy incorporating both routine histopathology and DIF, ideally from perilesional or adjacent normal-appearing gingival or buccal tissue rather than frankly ulcerated areas, since severely inflamed or ulcerated tissue frequently yields non-diagnostic or false-negative immunofluorescence results [20,21].

Management and referral pathway

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Body > Review
The management of DG operates on two complementary tracks: disease-specific pharmacotherapy directed at the underlying immune process, generally initiated and monitored by an oral medicine specialist or dermatologist, and non-pharmacological periodontal care, which falls squarely within the GDP's scope and materially affects patient comfort and disease activity, regardless of the causative diagnosis [2,5]. A systematic review of pharmacological treatments for DG identified topical clobetasol and tacrolimus as the most frequently studied and consistently effective first-line agents, both of which produced significant reductions in pain and lesion severity. Emerging adjunctive options, such as platelet-rich plasma and bioadhesive propolis- or nano-vitamin-based gels, have shown promising but preliminary results [2]. Systemic agents carry a materially higher risk profile, including candidiasis and hemolytic complications, reinforcing that escalation beyond topical therapy should occur under specialist supervision rather than general practice [2].

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Body > Review
The evidence base for non-pharmacological, GDP-deliverable care is well-established. A systematic review of oral hygiene instruction and professional prophylaxis across nine studies involving 224 patients with OLP, MMP, plasma cell gingivitis, and PV found statistically significant reductions in pain, lesion extent, gingival bleeding, and plaque scores following structured hygiene instruction and supragingival scaling, regardless of the underlying diagnosis [22]. Reported protocols emphasized a modified Bass brushing technique with a soft brush, chlorhexidine mouth rinse, and avoidance of sodium lauryl sulfate-containing toothpaste, with benefits demonstrated as early as one week and sustained improvement through 20 weeks of follow-up in several cohorts [22]. Clinical case reports further support guided biofilm therapy using erythritol-based air-polishing powders as a gentler, better-tolerated alternative to conventional mechanical debridement in patients with MMP, PV, and OLP, reducing procedural discomfort while achieving effective biofilm removal in an already fragile and painful gingival environment [23]. Comprehensive reviews of clinical findings in DG similarly stress that untreated plaque accumulation, itself a consequence of the pain-driven avoidance of oral hygiene, can independently drive periodontitis and tooth loss in these patients, making professional plaque control an essential rather than optional component of care [8].

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Body > Review
Practically, once DG is suspected, the GDP's role is to perform an atraumatic biopsy or arrange prompt referral for one, initiate gentle, individualized oral hygiene reinforcement using non-abrasive techniques, and establish a referral pathway to oral medicine, periodontology, or dermatology for definitive diagnosis and disease-specific pharmacotherapy [5,22]. Given the risk of ocular scarring in MMP and the potential for systemic morbidity across several of these conditions, referral should not await pharmacological failure but should be initiated promptly upon recognition of a DG pattern, in parallel with the institution of supportive periodontal care [5,6].

Desquamative Gingivitis: A Narrative Review of Practical Diagnostic Approach for General Dental Practitioners
Body > Conclusions
DG is a clinical sign rather than a diagnosis, most often signaling oral lichen planus, mucous membrane pemphigoid, or pemphigus vulgaris, although several rarer immune-mediated conditions can produce identical gingival appearances. For general dental practitioners, the diagnostic priority is pattern recognition rather than definitive labeling; a structured history and examination addressing lesion morphology, distribution, and extraoral involvement can substantially narrow the differential diagnosis before tissue is obtained. Because histopathology alone frequently underdiagnoses these conditions, biopsy planning should routinely incorporate direct immunofluorescence sampling from perilesional or uninvolved tissue using an atraumatic technique that preserves the fragile gingival epithelium. Diagnostic delay remains common and clinically consequential; therefore, prompt referral to oral medicine, periodontology, or dermatology should not be deferred pending trial therapy. Meanwhile, GDP can meaningfully improve patient comfort and disease activity through gentle, individualized oral hygiene reinforcement and professional plaque control, interventions supported by consistent evidence regardless of the underlying diagnosis. A working knowledge of this practical pathway equips general practitioners to shorten the diagnostic journey and serve as active partners rather than passive referrers in the long-term care of these patients.

Dental Pulp Stem Cells for the Management of Plaque Biofilm-Associated Infections : A Review
Abstract
This structured narrative review synthesises current evidence (2000-2025) on the antimicrobial, immunomodulatory, and regenerative properties of dental pulp stem cells (DPSCs) in the context of plaque-induced gingivitis and oral biofilm infections. We systematically reviewed peer-reviewed literature from PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science via keywords related to DPSCs, oral biofilms, antimicrobial peptides (eg, β-defensins, LL-37), and immunomodulation. Unlike conventional antimicrobial therapies that solely target pathogen eradication, DPSCs offer a dual-function strategy: (1) direct microbial control through the secretion of antimicrobial peptides that disrupt Porphyromonas gingivalis and Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans and (2) resolution of inflammation via macrophage M2 polarisation, suppression of IL-1β/TNF-α (Interleukin-1β and Tumor Necrosis Factor-α), and microbiome rebalancing. Additionally, DPSCs support periodontal tissue regeneration through trophic signalling and differentiation into periodontal lineage cells. Critically, no clinical trials to date have evaluated DPSCs for the management of gingivitis. This review highlights DPSCs as promising, antibiotic-sparing therapeutic candidate and outlines key knowledge gaps for future translational research.

Effectively managing the microbial aetiology of periodontal disease remains a key challenge. These diseases are driven by dysbiosis, an imbalance in the oral microbiome. While conventional antimicrobial treatments reduce pathogenic bacteria, they often lack specificity and may disrupt beneficial microbial communities.7 In contrast, DPSCs offer a more targeted approach. They secrete antimicrobial peptides AMPs, such as LL-37, which kill periodontal pathogens and modulate the oral microbiome to promote a balanced environment conducive to periodontal health.8 Furthermore, DPSCs play a significant role in modulating host immunity by promoting macrophage polarisation towards an anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype, which is essential for tissue repair and regeneration. This immunomodulatory function, which is partially mediated by the secretion of IL-10 and hepatocyte growth factor, contributes to resolving inflammation and enhancing periodontal tissue regeneration.9

DPSCs also positively influence the oral microbiome. Studies involving the injection of periodontal ligament stem cells (PDLSCs) into periodontal defects have demonstrated a reversal of dysbiosis, with increased levels of beneficial bacteria such as Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus. This rebalancing of the microbiota is correlated with improved periodontal regeneration, suggesting that stem cell therapies can modulate oral microbial communities in a beneficial manner.10 These comprehensive effects surpass the capabilities of conventional treatments. Nonetheless, further clinical trials are necessary to confirm the safety, efficacy, long-term outcomes, and underlying mechanisms before DPSCs can be established as a standard treatment for periodontal therapy.

Despite advances in stem cell biology, the dual capacity of DPSCs to simultaneously combat pathogenic biofilms and regenerate periodontal tissues remains underexplored in the context of gingivitis. Unlike conventional antimicrobials or even other types of MSCs, DPSCs uniquely integrate innate immune defense with tissue repair, a synergy that positions them as a promising antibiotic-sparing strategy. This review critically evaluates this emerging paradigm, with emphasis on molecular mechanisms, microbiome interactions, and translational prospects.

Gingival inflammation, a widespread condition affecting gums, is a major risk factor for periodontitis and a strong predictor of potential long-term tooth loss.11 Therefore, preventing gingival inflammation is crucial for both primary and secondary prevention of periodontitis. The majority of gingival inflammation cases are classified as dental plaque-induced gingivitis, which is further categorised on the basis of the presence or absence of modifying risk factors, such as systemic conditions, local irritants, or drug-induced influences.12

Dental plaque is a biofilm that forms on tooth surfaces and is primarily composed of bacteria embedded in a matrix of salivary glycoproteins and extracellular polysaccharides. While plaque formation is a natural biological process, inadequate oral hygiene can lead to excessive accumulation, resulting in oral diseases such as gingivitis and periodontitis.13 Gingivitis arises from the host’s immune response to the bacterial biofilm in dental plaque and is characterised by inflammation of the gingival tissue.14 Clinically, it presents as redness, swelling, tenderness, and bleeding of the gums, particularly during brushing or flossing. Importantly, gingivitis is a reversible condition, and appropriate oral hygiene practices such as regular brushing and flossing can resolve inflammation and restore gingival health.15

If left untreated, gingivitis may progress to periodontitis, a more severe and destructive form of periodontal disease that affects the supporting structures of the teeth, including the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone. This progression can lead to the formation of periodontal pockets, bone resorption, and eventual tooth loss. Although not all cases of gingivitis progress to periodontitis, every case of periodontitis is preceded by gingivitis.16 The primary aetiological factor in both conditions is the accumulation of dental plaque. Bacteria within the plaque biofilm release toxins and enzymes that trigger an inflammatory response in the gingival tissues. Over time, if plaque is not effectively removed, it may mineralise into calculus (tartar), which further exacerbates inflammation and provides an additional surface for microbial accumulation.17,18

These risk factors can modulate the host immune response, increasing the vulnerability of gingival tissues to inflammation.

Maintaining proper oral hygiene is essential in both the prevention and management of gingivitis and plaque-related infections. The recommended practices include brushing teeth at least twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, flossing daily to remove interdental plaque, and attending regular dental check-ups for professional cleaning and evaluation. In addition to oral care, lifestyle modifications such as adopting a balanced, low-sugar diet, abstaining from tobacco, and managing systemic health conditions can significantly reduce the risk of developing gingivitis and its progression to periodontitis. Emerging evidence also suggests strong associations between periodontal diseases and systemic health conditions, including cardiovascular diseases, diabetes mellitus, respiratory infections, and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Inflammatory mediators released in response to periodontal infections can enter the systemic circulation, potentially affecting distant organs and contributing to chronic systemic inflammation. Consequently, preserving periodontal health is essential not only for maintaining oral function but also for promoting overall systemic well-being. The oral microbial community is typically in a state of dynamic equilibrium. However, when this ecological balance is disrupted, pathological conditions may arise. Among the most common oral infections are dental caries and periodontal diseases, both of which are now better understood in terms of their microbial aetiology. Dental caries result from the demineralisation of enamel and, eventually, dentin due to acids produced by the bacterial metabolism of dietary sugars. The microorganisms most commonly associated with carious lesions include Streptococcus mutans, Streptococcus sobrinus, Lactobacillus spp., and Actinomyces spp.21,22

In contrast, periodontal diseases are among the most prevalent chronic inflammatory conditions affecting adults. In the absence of effective treatment, they may lead to progressive tissue destruction and eventual tooth loss. These conditions are generally categorised into two main types:

• Periodontitis extends to deeper supporting structures, such as the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone.

Gingivitis is primarily a nonspecific inflammatory response to the accumulation of bacterial biofilms (both gram-positive and gram-negative species) at or below the gingival margin.23 In contrast, periodontitis is typically initiated by the overgrowth of specific pathogenic gram-negative anaerobes, including members of the ‘red complex’.17,24

Dental plaque plays a central role in the pathogenesis of both caries and periodontal disease. A plaque is a complex microbial biofilm that forms on the tooth surface and comprises bacteria, salivary glycoproteins, food debris, and extracellular polysaccharides. It adheres firmly to the enamel and is difficult to remove without mechanical intervention. Its composition includes both organic components (eg, polysaccharides, proteins, glycoproteins and lipids) and inorganic constituents (eg, calcium, phosphate, sodium and potassium).25

When not properly removed, plaque undergoes calcification, forming dental calculus (tartar), which further facilitates bacterial colonisation and perpetuates inflammation. Plaques tend to accumulate in anatomically protected sites such as fissures, interproximal areas, and the gingival sulcus, regions that are often challenging to clean effectively.26,27 The acidogenic nature of plaque is the primary mechanism behind dental caries. After carbohydrate intake, plaque bacteria metabolise sugars and produce acids that lower the pH at the tooth surface, leading to enamel demineralisation. Repeated acid attacks, if unchecked, eventually result in cavity formation. Moreover, the bacterial toxins and enzymes in plaque can irritate the gingiva, initiating gingivitis and possibly progressing to periodontitis and tooth loss.28

The specific plaque hypothesis postulates that only certain microbial species within the biofilm are pathogenic and that their presence determines the disease potential of the plaque. This contrasts with the nonspecific plaque hypothesis, which attributes pathogenicity to overall biomass.29,30 Understanding the nature and formation of dental plaque is essential for devising effective strategies for oral disease prevention. Plaque formation begins within minutes after eating or drinking and follows a well-defined sequence of biological events:

➢ Pellicle formation: The acquired pellicle is a glycoprotein-rich film derived from saliva, gingival crevicular fluid, microbial byproducts, and host cells. It forms rapidly on all surfaces in the oral cavity, including teeth and restorations. While it serves as a protective barrier, the pellicle also facilitates bacterial adhesion and colonisation.31
➢ Initial bacterial colonisation: Early colonisers, such as Streptococcus sanguinis and Actinomyces spp., bind to pellicle receptors and initiate plaque development.32
➢ Secondary colonisation and biofilm maturation: Coaggregation of secondary colonisers leads to a more complex and structured biofilm. Over time, biofilms mature, with increased microbial diversity and potential pathogenicity.32

A biofilm can be defined as a layer of both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria that adhere to and grow on any firm biotic or abiotic surface surrounded by a self-produced mucilaginous matrix. Biofilms are ubiquitous and can have serious adverse effects on human health. They also form on inanimate surfaces, such as medical devices, dental implants, surgical sutures, catheters, and artificial joints.34,35

A prime example of this phenomenon is oral biofilms, or dental plaque, which are common in the oral cavity of all mammals. Natural dentition and dental prostheses, including dentures and implants, serve as substrates for biofilm formation. The consumption of carbohydrate-rich foods leads to increased secretion of organic acids by bacteria that form oral biofilms or dental plaques. As bacterial colonisation increases, there is an overproduction of matrix polysaccharides, such as alginate, and the resulting mucoid biofilm facilitates resistance to antibiotics and the host immune response. Bacteria also produce an extracellular polymeric substance (EPS), which contributes to chronic infection and complicates treatment. If left untreated, the biofilm demineralises the enamel, ultimately causing dental caries

Such signalling can result in coordinated gene expression within the microbial community, and these cell signalling strategies are currently considered potential targets for novel therapeutics.48,49

Stages of biofilm formation in dental plaques
content:
Dental Pulp Stem Cells for the Management of Plaque Biofilm-Associated Infections : A Review
Body > Methods > Dental plaque identified as a biofilm > Stages of biofilm formation in dental plaques > First stage: Adherence and lag
In the initial stage of oral biofilm formation, planktonic (free-floating) bacteria approach and attach to the tooth surface, specifically, to the acquired enamel pellicle. This adherence is initially reversible, mediated by weak physicochemical forces (such as van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions), and soon becomes irreversible as bacteria use surface structures such as pili and adhesins to secure their attachment. This phase also involves a genetic shift in bacteria, with the upregulation of genes related to biofilm survival and resistance. As a result, bacterial growth slows temporarily in what is termed a ‘lag phase’, allowing for the establishment of a stable colonising population.26,50,51

content:
Dental Pulp Stem Cells for the Management of Plaque Biofilm-Associated Infections : A Review
Body > Methods > Dental plaque identified as a biofilm > Stages of biofilm formation in dental plaques > Second stage: Accelerated growth
Once securely attached, bacteria begin to proliferate rapidly. This accelerated growth phase is characterised by active cell division, the recruitment and coaggregation of additional bacterial species, and the secretion of abundant EPSs, primarily polysaccharides and proteins. These secretions form a robust matrix that encapsulates the cells, fostering structural stratification and further complexity within the biofilm. The matrix not only supports additional bacterial adhesion but also enhances resistance to environmental stresses and antimicrobial agents.50,52

Dental Pulp Stem Cells for the Management of Plaque Biofilm-Associated Infections : A Review
Body > Methods > Dental plaque identified as a biofilm > Stages of biofilm formation in dental plaques > Third stage: Stable attachment
In the steady-state or stable attachment phase, the biofilm matures into a dense and highly organised microbial community. The growth rates of bacteria are slow, with metabolic activity often downregulated deep within the biofilm. At this point, the matrix becomes more complex and protective, and the established biofilm exhibits increased tolerance to antimicrobials and host immune defenses. Channels and pores develop, allowing for nutrient circulation. The mature biofilm can remain stable for extended periods and may occasionally release clusters of cells or single bacteria, contributing to colonisation elsewhere in the oral cavity.26,50,52

The enamel surface predominantly contains negatively charged phosphate groups that interact directly or indirectly with positively charged components of salivary and crevicular fluid macromolecules. Within a few hours of pellicle formation, bacteria colonise the pellicle-coated tooth surface. These initial colonisers are mainly gram-positive microorganisms, such as Actinomyces viscosus and S. sanguinis. These primary colonisers adhere to the pellicle via specific surface molecules called adhesins, which interact with receptors in the dental pellicle. The major constituents of the pellicle include salivary glycoproteins, phosphoproteins, and lipids, such as statherin, amylase, and proline-rich peptides.53

For example, A. viscosus cells possess fibrous protein structures termed fimbriae, which extend from their surface. Protein adhesins on these fimbriae specifically bind to proline-rich proteins within the dental pellicle, facilitating bacterial attachment to the pellicle-coated enamel surface.45,54 Following initial colonisation, the plaque mass matures through the growth of these attached species and colonisation by additional microbial species. Microorganisms are predominantly transported passively to the tooth surface via saliva flow; few oral bacterial species are motile (eg, possessing flagella), mainly inhabiting subgingival sites. Dental plaque can typically be visualised on teeth after 1 to 2 days without oral hygiene measures. It appears white, grayish, or yellowish and has a globular morphology. Effective oral hygiene can remove these pellicle and plaque layers.55,56

Several treatment modalities aim to remove plaque and extrinsic stains; patient-friendly approaches are generally better accepted than clinical interventions are. Certain chemical toothpastes inhibit plaque adherence by altering the tooth surface environment. For example, hydrogen peroxide acts by releasing nascent oxygen, whereas abrasive agents such as baking soda or silica mechanically cleanse the tooth surface. Some toothpastes contain specific enzymes believed to degrade plaque and stains, thereby improving gingival health. These formulations are biocompatible with the tooth surface and surrounding soft tissues.57

The initial colonisers represent a highly selected subset of the oral microflora. Within minutes after pellicle formation, coccal bacteria primarily streptococci of the mitis group (eg, S. sanguinis, S. oralis, and S. mitis biovar) are detectable on the surface. S. sanguinis and S. oralis produce IgA1 protease, which may help these bacteria evade a key element of host immune defense during early plaque formation.58

Other species, such as Actinomyces spp., typically appear after approximately 2 hours, along with Haemophilus and Neisseria spp. Obligate anaerobic species are rarely detected at this stage and generally remain in low numbers.47 Mixed-cell aggregates may also attach concurrently. Once adhered, these pioneer populations initiate cell division and form microcolonies. These early colonisers become embedded within extracellular bacterial slimes and polysaccharides, mixed with additional layers of adsorbed salivary proteins and glycoproteins.59,60 The streptococcal mitis group possesses multiple glycosidase activities that enable them to interact with and utilise salivary glycoproteins as substrates. The highest rates of bacterial multiplication occur during these early stages of plaque development.47

In addition to maintaining good oral hygiene habits, several other effective measures are available to prevent dental plaque accumulation. These include reducing the intake of sugary and starchy foods and beverages, drinking sufficient amounts of water, and chewing sugar-free gum after meals to stimulate saliva production, which helps neutralise acids in the oral cavity.

The human oral cavity harbours over 500 distinct bacterial species spanning diverse phyla, such as Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, Tenericutes, Actinobacteria, Proteobacteria, Euryarchaeota, Chlamydiae, and Spirochaetes. Many of these microorganisms colonise the gingival sulci and tooth surfaces, forming biofilms that lead to dental plaque formation. The metabolic activities of these bacteria result in acid production, which demineralises enamel and causes caries and potentially infections. The diagnosis of oral bacterial infections is largely clinical, and antibiotics are often prescribed empirically for treatment or prophylaxis. However, definitive characterisation, precise diagnosis, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing are essential for guiding appropriate therapy and preventing disease progression.61
