Body > Material and Methods
Studies were selected based on inclusion criteria, specifically those that addressed third molar mineralization, the presence of impacted third molars, and age estimation based on dental development in adolescent and young adult samples, as well as the potential influence of impaction on the mineralization process or third molar development. There were no restrictions regarding the language of the articles or the type of imaging examination used. Exclusion criteria included systematic reviews, meta-analyses, books or book chapters, papers that have been presented at a conference and subsequently included in that conference's published proceedings, dissertations, thesis, and case reports. In addition, in vitro studies, studies involving cells, animals, or drug interventions were excluded, as well as studies that analyzed teeth other than the third molar or included pediatric samples.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Material and Methods
The studies retrieved from the database search were imported into the Rayyan application (https://www.rayyan.ai/) for duplicate removal and implementation of eligibility criteria. Subsequently, the study selection process was carried out based on title and abstract, respectively. The selection was performed by two independent reviewers, and any disagreements between them were discussed and resolved through consensus meetings. For the included studies, the reviewers independently conducted full-text reading, and any differences regarding the study selection were solved through discussions and analyses of eligibility criteria.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Material and Methods
After screening by title, abstract, and full-text reading, the relevant extracted data were tabulated using Microsoft Excel© (Microsoft Corp., Redmond, WA, USA). The extracted information included: study identification, year of publication, study title, scientific journal, sample size, method, country of origin, sex, age, type of tooth and whether an influence of impaction on tooth mineralization was identified.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Material and Methods
The risk of bias in the selected studies was independently assessed by the reviewers using the approach proposed by The Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) (20). For a thorough analysis, the reviewers answered eight pre-established questions, each with four possible responses: “yes,” “no,” “unclear,” or “not applicable.” This process allows for a critical appraisal of the studies, ensuring that they meet quality methodological standards.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Material and Methods
Accordingly, studies were classified as having a high risk of bias (when the percentage of “yes” responses was less than or equal to 49%), moderate risk of bias (between 50% and 69%), and low risk of bias (greater than 70%). In cases of disagreement between reviewers’ responses, the divergences were discussed, resolved, and a consensus response was established. Finally, the risk of bias for each selected study was calculated.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Results
A total of 5,314 studies were identified across the six databases. Among these, 1,280 potential duplicates were identified, of which 715 were confirmed and removed, resulting in 4,599 studies to be screened by title. Following the initial analysis, there was disagreement between reviewers regarding the selection of 12 studies based on their titles. These cases were discussed and solved jointly using the eligibility criteria. As a result, 150 studies were included at this stage, and 4,449 were excluded. The next step was abstract screening, which resulted in 33 studies being selected for full-text reading.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Results
Upon full-text reading, it was found that one study was a systematic review and another literature review; both were only identified at this stage. Access to two studies was requested from the corresponding authors, but no response was received, and ten studies were not fully available in databases, resulting in the exclusion of 14 studies. Thus, a total of 19 studies were initially included for the development of this systematic review. Of these, eight studies were excluded because they addressed the influence of third molar impaction from a purely clinical perspective, which did not align with the purpose of this systematic review. In the end, 11 articles met the inclusion and exclusion criteria and were selected for data extraction and tabulation using Microsoft Excel© (Microsoft Corp., Redmond, WA, USA) (Figure 1).

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Results
After data extraction from the 11 studies, it was observed that all of them evaluated third molars. The difference lay in the position of the dental element: six studies assessed both upper and lower third molars, while five studies focused exclusively on lower third molars. Regarding the age range of the individuals analyzed in the article, it is relevant to highlight that the youngest age evaluated was 10 years in the article by Olze et al. (2012), (17) while the oldest was 40 years in the study by Olze, Otto e Tsokos (2012) (21). In this regard, it is important to emphasize that, although Olze, Otto, and Tsokos (2012) (21) included individuals up to 40 years of age in their sample, it is expected that by this age the third molar has already completed its development, regardless of whether it is impacted or not. In other words, impaction may cause a delay in the mineralization process, postponing the attainment of the final stage of development, but it does not prevent it from occurring.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
By the time an individual reaches adulthood, in the second decade of life, the eruptive process of the dentition has typically ceased except for the third molar, which has a prolonged period of development and maturation, and is also susceptible to impaction. According to Balla et al. (2022), (22) third molar impaction has a high prevalence in the Indian population, which is relevant when discussing the impact of mineralization on age estimation. In conducting this systematic review, some studies were selected that addressed the potential influence of impaction on the mineralization process or development of the third molar and its applicability in age estimation.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
Dental impaction is a dental condition in which teeth do not erupt properly and fail to achieve correct positioning within the oral cavity (28, 29). In general, the third molar shows a higher prevalence of impaction in the lower dental arch (28-32), and it is believed that third molar impaction specifically occurs due to a reduction in mandibular size, thereby preventing proper positioning of the tooth within the dental arch (32).

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
In 1956, Björk et al. (33) investigated the causes of third molar retention using lateral cephalometric radiographs in Swedish male individuals. In the first phase of dental evaluation, the participants were 12 years old, and in the second phase they were 20 years old. The objective was to assess whether the mineralization of the retained teeth was significantly delayed (33). More recently, Idris et al. (2021), (32), emphasized that the causes of dental impaction may range from skeletal growth patterns to dietary habits.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
According to Marchiori et al. (2016), there is a correlation between the lack of space in the dental arches for root development—particularly the absence of space in the retromolar region—and the impaction of the lower third molar. Furthermore, this study found that such impaction affects the rate of the mineralization process. Gopalaiah et al. (2022), (25) analyzed the relationship between eruption delay and the type of impaction, but this association proved to be weak and not significant in some of the developmental stages assessed. Other studies, such as those by Friedrich et al. (2003) (6), Meghana et al. (2022) (26), Guo et al. (2014) (2), Balla et al. (2022) (22), and Olze et al. (2010) (18), investigated additional contributing factors. These include the mineralization stage of the third molar, crown size, mandibular positioning, genetic factors, available space, and individual stages of skeletal maturation. Thus, although all studies addressed the prolonged time required for third molar development, the influence of dental impaction on mineralization rate remains a subject of ongoing debate, as discussed by the authors across different population groups and using varied methodologies (2, 6, 8, 18, 21-23, 25-27).

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
Lauesen et al. (2013), (23), applied the method proposed by Haavikko et al. (1970), (24), which evaluates 12 stages of dental development; six related to crown formation and six to root development. Meanwhile, Balla et al. (2022), (22), used the method introduced by Cameriere et al. (2008), (12), which estimates dental maturation by measuring tooth length and the openings of the root apices. The remaining studies applied the method proposed by Demirjian et al. (1973) (13), based on the process of tooth mineralization. This method was originally developed for dental age estimation using seven permanent mandibular teeth, excluding third molars. Its widespread use may be attributed to the possibility of assessing the effect of impaction at each developmental stage defined in the classification. However, it is important to distinguish between the original method and Demirjian’s developmental scale (stages A–H), which describes general phases of tooth mineralization and is not tooth-specific. Thus, although the original method did not include third molars, the developmental scale can be applied to them, thereby extending the applicability of mineralization-based dental age estimation.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
In total, eight studies adopted this methodology, applying the developmental scale described by Demirjian et al. (1973), (13) to evaluate the stage of development of the third molars (2, 6, 17, 18, 21, 25-27). As shown in Table 2, most studies found an influence of dental impaction on mineralization. However, studies (2, 6, 17, 18, 21, 25-27) that applied the method proposed by Demirjian et al. (1973) (13) reported only small differences between developmental stages in both impacted and non-impacted teeth. The study conducted by Guo et al. (2022), (2) in a population from northwest China, which employed Demirjian’s method (13), showed that the mean ages of individuals with impacted third molars at stages C-H were higher than those with non-impacted third molars. The results demonstrated that impacted third molars in the Chinese population reached mineralization stages C–H later than non-impacted molars, reflecting delayed mineralization associated with impaction. Similarly, Meghana et al. (2022), (26) demonstrated that there was a developmental delay in impacted molars compared to non-impacted ones in stages D-H of the Demirjian´s developmental scale method (13).

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
Thus, it is evident that each study demonstrated some degree of influence of impaction on the mineralization process, whether to a greater or lesser extent but at different stages of the Demirjian´s developmental scale method (13). These differences in the point at which impaction interfere with third molar mineralization may be attributed to sociogeographic variations among the populations analyzed (34, 35) (Table 2). Guo et al. (2014), (2) for example examined a population from northwest China and found that impacted third molars mineralized more slowly than non-impacted ones. This finding was similar to those reported in European populations studied by Knell and Schmeling (2010), (18) in African male populations analyzed by Olze et al. (2012), (17) and in the Lebanese population investigated by Angelakopoulos et al. (2023), (27).

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
In addition, a difference in impaction between lower and upper third molars was observed in several studies (8, 17, 26, 27), with a higher prevalence of impaction in the lower third molars. Regarding the type of tooth selected for analysis, some studies focused exclusively on the lower third molars, such as those by Angelakopoulos et al. (2023), (27); Meghana et al. (2022), (26); Marchiori et al. (2016), (8) and Knell and Schmeling (2010), (18) (Table 2). Studies that examined all four third molars such as Gopalaiah et al. (2022), (25); Guo et al. (2014), (2); Friedrich et al. (2003), (6); Balla et al. (2022), (22); Olze et al. (2012), (17) and Olze, Otto and Tsokos (2012), (21) did not identify significant differences specifically in impacted upper third molars, but rather confirmed a tendency for impaction to occur more frequently in the lower third molars (22) (Table 2).

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
Friedrich et al. (2003), (6) analyzed all four third molars, focusing on the differences in root mineralization. Their study demonstrated that upper molars are more advanced than their antagonists, completing their full development approximately six months earlier.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
The most recent study included in this review that met the eligibility criteria was conducted by Angelakopoulos et al. (2023), (27) using a sample from the Lebanese population, while the earliest study was by Friedrich et al. (2003), (6) based on a German population. Both studies confirmed the effect of impaction on third molar mineralization in their respective populations, the former in relation to the entire dental element, and the latter specifically in relation to the root. However, in the study by Angelakopoulos et al. (2023), (27) the difference in mineralization timing between impacted and non-impacted third molars was not statistically significant.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
Furthermore, Angelakopoulos et al. (2023), (27) observed that dental impaction holds greater relevance for clinical practice in dentistry than for its application in dental age estimation. This is because, in forensic analysis, preference is given to non-impacted teeth, as they are more likely to exhibit normal developmental patterns, thereby allowing the chosen methodology to be applied with greater reliability (27).

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
It is evident that the mineralization process of the third molar in age estimation has been studied for a long time, using various methodologies and across different populations (2, 6, 17, 18, 21, 25-27, 36). Research such as Shi et al. (2024) (37) that compare the methods of Olze, Haavikko, and Demirjian show that methodological accuracy can vary considerably according to the population, thus highlighting the importance of specific validations for each group.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
Therefore, when analyzing different populations, the applied methodology may or may not exhibit adequate compatibility and accuracy. Its precision can be influenced by factors such as geographic region, age range, and sex, as well as the presence of syndromes or other systemic conditions that affect dental development. Consequently, specific population characteristics, such as regional variations, age differences, as observed in the study by Olze, Otto, and Tsokos (2012) (21); sexual dimorphism, or alterations associated with systemic diseases, may result in distinct patterns of third molar development. In this context, Pereira et al. (2019) (38) aimed to estimate the chronological age of a population with special needs, recognizing that certain syndromes and clinical conditions can modify the expected pattern of dental mineralization, which may impact the application and interpretation of age estimation methods.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
Thus, impaction of this tooth and its associated slowing effect on mineralization may influence the accuracy of age estimation methods. Most of the studies included in this systematic review confirm this association, although the impaction occurs at different stages of dental development depending on the population analyzed (2, 6, 17, 18, 21-23, 25-27, 34).

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
However, the factor responsible for this effect on mineralization may be related to specific genetic or phenotypic characteristics of each population analyzed (2, 6, 8, 17, 21, 22, 25-27). Another perspective is the possibility that human evolution is moving toward the eventual disappearance of this organ. Studies such as those by Björk et al. (1956), (33); Carter and Worthington (2015), (39); Marchiori et al. (2016), (8); Raloti et al. (2013), (40); Scheiwiller et al. (2020), (41) and Kanavakis et al. (2024), (42) the retromolar space and how the reduction in mandibular size affects the eruption of this tooth into the dental arch, potentially resulting in impaction, dental anomalies, and agenesis of this tooth. Nevertheless, the exact determinant responsible for the differences observed among populations regarding mineralization stages, particularly the delayed development of impacted third molars, remains unclear (2, 6, 17, 18, 21-23, 25-27, 34-36, 43).

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
A systematic review and meta-analysis conducted by Balla et al. (2025) (44) addressed the effect of impaction on the mineralization of third molars, with a focus on forensic age estimation. The study reached a conclusion similar to the present study: impaction delays the development of the lower third molar compared to non-impacted teeth. This delay in maturation time is consistently reported in the studies analyzed (2, 6, 8, 17, 18, 21, 22, 25-27).

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
Our systematic review and the study published by Balla et al. (2025), (44) address the same topic, although Balla et al. (2025), (44) formulated a different research question. Both investigations searched similar databases, including PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, SciELO, Scopus, and Web of Science. The main methodological difference is that the present review also included the Lilacs database, whereas Balla et al. (2025), (44) consulted the Open Access Theses and Dissertations (OATD). Minor discrepancies in the number of retrieved articles are further explained by the use of different keywords in each search strategy. In our systematic review, a meta-analysis was not performed due to the limited number of articles identified and considered potentially eligible for such an analysis.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
Despite these differences, it is important to highlight that both, our study and that of Balla et al. (2025), (44) demonstrate that impacted third molars exhibit a slower process of dental development and maturation. Therefore, the delayed mineralization associated with third molar impaction must be taken into account when this tooth is used in age estimation methodologies. In other words, impacted third molars should not be preferred for analysis in forensic assessments, especially when other options are available (27). This delay in the mineralization process may influence the size of the pulp chamber, root pulp, root formation time, and apical closure, all of which are features commonly used in dental age estimation methods (2, 6, 17, 18, 21-23, 25-27, 36).

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Discussion
Methods such as those of Cameriere et al. (2008), (12) which perform measurements of root apex openings and tooth length; those of Köhler et al. (1994), (10) and Gunst et al. (2003), (11) both based on root development observed in orthopantomographs and on the classification of root formation stages and apical closure; and the method of Demirjian et al. (1973), (13) which uses crown and root formation stages, are proposed methods for age estimation based on the third molar tooth. The latter was adopted by most studies included in this systematic review to identify at which stage of development impaction acted as a factor in slowing down the mineralization process.

Third Molar Impaction Influence on Dental Estimation: A Systemic Review
Body > Conclusion
It can be concluded that third molar impaction may be associated with delayed dental mineralization, although the current scientific evidence remains inconsistent. Consequently, caution is advised when using impacted third molars as indicators for dental age estimation, as their use may lead to underestimation of chronological age.

This review adhered to PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies published within the last eight years were screened across multiple databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, and Science Direct. The studies eligible were: randomized controlled trials; cohort; and longitudinal designs comparing PRP with other treatment modalities of which six clinical studies were included which had 129 participants in total. Abstract > Results:
Clinically, both control and intervention groups exhibited a pooled mean difference of 0.61, 95% CI (0.22-0.99). As there were variations within the studies, the fixed effects model was chosen for analysis. Comparative analysis of the results demonstrated that both the platelet-based therapies and the topical corticosteroid approach improved patient satisfaction and comparably reduced pain and lesion size in individuals with erosive OLP in similar measures.

Efficiency of platelet-rich plasma in management of oral lichen planus: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Abstract > Conclusion:
Oral lichen planus can be safely and perhaps effectively treated with platelet-rich plasma. Future studies should adopt a standardised approach in evaluating efficacy of PRP in OLP. Rigorous clinical trials less heterogeneity in the methodology is required for high-quality evidence.

Beyond that, OLP poses a 0.5% to 2% risk of malignant transformation, which is particularly prevalent in middle-aged women (female-to-male ratio of 2:1). 2 The essential search for a definitive intervention that achieves a complete and sustained cure for OLP remains a primary concern. 3

In addition to pain relief, some of the included studies also yielded positive outcomes on lesion size reduction and mucosal healing. Again, since measurement methods as well as scores varied, these results could not be combined quantitatively. Recurrence rates post-PRP therapy also were not consistently reported among the studies, so we could conclude little about the long-term persistence of the effect achieved. 11 There was one study that reported a statistically significant superiority for the injectable PRF group over the steroid group. Conversely, a separate included study noted that patients treated with PRP exhibited higher rates of disease recurrence and adverse effects compared to those treated with intralesional triamcinolone acetonide (TA) after three months of follow-up. Results of our review are consistent with earlier reports that emphasize PRP's autologous nature and low immunogenicity. 18-20 However, it was also noted that the included studies had small sample sizes, with lack of blinding or placebo controls along with shorter follow-up period. There was wide variation in PRP preparation methods (single spin vs. double spin), platelet concentration and its application technique (topical vs. injectable). 21-24 This makes direct comparisons and pooled analysis more challenging.

Efficiency of platelet-rich plasma in management of oral lichen planus: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > DISCUSSION > Clinical Implication
Our systematic review and meta-analysis suggest that Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) yields significant improvements in pain relief (measured by Visual Analog Scale (VAS) scores), lesion size decrease or mucosal healing, as well as global patient satisfaction and quality of life. 25,26 This is similar to the findings from few other studies which observed faster healing and decreased symptoms after PRP treatment in erosive OLP. 27,28 However, it was also noted that the included studies had small sample sizes, with a lack of blinding or placebo controls and short follow-up durations. Hence, future studies with more stringent protocols, large sample size and long term follow up are recommended.

Efficiency of platelet-rich plasma in management of oral lichen planus: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > DISCUSSION > Strength and Limitations
This review has several strengths, including the comprehensive search strategy, rigorous inclusion criteria, and quantitative synthesis of outcomes where possible. Unlike earlier narrative or scoping reviews, our study conducts a quantitative meta-analysis, adding a higher level of evidence. 29,30

Efficiency of platelet-rich plasma in management of oral lichen planus: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > DISCUSSION > Strength and Limitations
However, there are important limitations that must be acknowledged. Included studies showed small sample sizes, limited follow-up intervals, and variable PRP methods of production, which added clinical heterogeneity and affected the generalizability of the results. Direct comparisons were also difficult due to inconsistent result reporting and different methods of scoring used to evaluate clinical improvement.

Efficiency of platelet-rich plasma in management of oral lichen planus: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > CONCLUSION
The results of our systematic review suggest that platelet-rich plasma is a potentially efficacious and safe treatment modality for oral lichen planus, specifically regarding alleviation of pain as well as mucosal healing improvement. However, due to methodological variation as well as the lack of high-quality evidence, further rigorous clinical trials must be carried out to confirm these inferences and establish standardized guidelines for treatment.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Abstract > Background
Oral mucosal diseases include autoimmune, inflammatory, and infectious disorders that can substantially affect patients’ physical, psychological, and social well-being. Psychological factors are reported to influence oral health-related quality of life in affected individuals, particularly through pain, visible lesions, and impaired social functioning.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Abstract > Methods
This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261288659). The review question was structured using the PECO framework. Population included patients with oral mucosal diseases, specifically recurrent aphthous ulcer, oral lichen planus, oral leukoplakia, and oral submucous fibrosis. Exposures included psychological factors such as distress, depression, anxiety, and psychological interventions. Comparators were patients without psychological intervention or healthy controls. Outcomes were oral health-related quality of life and patient-reported psychological status. Six electronic databases, including CNKI, WanFang Data, PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library, were searched from inception to 30 August 2025, limited to English or Chinese studies. Eligible studies included cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional studies involving patients with diagnosed oral mucosal diseases and clearly reported outcomes. Risk of bias, heterogeneity, and evidence certainty were assessed using design-appropriate tools.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Abstract > Results
A total of 468 records were identified. After removal of 183 duplicates, 235 records were excluded during title and abstract screening and 11 were excluded following full-text review. Ultimately, 39 studies published between 2014 and 2025 were included in the final synthesis. Thematic analysis identified three major domains: Disease characteristics, psychological factors, and quality-of-life outcomes. Across oral mucosal disease subtypes, the included studies suggested a close association between disease burden, psychological distress, and poorer patient-reported outcomes.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Abstract > Conclusion
Psychological factors are influential to oral health-related quality of life in patients with oral mucosal diseases. Combining generic and disease-specific assessment tools could support a more comprehensive evaluation of psychological status and quality of life. Greater awareness of psychological problems, together with symptom management and social support, could help improve overall well-being and quality of life in this population.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Background
Oral mucosal diseases (OMDs) are a group of disorders affecting the oral mucosa and associated soft tissues. These conditions typically present as various lesions triggered by multifactorial influences [1]. OMDs are recognized as psychosomatic conditions, involving complex interactions between physiological and psychological factors. These disorders are fairly prevalent and are frequently associated with substantial psychological, physical, and social burdens. Impairments in oral functions caused by OMDs can lead to reduced life satisfaction, heightened emotional distress, and diminished overall well-being [2]. Consequently, quality of life (QoL) is often significantly compromised, particularly in areas related to oral functionality, facial appearance, and social interaction.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Background
Despite the substantial disease burden, most OMDs are managed symptomatically, with limited attention paid to psychological issues or oral health-related quality of life (OHRQoL). Approximately 30% of patients exhibit psychopathological symptoms, which often go unrecognized and untreated [3]. Addressing the psychological issues of patients with OMDs is crucial to improve overall OHRQoL. However, existing research remains limited, as it lacks in-depth exploration of the pathways linking psychological factors to OMDs progression and OHRQoL decline, sufficient high-quality long-term randomized controlled trials (RCTs) validating psychological intervention efficacy for specific OMDs subtypes, and unified OMDs-specific protocols for psychological comorbidity screening and integrated care. Further studies are warranted to elucidate the underlying mechanisms by which psychological factors affect quality of life and to develop tailored psychosocial interventions that promote recovery, emotional well-being, and long-term life satisfaction in affected individuals.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Methods
This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the “Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis” (PRISMA 2020 statement) [4], with its protocol prospectively registered on PROSPERO (ID: CRD420261288659). The review question was defined using the PECO framework: Population-Patients with OMDs, specifically Recurrent Aphthous Ulcers (RAU), Oral Lichen Planus (OLP), Oral Leukoplakia (OLK), and Oral Submucous Fibrosis (OSF); Exposure-Psychological factors (anxiety, depression, fear of disease progression) and psychological interventions; Comparator- OMDs patients without psychological intervention or healthy controls; Outcome-OHRQoL scores, clinical disease outcomes, and neuroendocrine/immune mediators. The review also assessed the clinical applicability of various OHRQoL assessment tools to these populations. Body > Methods > Risk of bias assessment
Two reviewers independently assessed the methodological quality of the included studies using standardized tools. Specifically, the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool was used for randomized controlled trials, and the COnsensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement INstruments(COSMIN) Risk of Bias checklist was applied to evaluate the measurement properties of the patient-reported outcome measures. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion until a consensus was reached or, when necessary, by arbitration from a third reviewer. For details, see Appendix Tables 1 and 2.

Body > Methods > Literature search
A comprehensive search was conducted across six databases: CNKI, WanFang Data, PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library. Keywords included “oral mucosal diseases,” “psychology,” “oral health-related quality of life,” “RAU,” “OLP,” “OLK,” “OSF,” and relevant assessment tools.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Methods > Study retrieval
The initial database search identified a total of 468 studies (CNKI: 68, WanFang Data: 143, PubMed: 88, Web of Science: 41, Scopus: 61, Cochrane: 67). After removing 183 duplicate records, 285 unique records remained. In the first screening, two reviewers (WU, GAO) independently assessed the titles and abstracts of these 285 records, excluding 235 studies that were clearly irrelevant to the research topic. This resulted in 50 full-text articles that were then assessed for eligibility. During the full-text evaluation, 11 articles were excluded: 9 due to inadequate results and 2 due to unclear research questions. Ultimately, 39 studies were selected for inclusion in this review, ensuring a balanced representation of both domestic and international perspectives on OMDs (Fig. 1).

Body > Methods > Data synthesis
A structured narrative synthesis was undertaken to synthesize evidence on the psychological factors modulating OHRQoL in four core OMD subtypes (RAU, OLP, OLK, OSF). This synthesis focused on two key themes: The clinical applicability of generic and disease-specific OHRQoL assessment tools for each subtype, and the psychometric performance of these tools in capturing subtype-unique psychological burdens and distress. Additionally, mechanistic links between psychological factors and OMD pathogenesis, and their implications for OHRQoL, were integrated into the synthesis to inform clinical translation.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Results > Four common categories of oral mucosal diseases in outpatient settings > Recurrent Aphthous Ulcers (RAU)
RAU, also known as recurrent aphthous stomatitis, is the most prevalent type of oral mucosal disease, affecting approximately 25% of the general population [5]. RAU is characterized by repeated episodes of painful ulcers on the oral mucosa. The lesions are typically round or oval with yellow centers and erythematous borders, often described by the clinical features of “yellow, red, depressed, and painful [6]”. It is characterized by its periodicity, recurrence, and self-limiting nature.

heading_path: Four common categories of oral mucosal diseases in outpatient settings
content:
Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Results > Four common categories of oral mucosal diseases in outpatient settings > Recurrent Aphthous Ulcers (RAU)
During disease flare-ups, RAU significantly impairs essential oral functions such as chewing, swallowing, and phonation, which in turn hinders social interaction and deteriorates patients’ mood [7]. In severe or prolonged cases, patients may experience increased ulcer size and number, exacerbated pain, prolonged healing time, and shortened remission periods [8], all of which collectively compromise oral function and reduce overall quality of life. The high recurrence rate and associated pain of RAU often lead to social withdrawal, communication difficulties, and negative emotional responses, with psychological factors closely intertwined with disease pathogenesis through complex neuroendocrine and immunological pathways.

heading_path: Four common categories of oral mucosal diseases in outpatient settings
content:
Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Results > Four common categories of oral mucosal diseases in outpatient settings > Oral Lichen Planus (OLP)
OLP is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the oral mucosa, predominantly affecting women aged 30–60 years with a global prevalence of approximately 0.5%–3% [9]. Clinically heterogeneous, OLP is classified as a potentially malignant disorder by the WHO, with a malignant transformation rate of up to 2% [10]. It can involve any site of the oral mucosa (most commonly the buccal mucosa) and typically presents as bilateral, symmetrical gray-white papules forming reticular, annular, or plaque-like patterns [11], which may be accompanied by erythema, atrophy, ulceration, or vesicles [12].

heading_path: Four common categories of oral mucosal diseases in outpatient settings
content:
Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Results > Four common categories of oral mucosal diseases in outpatient settings > Oral Lichen Planus (OLP)
Immune dysregulation is recognized as the central pathogenic driver of OLP, with genetic, infectious, and psychosocial factors also contributing [13]. Patients with OLP frequently report oral discomfort, such as persistent burning or stinging pain, which—combined with the chronic disease course, limited therapeutic efficacy, and fear of malignant transformation—impairs daily functioning and quality of life. Psychological factors further modulate disease progression and patient well-being through bidirectional interactions with the immune system and mucosal microenvironment.

heading_path: Four common categories of oral mucosal diseases in outpatient settings
content:
Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Results > Four common categories of oral mucosal diseases in outpatient settings > Oral Leukoplakia (OLK)
OLK is defined as non-scrapable white lesions of the oral mucosa that cannot be clinically or histopathologically diagnosed as any other specific disorder [14, 15]. As a potentially malignant lesion, it excludes reversible white patches caused by identifiable local factors such as tobacco use, alcohol consumption, or mechanical irritation [16]. OLK is most common in individuals aged 40–69 years [17], with high-risk groups including those with long-term habits of smoking, alcohol consumption, betel nut chewing, or intake of excessively hot or spicy foods [18, 19].

heading_path: Four common categories of oral mucosal diseases in outpatient settings
content:
Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Results > Four common categories of oral mucosal diseases in outpatient settings > Oral Leukoplakia (OLK)
Reported malignant transformation rates of OLK range from 0.13% to 17.5% [18]. This cancer risk, together with persistent pain from keratinized or ulcerated lesions, significantly impacts patients’ daily lives, as involuntary chewing or stimulation of lesion areas can induce spontaneous or provoked pain, interfering with eating and routine activities [20]. Psychological distress, often exacerbated by concerns over malignant transformation and high-risk behavior-related guilt, further compromises patient outcomes.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Results > Four common categories of oral mucosal diseases in outpatient settings > Oral Submucous Fibrosis (OSF)
OSF is a potentially malignant disorder characterized by mucosal burning sensations, recurrent ulcers, vesicles, and progressive fibrosis of oral and oropharyngeal tissues [6]. The fibrotic process leads to mucosal pallor, restricted mouth opening, severe oral dysfunction, and compromised QoL, with a 7%–13% risk of malignant transformation to oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) [21, 22]. It constitutes a major global public health concern, particularly in East and Southeast Asia where betel nut chewing is prevalent.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Results > Four common categories of oral mucosal diseases in outpatient settings > Oral Submucous Fibrosis (OSF)
The progressive functional impairment of OSF—including restricted jaw mobility and difficulties in eating and speaking—combined with its strong association with betel nut addiction, imposes a unique burden on patients. Betel nut chewing serves as a key etiological factor, while psychological stress and addiction-related distress further perpetuate disease progression through neuroendocrine-mediated fibrotic pathways [23, 24] (Fig. 2; Table 2).

Over the past two decades, research into the associations between psychological factors and OHRQoL in patients with OMDs has advanced substantially. Global multicenter investigations link psychological factors to OMDs etiology using validated instruments like the HADS and Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10) [32, 34]. Anxiety and depression heighten disease susceptibility through inflammatory dysregulation, with observational data confirming reciprocal OHRQoL impacts [63, 64]. Chinese research adapts tools to cultural contexts, such as validating OHRQoL scales for oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs) [53, 65], whereas international studies emphasize immune-neuroendocrine interactions [36].

RAU has adverse psychological impact, including anxiety and depression [5, 41]. Patients were found to exhibit social withdrawal, communication difficulties, and emotional disorders such as anxiety and depression [43]. Other research has explored psychological triggers of RAU, particularly the correlation between mental state and ulcer occurrence [42, 44]. Compared to healthy individuals, RAU patients tend to score higher on self-rating scales for anxiety and depression, indicating a strong association between RAU and negative psychological states. Such psychological burdens contribute to the reduced oral health status and overall quality of life in affected individuals [66]. Additional mechanistic evidence indicates that RAU-related chronic pain triggers anticipatory anxiety and social avoidance due to eating-related embarrassment [2].

Similarly, for OLP, current research has established its association with anxiety and depression [67, 68]. Due to chronic oral pain, prolonged disease course, limited therapeutic effects, and fear of malignancy, many patients experience fatigue, psychological stress, and cancer-related anxiety [45], which together impair mental well-being and reduce quality of life. Unlike RAU, the psychological mediation of QoL decline in OLP is intertwined with its chronic, potentially malignant, and immune-mediated pathology, primarily via OLP-specific psychoneuroimmunological (PNI) pathways driven by cancer-related anxiety, chronic stress, and depression. A key trigger is fear of malignant transformation (FMT), which induces hypervigilance, catastrophic thinking, and avoidance of follow-ups, escalating distress independent of lesion severity [47, 69]. Additionally, OLP’s persistent burning/stinging pain—distinct from RAU’s ulcerative pain—and incurable course lead to helplessness, impairing the social and emotional dimensions of patients’ QoL [49]. Psychological distress in OLK interacts with etiological agents and malignant transformation risk, transcending a simplistic psychology-immunity loop. The predominant psychological load stems from deterministic anxiety over malignant transformation—differing from OLP’s ambiguous malignancy fear—eliciting excessive prognostic apprehension, hypervigilance toward lesions, and catastrophic cognitions [71, 72]. OLK’s strong association with high-risk behaviors (e.g., tobacco use, betel quid chewing, alcohol consumption) engender guilt and shame from unsuccessful cessation attempts, compounded by social avoidance, thereby intensifying distress and isolation—notably absent in OLP or RAU [73]. Chronic anxiety undermines adherence to habit modification, sustaining carcinogen exposure (e.g., tobacco-derived nitrosamines, arecoline), which accelerates keratinocyte hyperproliferation and hyperkeratosis, advancing lesions toward dysplasia [52].

OSF is accompanied by anxiety. It imposes a unique dual psychological burden tied to its etiology: first, anxiety from progressive functional impairment, as advancing fibrosis tightens the mucosa and restricts jaw mobility, triggering despair over impending eating/speaking dysfunction—distinct from OLK-related fear of malignant transformation or RAU-associated recurrence anxiety [56]; second, guilt from entrenched betel quid addiction (more severe than in OLK), driven by conflicting awareness of its carcinogenicity amid failed cessation attempts, and compounded by social stigma from oral rigidity and pallor [54]. OSF correlates with anxiety, depression, and areca nut dependence, with sociodemographic factors modulating these psychological burdens; notably, addiction severity and functional anxiety independently predict OHRQoL deficits post-adjustment for fibrosis and pain [38, 51, 74, 75], and research on OSF-OHRQoL links remains nascent [39].

A key distinction between domestic and international research on psychological factors in OMDs lies in their focuses. International studies predominantly center on exploring the underlying neuroendocrine-immune mechanisms linking psychological distress to OMD onset, progression, and malignant transformation, while employing standardized, validated assessment tools (e.g., HADS, PSS-10, OHIP-14) across multicenter cohorts to ensure the generalizability and comparability of findings [32–34, 39]. In contrast, Chinese research prioritizes the adaptation and validation of psychological and OHRQoL assessment tools to fit cultural contexts (e.g., OHRQoL scales tailored for OPMDs) and the investigation of psychological burden profiles specific to domestic OMD subtypes (e.g., betel quid addiction-related guilt in OSF, malignancy-related anxiety in OLK) [20, 53]. Limitations of current domestic research include relatively small sample sizes and single-center designs, which hinder the generalizationof results, whereas international studies are constrained by potential inconsistencies in the cultural adaptability of assessment tools, e.g., when applied to Asian populations with distinct etiological characteristics (e.g., high betel quid consumption in OSF patients) [24]. The bidirectional relationship between psychological factors and OMDs involves complex pathophysiological pathways. Chronic stress activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, raising cortisol levels that impair immune function and heighten inflammation, promoting OMDs development and progression [63].

In RAU, anxiety correlates with salivary cortisol-dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) imbalance, inhibiting epithelial proliferation and increasing mucosal vulnerability via stress-induced release of IL-6 and TNF-α, which amplifies inflammation and pain sensitivity [7, 76]. Biomarkers link elevated cortisol, reduced DHEA, and OHRQoL decline in RAU, creating cycles where negative affect aggravates disease chronicity. For OLP, psychosocial stressors trigger T-cell-mediated autoimmune responses, inducing erosive lesions; HPA and sympathetic activation disrupts Th1/Th2/Th17 balance, elevating cortisol and catecholamines to favor proinflammatory shifts, boost autoantibodies, increase lymphocytic infiltration, and promote keratinocyte apoptosis through cytokines like IL-1β, IFN-γ, and TNF-α [25, 50, 77]. In OLK and OPMDs, depression-related oxidative stress accelerates carcinogenesis via genetic and epigenetic changes; stress engages the sympathetic-adrenal medullary axis, upregulating proliferation genes (e.g., Cyclin D1), perpetuating keratinocyte hyperproliferation, hyperkeratosis, and dysplasia amid sustained carcinogen exposure from

OSF features anxiety, depression, and areca nut dependence synergistically intensifying fibrosis; elevated cortisol activates the fibroblast TGF-β/Smad pathway, upregulating TGF-β, accelerating collagen cross-linking, and inhibiting matrix degradation, forming a vicious cycle of stress-induced fibrosis and functional decline unrelated to episodic inflammation in RAU or T-cell dysregulation in OLP [57–59].

Mental health-focused strategies aim to mitigate OMDs impacts, often using assessment tools for baseline and endpoint evaluations. Globally, cognitive behavioral therapy, stress modulation, and relaxation techniques improve outcomes, with pain scales sensitively reflecting changes [78]. Such approaches can be tailored to OMD subtypes and patient psychological profiles based on mechanistic links between psychological stress and disease pathogenesis. For RAU, where HPA axis activation and IL-6/TNF-α upregulation drive mucosal inflammation and ulcer recurrence, clinicians should prioritize anxiety screening and deliver CBT to modulate stress responses, thereby reducing inflammatory activity and recurrence risk [42, 43]. In OLP, psychosocial stress-induced Th1/Th2/Th17 immune imbalance underscores the value of combining immune-modulating therapies with stress management interventions to alleviate erosive lesions and mitigate disease-related distress [45, 49]. Chinese methodologies integrate positive psychology (verbal reinforcement, video-assisted education) to enhance compliance and resilience [26, 30, 40]. Non-pharmacological interventions like music therapy effectively reduce depression in OPMD patients complemented by humanistic care that boosts satisfaction [27]. International strategies advocate interdisciplinary collaboration [55], differing from

In summary, psychological factors mediate OMDs pathophysiology and OHRQoL, calling for integrated assessments and subtype-tailored psychological intervention strategies Chinese burgeoning research addresses earlier gaps but remains predominantly observational with limited trial designs. International advances in mechanistic elucidation of stress-disease pathways provide critical models for cross-regional collaboration to refine evidence-based intervention frameworks. Future research should prioritize cultural impacts on stigma, multinational RCTs, and optimized assessment tools to advance patient-centered outcomes.

OHRQoL [79] refers to the impact of oral health status on an individual’s overall quality of life. It encompasses a comprehensive assessment from multiple dimensions, including physical, psychological, and social functioning. OHRQoL represents a subjective evaluation system aligned with modern health concepts and medical models. In 2016, the FDI World Dental Federation redefined oral health and officially included OHRQoL as a core component [80]. The OHIP [81] is widely used to assess OHRQoL in patients with oral mucosal diseases, aiming to combine objective clinical indicators with patients’ subjective experiences to guide individualized treatment strategies. However, the OHIP scale has certain limitations, such as its potential inability to fully capture disease-specific symptoms of rare oral mucosal disorders and its reliance on self-reported data which may be influenced by patients’ recall bias or subjective interpretation (Table 4).

Body > Results > Oral health-related quality of life instruments > OHIP-49 (Oral Health Impact Profile-49)
Among various OHRQoL instruments, the OHIP-49 [82] is one of the most comprehensive. It evaluates seven domains: Functional limitation, physical pain, psychological discomfort, physical disability, psychological disability, social disability, and handicap, with a total of 49 items. Each item is rated on a 5-point Likert scale (0 = never, 1 = hardly ever, 2 = occasionally, 3 = frequently, 4 = very often). Higher scores indicate poorer OHRQoL. The Chinese version of OHIP-49 was translated by Sun Yat-sen University in 2011 and has demonstrated good reliability and validity in both community and patient populations. It is widely used and regarded as one of the most accurate instruments for evaluating OHRQoL. Shortened versions of OHIP-49 have also been developed to apply to different research settings.

content:
Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Results > Oral health-related quality of life instruments > OHIP-14 (Oral Health Impact Profile-14)
Developed by Slade [83, 84] based on the OHIP-49, the OHIP-14 contains 14 self-reported items across four dimensions: Functional limitation (3 items), pain and discomfort (3 items), psychological discomfort (3 items), and reduced capability (5 items). It uses the same 5-point Likert scale. Selecting “frequently” or “very often” suggests a negative impact. The total score ranges from 0 to 56, with higher scores indicating worse OHRQoL [85]. The Chinese version was translated by Xin Weini and colleagues in 2006 [86], showing good reliability in the general population. Although widely used in dental, periodontal, malocclusion, and temporomandibular joint studies, its application in mucosal diseases remains limited, with validation mainly focused on OLP. Some rating categories of OHIP-14 fail to meet Rasch criteria for category functioning, and certain items lack local independence, with suboptimal reliability in some dimensions and weak invariance across different samples.

To enhance efficiency in epidemiological and clinical research, John et al. [86] proposed the OHIP-5, which includes five key items: Difficulty chewing, significant pain, discomfort during eating, taste disturbances, and limitations in daily activities. Though only 10% the length of OHIP-49, OHIP-5 captures nearly 90% of its information. Lv Hao et al. [87]. validated the Chinese version and recommended its broader application in clinical and population studies. OHIP-5 demonstrates insufficient internal consistency and only fair to good test-retest reliability, performing less well than OHIP-49 and OHIP-14 in psychometric properties.

Each item is rated on a 5-point Likert scale, with total scores ranging from 0 to 88. Higher scores reflect worse OHRQoL. For individual items, scores of 3 or 4 indicate a negative impact. Body > Results > Oral health-related quality of life instruments > SF-36 (Short Form Health Survey-36)
The SF-36 is a widely used generic health-related quality of life instrument [90]. It includes 36 items divided into eight dimensions: Physical functioning, role limitations due to physical health, bodily pain, general health perceptions, vitality, social functioning, role limitations due to emotional problems, and mental health. The first four form the Physical Component Summary (PCS), and the last four the Mental Component Summary (MCS). The total score reflects the overall quality of life, with higher scores indicating better outcomes. The Chinese version has good reliability and validity in oral health studies [91].

The SF-12 is a shortened version of SF-36, with 12 items covering the same eight dimensions [92]. It requires less time to complete and reduces respondent burden. The first four dimensions comprise PCS, and the remaining four form MCS. Although SF-12 has shown reliability and validity in the general Chinese population, its application in oral health remains limited and merits further exploration [93, 94].Comparing with SF-36, theSF-12 standard scoring algorithm incorrectly assumes uncorrelated physical and mental health, leading to score distortion and erroneous statistical inferences.

Body > Results > Oral health-related quality of life instruments > COMDQ (Chronic Oral Mucosal Disease Questionnaire)
In 2020, Wiriyakijja [95] developed the COMDQ-15, a shortened version of the original COMDQ for chronic OMDs. The Chinese version was created by Wang et al. [96], through translation and back-translation. The full COMDQ includes 26 items across four domains: Pain and functional limitations (9 items), treatment and medication effects (6 items), social and emotional impact (7 items), and support from others (4 items). Each item is scored from 0 to 4 (0 = not at all, 4 = extremely), with total scores ranging from 0 to 104. Higher scores indicate poorer quality of life. COMDQ can be used to evaluate pre- and post-treatment changes and assess sensitivity to interventions. Nevertheless, COMDQ scale has a significantly narrower application scope as it is only applicable to evaluating the quality of life related to chronic oral mucosal diseases and cannot be used for the general population or patients with other oral diseases.

All instruments are stratified by evidence strength to guide context-appropriate selection, with their core comparative advantages aligning to the heterogeneous clinical and research needs of OMD evaluation.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Results > Clinical significance
Given the significant role of psychological factors in OMDs, psychological assessment has become an important part of comprehensively evaluation of patients’ quality of life. OHRQoL is a multidimensional concept typically measured using well-established scales with proven reliability and validity, categorized into generic and disease-specific instruments. With ongoing research, various versions of OHIP scales have been developed, including disease-specific tools such as Oral Health Impact Profile for Oral Lichen Planus (OHIP-OLP) [99], the Oral Health Impact Profile for Temporomandibular Disorders (OHIP-TMD) [100], the Oral Health Impact Profile for Edentulous Patients (OHIP-EDENT) [101], the Oral Health Impact Profile for Denture Patients (OHIP-DP) [102], the Oral Health Impact Profile for partially edentate patients with Implant-supported prostheses(OHIP-I) [103], and the Oral Health Impact Profile for Chronic Periodontitis (OHIP-CP) [104]. These tools enable clinicians and researchers to better quantify the impact of oral diseases on patients’ quality of life.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Results > Clinical significance
These instruments assess how oral health affects functional ability, psychological state, and social interactions, providing a quantitative foundation to gauge the degree of life quality disruption. In clinical research, combining generic tools (e.g., OHIP-14 [36, 79]) with disease-specific scales (e.g., COMDQ-15 [95, 96] or Liverpool Oral Rehabilitation Questionnaire version 3(LORQv3) [105, 106]) is recommended to yield more comprehensive insights. Moreover, cross-cultural adaptation and local validation are essential to ensure scientific rigor and test applicability, particularly in international multicenter studies or cross-population comparisons. Clinically, use of OHRQoL instruments can facilitate the identification of mental health issues and support evidence-based adjustments to treatment strategies. Multidisciplinary collaboration and integration of mental health care into oral disease management will enhance patient outcomes and overall well-being. Digital health tools offering continuous support appears to be a promising direction for improving care in the future.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Results > Clinical significance
Nonetheless, current OHRQoL instruments have limitations: (1) Insufficient coverage of psychological domains, with many scales emphasizing functional or general quality of life over specific psychological aspects such as social anxiety and emotional distress; (2) limited cultural adaptability, as different populations may interpret questionnaire items differently; and (3) emphasis on symptoms and short-term outcomes, with less focus on long-term follow-up or evaluation of the effectiveness of psychological interventions on OMDs.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Discussion
This systematic review synthesizes evidence on the bidirectional interaction between psychological factors, OHRQoL, and four core oral mucosal disease (OMDs) subtypes—RAU, OLP, OLK, and OSF. The well-established links between OMDs and psychological issues has driven the need for systematic assessment, leading to the proliferation of OHRQoL tools [3, 71, 95, 107]. A critical insight is the inherent trade-off in OHRQoL tools: Generic scales (OHIP series, SF-36/SF-12) enable broad coverage and cross-disease comparability but lack the measure of subtype-specific burdens (e.g., OLK premalignant anxiety, OSF functional disability), while disease-targeted tools (OHIP-OLP, OHRQoL-OSF, COMDQ) enhance subtype-specific sensitivity yet hinder cross-subtype analyses [62, 83, 90, 91]. Given this trade-off and subtype-unique neuroendocrine-immune-behavioral pathways (e.g., HPA axis activation in RAU, TGF-β/Smad induction in OSF, comprehensive OMDs management must extend beyond symptom treatment to include subtype-specific psychological interventions and stratified OHRQoL tool selection in accordance with each subtype’s pathogenic and psychosocial profile [57].

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Discussion
Subtype-specific mechanistic pathways linking psychological factors to oral mucosal disease (OMDs) pathogenesis are stratified by evidentiary strength—strong (supported by randomized controlled trials or large cohort studies), moderate (well-designed observational investigations), and weak (preliminary or exploratory data)—with established pathways (e.g., T-cell-mediated autoimmunity in OLP) clearly distinguished from emerging mechanistic insights (e.g., TGF-β/Smad-driven fibrosis in OSF). This evidence-based stratification directly informs tailored clinical practice for the four core OMDs subtypes, with mechanistically aligned interventions and OHRQoL assessment strategies to address subtype-unique pathophysiological and psychosocial burdens. For RAU, targeted anxiety screening and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) are recommended to modulate hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis hyperactivation, thereby reducing mucosal inflammatory activity and ulcer recurrence [9, 34, 41]. For OLP, combined immunomodulatory therapy and stress management interventions serve to rectify Th1/Th2/Th17 immune imbalance, alleviating erosive mucosal lesions and mitigating disease-related psychological distress [13, 25, 49]. OHRQoL assessment tools are similarly stratified by disease course and

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Discussion
disease-related psychological distress [13, 25, 49]. OHRQoL assessment tools are similarly stratified by disease course and clinical utility to optimize evaluative precision: The OHIP-49 for chronic progressive OMDs (OLP, OLK, OSF) [83, 85], the OHIP-14 for acute and recurrent presentations such as RAU [39, 79], and the OHIP-5 for large-scale epidemiological surveys and routine clinical follow-ups [87]. Disease-specific instruments—including the COMDQ [33, 95], OHIP-OLP [88, 89], and OHRQoL-OSF [62, 97]—further enable subtype-adapted evaluation by capturing disease-specific symptomatic and functional burdens that generic scales fail to quantify. Corresponding psychological interventions are tailored to address the unique psychosocial challenges of each OMDs subtype: CBT for anxiety management in RAU and OLP patients [34, 47], music therapy for depressive symptoms in OLK [40], and positive psychology interventions to mitigate betel quid addiction-related guilt in OSF [30].

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Discussion
Psychological distress exacerbates OMDs severity and OHRQoL impairment by amplifying pain, disrupting self-worth, and limiting social participation—mediated via subtype-specific mechanisms: Psychoneuroimmunological imbalance in OLP, catecholamine-driven proliferation in OLK, and bidirectional cortisol-fibrosis/betel quid addiction cycling in OSF [38, 51]. These pathways highlight the limitations of one-size-fits-all strategies and gaps in elucidating variables mediating the mental health-OMDs outcome interplay [61, 107].

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Discussion > Strengths and limitations
This review has several key limitations. One limitation is associated with the methodological constraints of the included studies: most had small sample sizes and single-center designs, reducing statistical power and generalizability, and heterogeneity across studies (in assessment tools, designs, and outcome measures) precluded meta-analysis of overall effect sizes. In addition, our review focused predominantly on Asian, particularly Chinese, populations. While this reflects the high prevalence of OMDs in these regions and provides context-specific insights, the generalizability of findings to other ethnic or regional populations merit further confirmation.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Discussion > Strengths and limitations
Despite these limitations, our review has notable strengths. We adopted PRISMA guidelines during literature screening to ensure rigor, and supplemented structured tables (Tables 3 and 4) to summarize mechanisms, evidence strength, and study quality, enhancing transparency. We also provided evidence-based, subtype-tailored guidance for OHRQoL tool selection and psychological interventions, offering practical insights for clinicians and policymakers.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Conclusion
Numerous factors mediate the bidirectional interaction between psychological factors, OHRQoL, and four core oral mucosal disease (OMDs) subtypes—RAU, OLP, OLK, and OSF. Essential strategies have been identified to address these challenges, including subtype-tailored psychological interventions and stratified OHRQoL tool selection based on instrument psychometrics and clinical needs.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Conclusion
The evidence synthesized in this review highlights the importance of integrating psychosocial management into comprehensive OMDs care. Therefore, clinicians and policymakers, in their role as healthcare stewards, should adopt the evidence-based guidance provided in this review to optimize OHRQoL assessment and psychological intervention for OMDs patients, facilitating precision care that addresses both clinical and psychosocial dimensions of these diseases.

Psychological factors and quality of life in oral mucosal diseases: A systematic review of assessment tools and clinical implications
Body > Conclusion
Future research should prioritize three directions: first, identifying subtype-specific mediators (e.g., neuroendocrine markers, immune subsets) to clarify the stress-OMDs progression causal chain; second, developing hybrid OHRQoL tools balancing cross-subtype applicability and disease-specific sensitivity via mechanistically tailored components [82]; third, designing and validating tailored psychological interventions (e.g., Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) for OLK premalignant anxiety, adherence support for OSF betel quid cessation) that target subtype-specific pathways [29, 30]. Integrating these into clinical practice enables early high-risk patient stratification, facilitating precision care to address both clinical and psychosocial OMDs dimensions.
