Diagnosis-based pathways for conservative and minimally invasive management of temporomandibular disorders: a scoping review
Body > 4. Discussion > 4.1 Summary of key findings > 4.1.4 Management of disc displacement with reduction
Disc displacement with reduction mainly causes joint clicking due to disrupted disc-condyle coordination. RCTs show structured conservative management is the most effective and least invasive first-line treatment. PE/BT/SC interventions reduce clicking, improve perceived effectiveness, and enhance jaw function, with counselling plus jaw exercises proving more effective than counselling alone [93, 94, 95, 96]. Physiotherapy particularly supervised jaw exercises yielded greater improvements in pain, neck disability, mood, and somatization than home-based exercise programs, reflecting the importance of therapist-guided motor control in disc recapture and muscular relaxation [94, 95, 96]. ARS demonstrated greater improvements in mouth opening and unique suppression of joint clicking compared with self-care alone [93, 97], consistent with external literature showing ARS can temporarily stabilize disc-condyle alignment and effective in reducing pain and popping symptoms compared to physical or behavioral therapy [156]. Conventional occlusal splint also reduced clicking severity and significantly more effective at improving mouth opening [157, 158]. LLLT and US provided additional early-phase analgesia and functional gains, consistent with recent evidence reporting improved pain relief and mandibular function following LLLT in patients with TMD, particularly with higher laser wavelengths [159]. Although propranolol

Body > 4. Discussion > 4.1 Summary of key findings > 4.1.4 Management of disc displacement with reduction
Minimally invasive options are reserved for DDR cases that continue to produce painful clicking or functional limitation after optimized conservative care. Injections including 25% dextrose, BoNT/A, and Saline offered variable benefits. Dextrose prolotherapy was effective, easy to administer, and safe, improving pain and maximum interincisal opening (MIO) with high patient satisfaction; however, effects did not consistently exceed arthrocentesis [99, 160]. BoNT/A was shown to reduce clicking and joint pain, with some studies reporting faster symptom relief compared to ARS [97]. External sources also support its effectiveness in relieving pain and significantly decreased muscle activity and biting force [161].

heading_path: 4.1.5 Management of disk displacement without reduction
content:
Diagnosis-based pathways for conservative and minimally invasive management of temporomandibular disorders: a scoping review
Body > 4. Discussion > 4.1 Summary of key findings > 4.1.5 Management of disk displacement without reduction
DDWoR often presents with acute limitation in mouth opening, and conservative therapy remains an essential first-line intervention. PE/BT/SC approaches improved pain, mandibular movement patterns, and functional disability [61, 77, 102, 103]. Jog manipulation added short-term improvement in mouth opening but showed no long-term superiority over conventional exercise-based rehabilitation [61]. ARS, OS, and CAD/CAM splints all reduced pain and improved oral health-related quality of life. However, CAD/CAM splints did not show better clinical outcomes than conventional splints [66], LLLT and TENS reduced pain and improved function, with LLLT demonstrating greater mid-treatment improvement than TENS [110]. Studies confirm that LLLT is a safe, effective, and non-invasive treatment for TMD, providing significant pain relief and functional improvement [162].

content:
Diagnosis-based pathways for conservative and minimally invasive management of temporomandibular disorders: a scoping review
Body > 4. Discussion > 4.1 Summary of key findings > 4.1.5 Management of disk displacement without reduction
DDWoR trials revealed minimally invasive procedures that primarily arthrocentesis and adjunctive injectables provide substantial benefit. Conventional double-puncture, single-puncture, and US-guided techniques provide equivalent reductions in pain and similar improvements in maximal interincisal opening [105, 106, 107], although single-puncture and US-guided methods were faster and required fewer needle manipulations [108]. Both double- puncture and single-puncture arthrocentesis methods are equally effective for patients during the procedure [163]. PRP Lavage consistently produced the greatest long-term improvement in pain, mastication efficiency, and mandibular function, outperforming HA and lavage alone [164]. Findings strongly supported by meta-analytic evidence demonstrating PRP’s regenerative and anti-inflammatory effects in chronic intra-articular pathology [153]. HA injections also significantly improved pain and MMO, though their durability was less than PRP [109].

Diagnosis-based pathways for conservative and minimally invasive management of temporomandibular disorders: a scoping review
Body > 4. Discussion > 4.1 Summary of key findings > 4.1.6 Management of degenerative joint disease
DJD represents a chronic, inflammatory degenerative process of the TMJ, and conservative therapy remains the essential foundation of care. Across the included RCTs, PE/BT/SC protocols reduced pain intensity, improved function, and optimized mandibular movement patterns, particularly in women with chronic painful TMDs, where education and self-care strategies effectively corrected dysfunctional mechanics [59, 77, 78, 103]. Physical therapy further enhanced mandibular mobility and reduced joint loading [59, 77]. ARS therapy demonstrated potential for condylar repair and remodeling in adolescents and young adults with early DJD [103]. LLLT show superior pain reduction compared with ultrasound and TENS consistent with recent literature [159]. Long-term pulsed radiofrequency improved pain and patient satisfaction [78]. Oral glucosamine hydrochloride provided additional benefit when combined with intra-articular HA, consistent with studies reporting favorable symptomatic and functional outcomes in patients with TMD compared with ibuprofen and paracetamol [165]. The study supports a hybrid biochemical approach, like peripheral joint osteoarthritis management, by confirming glucosamine’s role as a chondroprotective agent [166].

Diagnosis-based pathways for conservative and minimally invasive management of temporomandibular disorders: a scoping review
Body > 4. Discussion > 4.1 Summary of key findings > 4.1.6 Management of degenerative joint disease
When conservative measures fail to provide adequate relief, minimally invasive interventions particularly arthrocentesis and biologic injectables offer significant benefit. Conventional arthrocentesis effectively reduces joint pain and improves mouth opening by eliminating inflammatory mediators and adhesions within the superior joint space [77]. Adjunct HA injections enhance lubrication and joint biomechanics, with studies demonstrating greater improvements in pain and function compared with arthrocentesis alone [78]. DJD data revealed durable pain relief when arthrocentesis or HA injection was combined with oral glucosamine [111]. Regarding injectables, BoNT/A showed no superiority to saline in chronic muscular TMD and lacks evidence for intra-articular use in DJD [75].

heading_path: 4.1.7 Management of headache attributed to TMD
content:
Diagnosis-based pathways for conservative and minimally invasive management of temporomandibular disorders: a scoping review
Body > 4. Discussion > 4.1 Summary of key findings > 4.1.7 Management of headache attributed to TMD
Headache attributed to TMD frequently coexists with masticatory muscle hyperactivity and central sensitization, making conservative care the essential foundation of treatment. RCTs show that PE/BT/SC programs lower headache frequency, facial pain, and functional limitations, similar to results in general myogenous TMD treatment. Pulsed radiofrequency combined with conventional conservative therapy provided durable pain reduction and patient satisfaction [78], BoNT/A injections provided short-term relief of tender points and headache intensity [112]. But in other study its pain relief compared to saline placebo does not provide extra relief over saline [74].

Diagnosis-based pathways for conservative and minimally invasive management of temporomandibular disorders: a scoping review
Body > 4. Discussion > 4.1 Summary of key findings > 4.1.8 Management of mixed TMD
Mixed TMD, which are the most frequently encountered clinical presentations, characterized by both muscular and joint symptoms [6]. PE/BT/SC interventions consistently reduced pain intensity, improved sleep quality, and enhanced quality-of-life parameters [113, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118], internet-based behavioral therapy still understudied [113]. Cervical-mandibular manual therapy, Post-Isometric Relaxation (PIR), and structured exercise programs, yielded significant improvements in pain, mandibular range, and psychological outcomes. Findings aligned with broader literature show that addressing cervical mandibular interactions enhances TMD recovery [167]. Manual therapy generally outperformed Bowen’s technique, highlighting the importance of targeted joint–muscle mobilization [121]. Michigan splint, stabilization splint, SOVA, CAD/CAM, and BFB splints shows reduced pain, bruxism activity, muscle tenderness, and sleep disturbances [113, 115, 116, 117, 118, 123, 124], The Michigan splint is a type of stabilization splint, not a separate intervention. Both are hard-acrylic maxillary occlusal appliances designed to reduce parafunctional loading and muscle hyperactivity. The BFB splints demonstrate specific benefits in reducing nocturnal bruxism bursts and improving patient-reported pain

Body > 4. Discussion > 4.1 Summary of key findings > 4.1.8 Management of mixed TMD
hyperactivity. The BFB splints demonstrate specific benefits in reducing nocturnal bruxism bursts and improving patient-reported pain [125, 168]. The SOVA splint study found notable differences in sleep bruxism associated with TMD, possibly due to the SOVA’s softer material and larger occlusal contact areas compared to the Michigan splint [126]. LLLT, TENS, ozone therapy, PBMT, and ultrasound further contributed to pain reduction and improved mandibular function, with LLLT offering greater efficacy in muscle tenderness remission [169]. The Bioactive Ozone Therapy shows equal result in reducing pain and increasing MMO [123]. Pharmacologic therapy with duloxetine improved pain and function when used adjunctively but does not impact anxiety, depression, or IL-6 levels [122, 170]. These trials confirm that no single conservative therapy is best for all cases, but combining manual therapy, exercise, behavioral strategies, and splint therapy consistently yields the greatest benefit aligning with meta-analytic evidence that multimodal approaches are most effective for mixed TMD [135].

Diagnosis-based pathways for conservative and minimally invasive management of temporomandibular disorders: a scoping review
Body > 4. Discussion > 4.1 Summary of key findings > 4.1.8 Management of mixed TMD
If symptoms continue after thorough conservative care, minimally invasive procedures may be considered for selected mixed TMD cases. Arthrocentesis reduces joint pain and improves mouth opening, especially when combined with duloxetine, benefiting patients with central sensitization [122]. Needling-based therapies including scalp acupuncture and auricular acupuncture provided short-term pain reductions. But scalp acupuncture is not effective in improving sleep or quality of life [115]. Occlusal equilibration therapy demonstrated clinically significant improvements in facial pain and mouth opening with favorable safety, indicating potential benefit in selected patients with occlusal instability [119, 134].

Diagnosis-based pathways for conservative and minimally invasive management of temporomandibular disorders: a scoping review
Body > 4. Discussion > 4.2 Clinical implication
The most important part of managing TMD is still conservative care that is based on diagnosis and uses more than one method. Therapeutic integration and patient adherence are more crucial for achieving successful outcomes than any singular treatment. The results highlight the imperative of screening for psychological comorbidities, including anxiety, depression, and catastrophizing, which affect pain persistence and treatment efficacy. Clinicians should begin with PE/BT/SC, progress to behavioral therapy and multimodal physiotherapy, manual therapy and jaw exercises as needed, and consider occlusal splints and adjunct physical modalities for additional pain relief and functional improvement. If pain persists beyond 6–12 weeks its can be considered for using minimally invasive treatment. For Myofascial Pain, Dry needling is recommended due to its consistent impact on trigger-point pain and mouth opening, followed by auricular acupuncture for patients who prefer non-needling modalities. Lidocaine or collagen MD injections may be considered for short-term relief but should not replace comprehensive rehabilitation. Overall, emphasis should remain on multimodal, reversible therapies that address muscular dysfunction, psychosocial contributors, and functional impairments. For Myalgia, dry needling should be considered the preferred minimally invasive option, followed by acupuncture for patients favoring non-trigger-point approaches. BoNT/A is not recommended as a routine treatment due to limited superiority over placebo, and EGF

Body > 4. Discussion > 4.2 Clinical implication
BoNT/A is not recommended as a routine treatment due to limited superiority over placebo, and EGF injections remain investigational. For Arthralgia, arthrocentesis with HA is preferred as the minimally invasive first choice due to consistent efficacy, safety, and lower injection frequency. Steroid injections can be considered to use besides the other medicine. PRP may be recommended for refractory cases or suspected early degenerative changes, given its superior long-term analgesia. Acupuncture or dry needling may serve as supportive options but should not replace joint-directed intervention. For DDR, Dextrose prolotherapy may be suitable for patients seeking non-surgical intervention with good safety and functional benefit. BoNT/A may be considered only in selected refractory cases where muscular hyperactivity contributes to persistent clicking. For DDWoR, clinicians should escalate to arthrocentesis, with single-puncture or ultrasound-guided approaches preferred for procedural ease and efficiency. PRP is recommended as the most effective adjunct for long-term pain and function, followed by HA when PRP is unavailable. For DJD, arthrocentesis combined with HA, given its consistent improvement in pain and biomechanics, BoNT/A and saline injections are not recommended due to lack of therapeutic advantage. ARS may be considered only in early DJD with favorable disc–condyle relationships. For Headache attributed to TMD,

may be considered only in early DJD with favorable disc–condyle relationships. For Headache attributed to TMD, BoNT/A should only be considered for select refractory cases, given its variable benefit and no clear superiority to saline in trials. Saline or BoNT/A injections are not recommended as first-line or early escalation treatments. Conservative neuromuscular stabilization should be prioritized before minimally invasive procedures. For Mixed TMD, clinicians may consider arthrocentesis and combine duloxetine in cases with centralized or chronic pain features. Acupuncture may be used for short-term analgesia but should not be relied upon as a sole therapy for sleep or psychosocial impairment. Occlusal equilibration can be considered when occlusal disturbances contribute to chronic symptoms. Based on 11 RCTs, several therapeutic interventions are supported for the management of TMD specifically in female patients. These include stabilization splint therapy, BoNT/A injections, and various laser and light therapies such as HILT, LLLT, and PBMT. Physical interventions like kinesio tapping (KT) and mandibular exercise (MME) should also be considered. Treatment efficacy in this population must be rigorously monitored, primarily by assessing pain intensity using scales such as the VAS and NRS, and by evaluating functional capacity through measures like MMO and PPT. by evaluating functional capacity through measures like MMO and PPT. In addition, the prioritization of minimally invasive interventions should be guided by the specific TMD subtype. Identifying subtype hierarchies helps clinicians match minimally invasive treatments to the pathology, so escalation from conservative care stays logical and personalised.

Diagnosis-based pathways for conservative and minimally invasive management of temporomandibular disorders: a scoping review
Body > 4. Discussion > 4.3 Strength, limitation, and future direction
The strength of this review is that it looks at 129 RCTs covering conservative and minimally invasive interventions in a way that separates them by diagnosis. Aligning evidence with diagnostic categories, it establishes clinical pathways for personalized care, enhancing prior reviews of diverse TMD populations. Most studies reported pain intensity using validated scales such as VAS, alongside functional mobility measures such as MMO, enabling consistent comparison of clinical response across diagnostic subtypes. The review also captured outcomes related to psychological and emotional factors, including stress, catastrophizing, and depressive symptoms, as well as quality-of-life indicators, reflecting the biopsychosocial nature of TMD. Importantly, several RCTs incorporated physiological or objective markers including EMG activity, biomarkers such as IL-6, Salivary Oxidative Stress Markers, and Salivary Cortisol indices which provide valuable mechanistic insight into treatment response. This review is the use of the RoB2 framework to assess risk of bias in all included RCTs. The scoping design encompassed various modalities and innovative treatments, providing a thorough overview of the practice.

Diagnosis-based pathways for conservative and minimally invasive management of temporomandibular disorders: a scoping review
Body > 4. Discussion > 4.3 Strength, limitation, and future direction
There are a few limitations that need to be thought about. The variability in diagnostic criteria among studies requires the omission of the effective intervention, treatment dosage, and outcomes from quantitative analysis. The sample sizes were small, and the follow-up periods were rarely longer than six months, which made it hard to see what happened in the long term. However, many primary studies had methodological limitations. While a third of trials were low risk, most showed “some concerns” due to poor reporting of allocation concealment, difficulties blinding participants for certain interventions, and inconsistent adherence to home-exercise protocols potentially affecting treatment effect estimates. Modest sample sizes and limited long-term follow-up further restrict conclusions about sustained efficacy. This review also lacks to population differences, especially sex and region. Over 80% of RCT participants were women, which matches TMD epidemiology but hinders treatment comparisons by sex; women often report higher pain and psychosocial issues, so absence of sex-based analysis limits clinical relevance. Additionally, a quarter of studies were from Brazil, with little evidence from Africa, Southeast Asia, or other low-resource regions, raising concerns about global applicability where minimally invasive treatments may be unavailable.

Diagnosis-based pathways for conservative and minimally invasive management of temporomandibular disorders: a scoping review
Body > 4. Discussion > 4.3 Strength, limitation, and future direction
Future research should prioritize multicenter, randomized studies employing standardized DC/TMD diagnostics and core outcomes for pain, mandibular function, psychosocial distress, and quality of life, accompanied by long-term follow-up (≥12 months) and should include sex-specific data and recruit more diverse populations to improve generalizability. Incorporating psychosocial and biological markers will facilitate the development of precision medicine algorithms to forecast treatment efficacy for subsequent systematic review. Comparative analyses of multimodal treatments versus single-modality care will elucidate synergistic effects. Investigations should explore the mechanisms that connect joint pathology to central pain modulation. Implementation studies of tele-rehabilitation, digital platforms, and cost-effectiveness can enhance the accessibility and adherence to TMD care. Importantly, upcoming RCTs should focus on using robust randomization methods, enhancing blinding whenever possible, and ensuring reports follow Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) and RoB2 standards.

Diagnosis-based pathways for conservative and minimally invasive management of temporomandibular disorders: a scoping review
Body > 5. Conclusions
This scoping review demonstrates that the management is most effective when supported by a diagnosis-based framework. An analysis of 129 RCTs shows that conservative treatments, such as patient education, behavior modification, exercise therapy, and occlusal splints, can greatly reduce pain and improve jaw function. Patients with persistent symptoms can benefit from minimally invasive techniques, such as arthrocentesis, needling, and injections. Diagnosis-specific symptoms should be used as escalation rather than replacement strategies for suitable treatment approach. Evidence shows that effective TMD treatment requires personalized, holistic care that considers both physical and psychosocial aspects. Future studies should be focused on standardized diagnostic criteria, longer follow-up, and multidisciplinary strategies to enhance clinical outcomes.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Abstract > Background
Dentin hypersensitivity (DH) is a prevalent clinical condition characterized by short, sharp pain arising from exposed dentin in response to thermal, tactile, osmotic, or chemical stimuli. Conventional desensitizing agents often provide temporary relief, with inconsistent long-term effectiveness, prompting growing interest in advanced treatment modalities.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Abstract > Objective
To systematically evaluate and compare the efficacy of advanced treatment modalities with conventional or placebo interventions in reducing dentin hypersensitivity in adults.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Abstract > Methods
This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (Registration ID: CRD420250651753). Electronic searches were performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Google Scholar, with the date of final search being 30 September 2025. Randomized controlled trials involving adults with clinically diagnosed dentin hypersensitivity affecting permanent teeth were included. Advanced interventions such as laser therapy, photobiomodulation, bioactive glass, nano-hydroxyapatite, CPP-ACP, iontophoresis, Resin and varnish systems, were assessed. The primary outcome was reduction in hypersensitivity measured using validated pain assessment scales. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool, and quantitative synthesis was performed using a RevMan 5.4. software.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Abstract > Results
Thirty-one randomized controlled trials were included in the qualitative synthesis, and twenty-five studies were eligible for meta-analysis. Advanced treatment modalities demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in dentin hypersensitivity compared with conventional or placebo controls (pooled SMD = −1.02; 95% CI: −1.32 to −0.73; p < 0.001). Laser-based therapies showed the greatest effectiveness, followed by nano-hydroxyapatite and bioactive glass agents. Moderate heterogeneity was observed across studies.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Abstract > Conclusion
Advanced treatment modalities are more effective than conventional desensitizing agents in managing dentin hypersensitivity. Laser therapy provides the most consistent and sustained relief, supporting its clinical use, while further standardized long-term trials are recommended.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Introduction
Dentin hypersensitivity (DH) is a prevalent and clinically significant condition characterised by short, sharp pain arising from exposed dentinal surfaces in response to thermal, tactile, evaporative, osmotic, or chemical stimuli, pain that cannot be attributed to any other dental pathology.1 Despite decades of research, DH continues to challenge dental practitioners, largely because its multifactorial aetiology intersects with variability in patient susceptibility, lifestyle behaviours, and clinical presentation. Global prevalence estimates range from 10% to 30%, with higher figures reported in populations with active periodontal disease, erosive dietary habits, or following periodontal surgical and non-surgical therapy.2,3 This wide epidemiological burden underscores the urgency of identifying interventions that offer not only immediate symptom relief but also predictable, long-term benefit.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Introduction
Conventional desensitizing agents including fluoride varnishes, potassium nitrate dentifrices, strontium salts, oxalate compounds, glutaraldehyde-based preparations, and early-generation dentin bonding systems have been employed routinely for decades. Their accessibility, ease of use, and cost-effectiveness make them practical first-line options for mild to moderate DH.4,5 However, their long-term durability remains a recognised limitation: symptom relapse within weeks to months after application is commonly reported, and head-to-head comparisons with newer agents have generally not favoured traditional therapies over sustained follow-up periods.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Introduction
In response to these limitations, advances in dental materials science and laser technology have introduced an expanding repertoire of treatment modalities. Bioactive glass (NovaMin), casein phosphopeptide–amorphous calcium phosphate (CPP-ACP), arginine–calcium carbonate complexes, nano-hydroxyapatite (n-HAp), and advanced adhesive systems are increasingly investigated for their ability to promote remineralization, generate stable mineralised occluding layers within dentinal tubules, and produce sustained clinical relief.6 Laser-based therapies including diode, Nd:YAG, and Er,Cr:YSGG wavelengths have attracted considerable interest for their capacity to deliver immediate and durable desensitisation through neurological modulation and physical tubule obturation.7,8

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Introduction
Despite the proliferation of available modalities, the clinical evidence base remains fragmented. Three interrelated challenges undermine the translation of existing research into evidence-based guidelines. First, DH is inherently multifactorial: aetiological contributors including gingival recession, erosive wear, toothbrush abrasion, periodontal therapy sequelae, and parafunctional habits vary considerably between individuals, limiting the generalisability of treatment effects across heterogeneous patient populations.9 Second, methodological inconsistencies — encompassing disparate pain measurement scales, inconsistent provocation stimuli, variable follow-up durations, and non-uniform reporting of outcomes — impede cross-study comparisons and evidence synthesis.10 Third, most clinical trials assess outcomes over short post-treatment intervals, whereas DH is inherently recurrent due to ongoing dentinal exposure from dietary acids, mechanical abrasion, and erosive processes. Long-duration comparative evidence is therefore critically needed.11

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Introduction
There is a recognised scarcity of high-quality literature that clearly identifies the most effective and long-lasting treatment modality for DH. Traditional agents, while well established, often lack consistency in long-term outcomes. Conversely, modern agents and laser-based therapies show promising sustained efficacy but are frequently supported by smaller trials, limited follow-up periods, or non-standardised methodologies. This means that their true comparative effectiveness remains insufficiently understood.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Introduction
Prior systematic reviews have tended to examine DH treatment in siloed categories potassium nitrate, fluorides, or laser therapy rather than providing a unified comparative synthesis across the full clinical spectrum.12,13 Moreover, several newer modalities have entered the marketplace in advance of robust longitudinal validation: nanohydroxyapatite and bioglass formulations are widely marketed as superior options, yet long-term clinical data remain sparse. Similarly, laser therapy outcomes vary considerably across wavelengths, power settings, and study designs. These gaps collectively reinforce the need for a rigorously conducted, comprehensive systematic review.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Introduction
Another challenge is that several newer treatment modalities have been commercialised rapidly, often ahead of robust clinical validation. For instance, nanohydroxyapatite toothpastes and bioglass-based formulations are widely marketed as superior options, yet their long-term clinical effectiveness remains under investigation.14 Similarly, laser-based treatments demonstrate considerable variability in outcomes depending on wavelength, power settings, technique, and study design, making it difficult to draw consistent conclusions.15 These inconsistencies reinforce the need for an updated systematic review that evaluates advanced modalities alongside established agents using rigorous methodological standards.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Introduction
The present systematic review and meta-analysis was therefore designed to synthesise evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating both traditional and advanced DH treatment modalities, with an explicit emphasis on short-term and long-term clinical outcomes. In doing so, this review seeks to bridge the gap between available evidence and everyday clinical decision-making, and to provide a structured, methodology-driven framework that supports the selection of the most effective and durable intervention strategies for dentin hypersensitivity.16

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Study design
This systematic review and meta-analysis were methodically designed following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines and adhered to the methodological framework outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions.17 The review protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (Registration ID: CRD420250651753). The statistical analysis for this systematic review followed the Cochrane Handbook recommendations. Data from included randomized controlled trials were synthesized using both qualitative and quantitative approaches, depending on methodological homogeneity across studies.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Research rationale
Dentin hypersensitivity remains a clinically common condition for which conventional desensitizing agents offer inconsistent long-term relief. Advanced modalities including laser therapy and bioactive remineralising materials show clinical promise, but supporting evidence remains fragmented and not yet amenable to confident clinical recommendations. This systematic review and meta-analysis was therefore designed to critically compare advanced treatment modalities with conventional or placebo controls, with the objective of identifying interventions that offer effective and durable management of dentin hypersensitivity.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Research question
This systematic review was based on the following question: “What is the efficacy of advanced treatment modalities, compared with conventional or placebo treatments, in reducing dentin hypersensitivity in adults?”

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Research question
The search strategy was prepared based on Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome (PICO). Population (P) of interest were adults with clinically diagnosed dentin hypersensitivity affecting permanent teeth. The Intervention (I) included advanced modalities such as laser therapy, bioactive glass, nano-hydroxyapatite, CPP-ACP, iontophoresis, oxalate, arginine based, resin and varnish-based systems, and combination therapies. The comparison group (C) comprised of placebo, sham procedures, or conventional desensitizing agents. The outcome (O) focused on reduction in hypersensitivity measured using validated scales (VAS, Schiff Score), duration of symptom relief, and adverse effects. Only randomised controlled trials were included to ensure methodological rigor.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Research question
For the purpose of this review, “advanced treatment modalities” were defined a priori as interventions that employ enhanced biological, biomimetic, regenerative, energy-based, or delivery-assisted mechanisms beyond conventional desensitizing agents. These modalities were categorized into (1): Energy-based therapies (laser therapy and photobiomodulation); (2) Biomimetic and remineralising agents (nano-hydroxyapatite, CPP-ACP, and bioactive glass); (3) Delivery-enhanced systems (iontophoresis-assisted delivery); and (4) Advanced barrier-forming systems (resin- and varnish-based formulations designed to provide prolonged tubule occlusion). Conventional fluoride varnishes, potassium nitrate, and other traditional desensitizing agents were considered comparator interventions unless incorporated into modified delivery systems or combination therapies.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Inclusion criteria
a. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) only
b. Adult participants (≥18 years) with clinically diagnosed dentin hypersensitivity
c. Studies evaluating advanced desensitizing modalities, including laser therapy, bioactive glass, nano-hydroxyapatite, CPP-ACP, iontophoresis, oxalate, arginine based, resin and varnish-based systems and combination therapies
d. Studies with a comparison group (placebo, sham, no treatment, or conventional desensitizing agents)
e. Assessment of dentin hypersensitivity using validated pain scales (e.g., VAS, Schiff scale)
f. Studies reporting quantitative outcome data with at least one month follow-up evaluation
g. Full-text articles published in English

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Exclusion criteria
h. In vitro studies, animal studies, case reports, case series, reviews, editorials, or conference abstracts
i. Studies involving children or adolescents or primary teeth
j. Hypersensitivity secondary to caries, defective restorations, cracked teeth, pulpal involvement.
k. Studies lacking standardized or validated outcome measures
l. Studies with incomplete, unclear, or insufficient data for analysis

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Literature search strategy
A comprehensive, systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), supplemented by Google Scholar for citation tracking, from database inception through 30 September 2025 (date of final search). The search was restricted to publications in the English language. Both MeSH terms and free-text keywords were combined using Boolean operators. A representative PubMed search string was: ("dentin hypersensitivity" OR "tooth hypersensitivity") AND ("laser therapy" OR "bioactive glass" OR "nano-hydroxyapatite" OR "CPP-ACP" OR "iontophoresis" OR "photobiomodulation") AND (randomized OR RCT). The Cochrane CENTRAL search was performed using key terms including “dentin hypersensitivity,” “dentine hypersensitivity,” and “randomized controlled trial,” without a structured Boolean string, given the nature of the CENTRAL interface. Reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews were also manually screened to identify additional eligible trials. Grey literature and trial registries including ClinicalTrials.gov were also searched. All retrieved citations were imported into Zotero for deduplication, and the screening process was documented using a PRISMA 2020 flow diagram.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Study selection and data collection process
Prior to study selection and data extraction, reviewers independently screened and extracted data using standardized forms developed for this review. Disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus, with arbitration by a third reviewer when necessary. Although the kappa value were not calculated, independent duplicate screening and extraction were performed throughout the review process to minimize selection and extraction bias. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were documented systematically in accordance with PRISMA 2020 recommendations.

heading_path: Study selection and data collection process
content:
Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Study selection and data collection process
Data extraction was performed by the same two reviewers (VS and SS) using a standardised Microsoft Excel form. Extracted variables encompassed: study design and setting, participant demographics and diagnostic criteria, sample size, intervention and comparator characteristics, follow-up duration, outcome measures (mean VAS and Schiff score reductions with standard deviations), and details of adverse effects, funding sources, and conflicts of interest. When data were missing or ambiguous, corresponding authors were contacted to request clarification.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Risk of bias assessment
Methodological quality of included RCTs was independently evaluated by two reviewers (ST and PS) using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 1.0 (RoB 1.0) tool .The risk of bias was evaluated across seven domains: (1) random sequence generation (selection bias); (2) allocation concealment (selection bias); (3) blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias); (4) blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias); (5) incomplete outcome data (attrition bias); (6) selective reporting (reporting bias); and (7) other sources of bias. Each domain was judged as having a low, high, or unclear risk of bias. Any disagreements between the reviewers were resolved through discussion and consensus.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Statistical analysis and data synthesis
Meta-analysis was conducted using Review Manager (RevMan) version 5.4. Continuous outcomes were analysed using the standardised mean difference (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals. In anticipation of clinical and methodological heterogeneity across interventions, a random-effects model (DerSimonian–Laird method) was applied as the primary analytical approach. Statistical heterogeneity was quantified using the I2 statistic; values exceeding 50% were considered indicative of substantial heterogeneity. Subgroup analyses were pre-specified based on the category of advanced desensitizing modality. Publication bias was assessed visually using funnel plots. Formal statistical tests for funnel plot asymmetry (e.g., Egger's regression test) were not performed, as several subgroups contained fewer than ten studies, which renders such tests underpowered and their results unreliable per Cochrane Handbook guidance.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Methods > Statistical analysis and data synthesis
Because hypersensitivity outcomes were reported using different measurement scales, including Visual Analogue Scales (VAS; 0–10 and 0–100) and Schiff Sensitivity Scores, standardized mean differences (SMDs) were used to permit quantitative synthesis across studies while preserving the relative magnitude of treatment effects.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Results > Study selection and characteristics of included studies
The systematic database search retrieved a total of 305 records from the primary databases, comprising PubMed/MEDLINE (n = 137) and Cochrane CENTRAL (n = 71). An additional 125 records were identified through other sources, including manual reference list screening, yielding an initial pool of 430 citations. Following deduplication (n = 53 removed), 377 unique records remained for title and abstract screening. Of these, 239 records were excluded on the basis of irrelevance or failure to meet the predefined inclusion criteria, leaving 138 articles for full-text assessment.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Results > Risk of bias assessment
The risk of bias assessment of the included randomized controlled trials was performed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 1.0 tool, and the summary and graphical representation indicate an overall moderate methodological quality of the included studies.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Results > Risk of bias assessment > Random sequence generation (Selection Bias)
Nearly all included studies demonstrated a low risk of bias for random sequence generation, indicating that appropriate randomization methods were commonly used. Only a small proportion of studies had some concerns in reporting regarding the randomization procedure, while no major high-risk concerns were identified.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Results > Risk of bias assessment > Allocation concealment (Selection Bias)
Allocation concealment showed a comparatively lower proportion of low-risk studies than other domains. Although most studies adequately concealed allocation, a small percentage demonstrated high risk of bias, suggesting possible predictability in participant assignment. Some studies also lacked sufficient methodological details, contributing to some concerns judgments.

heading_path: Blinding of participants and personnel (performance Bias)
content:
Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Results > Risk of bias assessment > Blinding of participants and personnel (performance Bias)
This domain demonstrated one of the highest proportions of low-risk assessments. Most studies effectively blinded participants and study personnel, thereby minimizing the possibility of performance bias. Only a minimal proportion showed some concerns in reporting.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Results > Risk of bias assessment > Blinding of outcome assessment (Detection Bias)
Blinding of outcome assessment revealed moderate concerns. While the majority of studies were categorized as low risk, a noticeable proportion showed high risk of bias, indicating that outcome assessors were not adequately blinded in certain studies. This may have influenced outcome evaluation and introduced detection bias.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Results > Risk of bias assessment > Incomplete outcome data (Attrition Bias)
Most studies adequately addressed missing or incomplete data and maintained low attrition rates, resulting in a predominantly low risk of attrition bias. Very few studies showed some concerns, and high-risk attrition bias was uncommon.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Results > Risk of bias assessment > Selective reporting (Reporting Bias)
Selective reporting bias was generally low across the included studies. Most studies reported outcomes consistent with their objectives and methodology, indicating transparency in reporting practices. No substantial high-risk reporting bias was observed.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Results > Risk of bias assessment > Other Bias
The “other bias” domain also demonstrated predominantly low risk across studies. However, a moderate proportion of studies were judged as some concern due to insufficient methodological details or unidentified potential confounding factors.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Results > Risk of bias assessment > Overall
The ROB summary graph suggests that the included studies were generally of good methodological quality, with most domains demonstrating predominantly low risk of bias. However, some concerns were observed in the domains of allocation concealment and blinding of outcome assessment, where a small proportion of studies exhibited high risk of bias. These methodological limitations should be considered when interpreting the overall findings of the review.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Results > Meta-analysis: overall pooled effect
Meta-analysis of data from all 25 included trials demonstrated a statistically significant and clinically meaningful reduction in dentin hypersensitivity among participants receiving advanced treatment modalities compared with conventional or placebo controls. The pooled standardised mean difference was −1.02 (95% CI: −1.32 to −0.73; p < 0.001), representing a large effect size. Heterogeneity was substantial (I

Body > Results > Subgroup analyses by modality
A formal test for subgroup differences demonstrated statistically significant variation in treatment effects across intervention categories (Chi2 = 28.22, df = 7, P = 0.0002; I2 = 75.2%). This finding suggests that the magnitude of desensitizing effect differed significantly among the evaluated treatment modalities and supports the subgroup analyses performed according to intervention type.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Results > Subgroup analyses by modality > Iontophoresis based intervention
Two studies evaluating iontophoresis-based intervention yielded a pooled SMD of −1.25 (95% CI: −1.92 to −0.57), indicating moderate but statistically significant efficacy. These modalities consistently produced rapid initial desensitisation, often detectable within the first week of treatment. However, a degree of symptom recurrence was noted after 8–12 weeks in some trials, suggesting that iontophoresis may require periodic retreatment to sustain clinical benefit.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Results > Subgroup analyses by modality > Laser-based modalities
A total of sixteen studies evaluated laser therapies, including diode, Nd:YAG, and Er,Cr:YSGG lasers, pooled together as a single subgroup. The pooled SMD was −2.11 (95% CI: −2.96 to −1.26; p < 0.001), demonstrating a strong and statistically significant reduction in hypersensitivity. Laser-based therapies consistently produced both immediate and sustained desensitisation up to 6 months. The high within-subgroup heterogeneity (I2 = 93%) likely reflects variability in laser type, wavelength, power settings, and treatment protocols across included studies, and no further stratification by laser type was performed due to insufficient study numbers per device category.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Results > Subgroup analyses by modality > Calcium phosphate-based agents
Three studies assessing calcium phosphate–based formulations (primarily CPP-ACP) demonstrated a moderate and statistically significant reduction in dentin hypersensitivity, with a pooled SMD of −0.72 (95% CI: −1.09 to −0.34). Body > Discussion
This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized evidence from 25 randomized controlled trials evaluating the efficacy of advanced desensitizing modalities for dentin hypersensitivity. The pooled results demonstrate a statistically significant and clinically meaningful overall reduction in sensitivity scores among participants receiving advanced treatments compared with conventional or placebo controls (SMD = −1.02; 95% CI: −1.32 to −0.73; p < 0.001). Subgroup analyses revealed considerable variation in treatment effectiveness across modality categories, a finding that reflects both mechanistic differences and disparities in the evidence base supporting each treatment class.

The significant subgroup interaction test (P = 0.0002) indicates that treatment effects varied according to intervention category. However, although laser-based therapies demonstrated the largest pooled effect size, these findings should be interpreted cautiously because substantial within-subgroup heterogeneity remained, particularly among laser studies (I2 = 93%), reflecting differences in wavelength, power settings, treatment protocols, and follow-up periods.

Body > Discussion > Laser-based modalities
Laser therapies demonstrated the largest pooled effect sizes among the included interventions, producing the greatest magnitude of pain reduction across all subgroups (SMD = −2.11; 95% CI: −2.96 to −1.26; p < 0.001) however, these findings should be interpreted cautiously because of substantial heterogeneity and variations in laser parameters. All laser studies were pooled as a single subgroup; no further stratification by laser type was undertaken given the limited number of studies per device category. The substantial within-subgroup heterogeneity (I2 = 93%) reflects genuine variability in laser type, wavelength, power settings, treatment protocols, and follow-up durations across included trials, and prevents definitive conclusions about the relative superiority of any particular laser system.42,43

Body > Discussion > Laser-based modalities
Mechanistically, laser-based therapies are proposed to reduce hypersensitivity through a combination of neurological modulation and physical tubule obturation. Low-level diode lasers (810–980 nm range) are thought to thermally modulate intradentinal neural activity and partially seal tubule apertures without inducing pulpal injury.44 Higher-power ablative systems such as Nd:YAG and Er,Cr:YSGG lasers operate through different mechanisms including secondary dentin stimulation and surface modification, but their individual contributions could not be quantified in the present pooled analysis given the absence of device-stratified sub-analyses. Although complete operator and participant blinding is methodologically challenging in laser trials due to visible light emission and proprioceptive feedback, the consistency of pain reduction across included studies combined with a minimal adverse event profile (primarily transient mild warmth) supports the clinical reliability of laser therapy as a first-choice advanced modality, particularly for patients with moderate to severe DH refractory to conventional agents.

Biomimetic remineralising agents, specifically nano-hydroxyapatite (SMD = −0.87; 95% CI: −1.50 to −0.25) and bioactive glass (SMD = −1.08; 95% CI: −2.08 to −0.09), demonstrated the second-highest category of efficacy in this review. These agents act by releasing calcium and phosphate ions that precipitate as hydroxycarbonate apatite within and over dentinal tubule apertures, restoring mineral integrity at the dentin surface.45,46

Meta-analyses show that n-HAp toothpastes significantly outperform controls for evaporative and tactile stimuli.25 Previous studies have suggested that bioactive glass may provide longer-term tubule occlusion. However, heterogeneity in concentration (e.g., 5–15%), particle size, and application frequency limits direct comparability across trials. Iontophoresis enhances ionic diffusion (fluoride, calcium, phosphate) into dentin by means of low-intensity electrical current, resulting in deeper and more stable mineral deposition.47

Arginine–calcium carbonate formulations demonstrated consistent and reproducible efficacy across the two included trials, with a pooled SMD of −1.04 (95% CI: −1.37 to −0.72) and zero between-study heterogeneity (I2 = 0%). This homogeneity is noteworthy and likely reflects the well-characterised, physico-chemical mechanism of arginine a positively charged amino acid that adsorbs to the negatively charged dentinal surface, facilitating localised calcium carbonate precipitation to form a stable crystalline plug within tubule lumina. The practical advantage of its incorporation into commercially available toothpaste formulations also enhances adherence and real-world generalisability.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Non-significant modalities: oxalate and resin/varnish systems
Oxalate-based agents (SMD = −0.40; 95% CI: −0.92 to 0.12) and resin/varnish-based systems (pooled estimate: 0.50; 95% CI: −0.22 to 1.23) did not demonstrate statistically significant efficacy in the present meta-analysis. For oxalate compounds, the formation of calcium oxalate crystals at the dentin surface is theoretically sound as a tubule-occlusive mechanism; however, the durability of these deposits under acidic oral conditions and masticatory loading has been questioned. In the case of resin- and varnish-based systems, mechanical degradation over time and limited depth of tubule penetration may undermine their ability to provide sustained relief. These findings should not necessarily be interpreted as evidence of complete therapeutic ineffectiveness; rather, they may reflect insufficient statistical power within available trials, combined with real limitations in occlusion durability.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Emerging and combination therapies
Emerging therapies such as ozone therapy, and propolis-based bioadhesives also reported clinically meaningful reductions in hypersensitivity.49,50

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Emerging and combination therapies
Combination therapies particularly diode laser plus fluoride varnish or laser with nano-HAp produced superior improvements compared with single-modality interventions.51 These synergistic regimens may represent the future of multimodal DH management by combining rapid neural desensitisation with long-term remineralization. Future RCTs should formally evaluate such combination protocols with extended follow-up to determine their comparative long-term advantage.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Emerging and combination therapies
Although platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) was initially considered during protocol development because of its proposed regenerative potential and emerging application in dentin hypersensitivity management, no studies satisfied the predefined eligibility criteria for inclusion in the present review. Consequently, no conclusions can be drawn regarding the effectiveness of PRF for dentin hypersensitivity. The absence of eligible evidence highlights a gap in the current literature and underscores the need for well-designed randomized controlled trials evaluating PRF using standardized outcome measures and adequate follow-up periods.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Quality of evidence and limitations
The risk of bias assessment indicated overall moderate methodological quality across the 25 included trials: 12 studies were rated as low risk, 9 as presenting some concerns, and 4 as high risk. Incomplete blinding particularly in laser-based trials was the most consistently identified source of potential bias, followed by inadequate allocation concealment and selective outcome reporting in a minority of studies. Funnel plot inspection did not reveal substantial publication bias, although minor asymmetry consistent with the selective publication of small positive trials cannot be entirely excluded.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Quality of evidence and limitations
Several limitations warrant acknowledgement. The high overall heterogeneity (I2 = 91%) reflects genuine diversity in treatment protocols, populations, and follow-up periods rather than a methodological shortcoming, and is appropriately addressed by the random-effects model. The evidence base for several subgroups including iontophoresis, arginine, and bioactive glass remains limited to two or three trials, constraining the precision of pooled estimates. Additionally, the shortest mandated follow-up of one month may be insufficient to detect late relapse for some modalities, and the absence of standardised challenge stimuli across trials complicates direct outcome comparison.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Quality of evidence and limitations
Formal sensitivity analyses and meta-regression were considered but were not performed because several intervention subgroups contained only two to three eligible studies, which would have produced unstable and potentially misleading estimates. In addition, important study-level covariates including baseline hypersensitivity severity, stimulation methods, laser parameters, and follow-up schedules were inconsistently reported across studies. The substantial clinical heterogeneity among interventions with fundamentally different mechanisms of action further limited the interpretability of meta-regression outputs. Consequently, pooled findings should be interpreted cautiously, and the observed heterogeneity should be regarded as an important limitation of the present review.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Quality of evidence and limitations
Although statistically significant reductions in hypersensitivity were observed, interpretation of clinical relevance requires consideration of the minimal clinically important difference (MCID). Owing to variability in outcome measures and reporting methods across studies, a uniform MCID could not be established. Therefore, the present findings should be interpreted in terms of both statistical significance and the potential for clinically meaningful improvement as perceived by patients.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Quality of evidence and limitations
A formal GRADE assessment was not undertaken because the included evidence comprised highly heterogeneous interventions with substantially different mechanisms of action, outcome assessment methods, and follow-up periods. Several intervention categories were represented by only a small number of studies, and outcome reporting lacked sufficient uniformity to permit reliable certainty-of-evidence judgments across all comparisons. Application of the GRADE framework under these circumstances could have generated overly broad or potentially misleading certainty estimates. Nevertheless, methodological quality was systematically evaluated using the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool, and study limitations were considered when interpreting the findings.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Quality of evidence and limitations
Follow-up durations varied considerably among included studies, ranging from immediate post-treatment assessments to six months or longer. The subgroup analysis according to follow-up duration (short-, medium-, and long-term) was not feasible because outcome reporting time points were inconsistent and several categories contained insufficient studies for meaningful pooled analysis. Consequently, conclusions regarding long-term effectiveness should be interpreted cautiously.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Clinical implications
The findings of this review provide a clear evidence-based rationale for the clinical adoption of advanced desensitizing modalities, particularly for patients who have not achieved adequate relief from conventional agents. Laser therapy and biomimetic calcium-based materials (nano-hydroxyapatite, bioactive glass, arginine) stand out as the most robustly supported options for sustained DH management. Clinicians should tailor treatment selection to individual patient profiles, accounting for symptom severity, prior treatment response, availability of equipment, patient preference, and cost considerations. A personalized, multimodal approach combining rapid neurological desensitisation with longer-term mineralising occlusion is likely to optimise clinical outcomes and patient satisfaction.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Discussion > Future directions
Future research should focus on well-designed, large-scale randomized controlled trials with standardized intervention protocols and longer follow-up periods to assess the durability of treatment outcomes. Direct head-to-head comparisons between advanced desensitizing modalities are needed to establish relative effectiveness. Future studies should incorporate uniform pain assessment methods, patient-reported outcome measures, and cost-effectiveness analyses. Investigating combination therapies and emerging biomimetic materials may provide insights into achieving both immediate and long-term relief from dentin hypersensitivity.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Conclusion
This systematic review and meta-analysis provide comprehensive, high-level evidence that advanced treatment modalities may provide greater efficacy in reducing dentin hypersensitivity than conventional or placebo comparators. Among evaluated interventions laser therapy appeared to demonstrate larger pooled effect sizes whereas biomimetic agents including nano-hydroxyapatite, bioactive glass, and arginine-calcium carbonate showed promising and clinically meaningful benefits. However, considerable heterogeneity, variations in treatment protocols, and limited long-term follow-up warrant cautious interpretation of these findings. Iontophoresis and CPP-ACP offered moderate efficacy, whereas resin- and varnish-based systems and oxalate formulations did not achieve statistically significant superiority over controls in the available evidence.

Efficacy of advanced treatment modalities of dentin hypersensitivity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Body > Conclusion
The consistency of benefit observed across trials of moderate-to-high methodological quality supports the clinical integration of advanced modalities as a component of evidence-based DH management. However, high overall heterogeneity, limited long-term follow-up in several subgroups, and variable intervention protocols underscore the continued need for large-scale, standardised RCTs. In clinical practice, a personalized multimodal approach combining therapies with complementary mechanisms of action is most likely to deliver optimal and sustained long-term outcomes for patients with dentin hypersensitivity.

Abstract > Purpose
To determine the prevalence of dental erosion due to carbonated beverage consumption among adolescents and the association between both variables through a systematic review and meta-analysis.

Abstract > Methods and Materials
This study was conducted in accordance with the preferred reporting items for systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA) guidelines for systematic reviews. A comprehensive literature search was performed in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, LILACS, and SciELO. Observational studies were included, and the PEO framework was used to identify dental erosion and non-erosion (outcome) and intake of carbonated beverages (exposure) in adolescents (population). The prevalence of dental erosion and odds ratio (OR) with 95% confidence interval (95%CI) to determine the risk of carbonated beverages were estimated with MedCalc V.23.0.2 and Review Manager (RevMan V.5.4.1) software, respectively. A P value < 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance.

Abstract > Results
A total of 24 studies met the eligibility criteria. The pooled sample included 21,541 adolescents, and the overall erosion prevalence was 37.6% (95%CI 26.3, 49.7%). Body
Dental erosion is defined as the irreversible loss of tooth structure caused by the chemical action of acids and/or chelating agents of nonbacterial origin. Structural loss due to erosion is a progressive, localised, asymptomatic, and irreversible process. The acids responsible for this process do not originate from intraoral bacterial activity but rather from extrinsic sources such as diet and the environment or from intrinsic sources such as gastric acid.50 Among the extrinsic factors, the consumption of beverages with low pH is particularly relevant, as it initially affects the enamel and can reach the dentin and pulp in more advanced stages, leading to hypersensitivity, severe pain, discomfort during mastication, fractures, and even tooth loss.14,52

Prevalence and Risk of Dental Erosion Linked to Carbonated Drinks in Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Body
The increasing consumption of soft drinks and other carbonated beverages is a growing trend among adolescents, largely because of changes in dietary habits and lifestyles. The erosive potential of these drinks is linked to both their added sugars and acids and to the presence of carbon dioxide, which produces carbonic acid, and other factors that contribute to their erosive potential are pH, titratable acidity, and their calcium and phosphate concentration. The method, frequency of intake and duration of exposure in the oral cavity are important. There is a big difference between drinking very quickly versus drinking and holding or drinking and swishing in the mouth, which significantly increases the ability of these compounds to induce acid wear on dental enamel through their action on hydroxyapatite crystals, ultimately weakening the enamel. This process may be attenuated by the buffering capacity and mineral content of saliva.41

Epidemiological studies involving adolescents have revealed prevalence rates of dental erosion exceeding 30%, with higher susceptibility in males and an increasing trend with age.29,43 Although erosion mainly affects enamel, preventive strategies based on solid evidence are essential. Given the increased frequency of soft drink consumption among adolescents, previous systematic reviews have revealed a positive association between the consumption of carbonated beverages and the development of dental erosion.7,27 However, the evidence remains inconsistent because some studies have failed to find statistically significant associations. For instance, in an analysis of NHANES 2003–2004 data, Samman et al44 reported no clear link between carbonated beverage consumption and erosive tooth. These discrepancies underscore the need for more robust evidence to clarify the relationship between carbonated beverages and dental erosion.

The quality of each included study was independently assessed by the two analysts to evaluate the possible risk of bias, and the Newcastle–Ottawa scale (NOS), as it provides a comprehensive framework for observational studies that focuses on three key domains: selection of study groups, comparability of groups, and outcome assessment to obtain a final score.35 The NOS is a star rating system that assigns a maximum of nine stars across three categories. Studies scoring three or four stars in selection, one or two stars in comparability, and two or three stars in outcome/exposure were considered of good quality. Studies with two stars in selection, one or two stars in comparability, and two or three stars in outcome/exposure were classified as fair quality. When the studies scored no stars or one star in selection, no stars in comparability, and no stars or one star in outcome/exposure, they were considered of poor quality. In accordance with this method, a study is considered to have a low risk of bias (8 or 9 stars), a fair risk (5–7 stars), or a high risk of bias (< 5 stars). In this review, 24 studies with scores ≥ 5 were included for analysis.

Prevalence and Risk of Dental Erosion Linked to Carbonated Drinks in Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Body > MATERIALS AND METHODS > Statistical Analysis and Meta-Analyses
A standardised data extraction form was used for qualitative analyses to record the study characteristics (author and publication year), study design, and main findings. The meta-analysis of prevalence was conducted using MedCalc software version 23.0.2 (MedCalc Software), applying the Freeman–Tukey’s arcsine square-root transformation and the DerSimonian and Laird random-effects model. Publication bias was assessed through Egger’s test.

Prevalence and Risk of Dental Erosion Linked to Carbonated Drinks in Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Body > MATERIALS AND METHODS > Statistical Analysis and Meta-Analyses
To evaluate the association between dental erosion and carbonated drink consumption, OR and 95% confidence interval (95%CI) were calculated. The meta-analysis of ORs was performed using Review Manager (RevMan) software version 5.4.1 (Cochrane Collaboration),42 using the Mantel–Haenszel (M–H) method with a DerSimonian and Laird random-effects model. The I2 statistic was used to assess heterogeneity among studies, with values of ≤ 25%, 25–50%, 50–75%, and > 75% indicating no, low, moderate, and significant heterogeneity, respectively.

Prevalence and Risk of Dental Erosion Linked to Carbonated Drinks in Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Body > MATERIALS AND METHODS > Statistical Analysis and Meta-Analyses
For both meta-analyses, forest plots were generated, and a P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Body > RESULTS > Selection, Characteristics, and Quality of the Studies
A total of 131 articles were identified; after removing duplicates, 101 records remained. Titles and abstracts were screened for the eligibility criteria, resulting in the selection of 24 full-text articles for qualitative analysis. Among the included articles, 21 were cross-sectional studies, 2 were case–control studies, and 1 was a cohort study. For the prevalence meta-analysis, cross-sectional studies were used. To assess the association between dental erosion and carbonated beverages, only five articles were considered for the quantitative analysis of risk factors because they could be combined (Fig 1).

An analysis of the included studies revealed that 19 (74%) reported a statistically significant association between carbonated beverages and dental erosion. In the remaining 26%, the association was either not statistically significant or was the result of exposure to a combination of various acidic beverages.
